We evaluate this Program-Solve interface on MedCalc-Bench Verified (1,100 cases, 55 calculators) against direct model arithmetic and a hand-written 22-calculator library, using Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen2.5-32B-AWQ, after auditing the benchmark's formulas against current clinical guidelines and flagging 16 of 55 with version, use or coefficient concerns. With formulas and gold variables supplied and both routes reading the whole note, handing off to the solver is not a reliable advantage at 7B (75.31% against 72.02%, a paired +3.29 points with a 95% calculator-cluster interval of [-3.49, 10.38]) but is one at 32B (90.53% against 83.47%, +7.05 [0.47, 14.60], clear of zero). The hand-written library is exact on its 440 supported cases but abstains elsewhere (40.0% overall). Adding an executor thus helps some open-weight models more than others even under matched formula, variable and note access, and is not a substitute for verified formulas or reliable variable extraction either way.

AI.tldr: Program-Solve uses a restricted Python executor to run case-specific solver code; benefits depend on model size; not a universal substitute for verified clinical formulas.
AI.motivation: Improve numeric reliability of clinical calculators by separating arithmetic from model reasoning; reduce numerical errors in LLM outputs; evaluate whether a solver-executor approach boosts accuracy relative to direct model arithmetic and hand-coded libraries.
AI.method: Evaluate on MedCalc-Bench Verified (1,100 cases, 55 calculators) comparing direct model arithmetic vs. a programmatic solver that emits Python run by a restricted executor; tested with Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen2.5-32B-AWQ; audit formulas for version/coefficient concerns; measured accuracy and computed 95% calculator-cluster intervals.
AI.result: For 7B: 75.31% accuracy with executor vs 72.02% with direct arithmetic (delta +3.29, 95% CI [-3.49, 10.38]); not a reliable advantage. For 32B: 90.53% vs 83.47% (delta +7.05, 95% CI [0.47, 14.60]); significant advantage. Hand-written library is exact on 440 cases but abstains on the rest (40% overall). The executor helps some open-weight models more than others and is not a substitute for verified formulas or reliable variable extraction.
AI.conclusion: Executor-based solving yields model-size dependent benefits; does not universally outperform direct arithmetic or substitute for validated formulas. Larger models gain more, but careful formula validation and reliable variable extraction remain essential.

title: ObstaDiff: Generalizable Diffusion Policy Learning via Obstacle-aware Representations
comment: Accepted to the 10th Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL 2026), Austin, TX, USA. 16 pages, 5 figures
summary: Imitation learning has achieved impressive results in robotic manipulation, yet most existing approaches assume clean backgrounds and lack explicit mechanisms for obstacle-aware motion generation. Extending such policies to cluttered, real-world scenes with unstructured obstacles remains a key generalization challenge. We present ObstaDiff, a decomposed diffusion-policy framework with a lightweight obstacle-aware visual encoder. ObstaDiff extracts a structured target-obstacle-background representation, enabling the downstream alignment policy to generate end-effector trajectories toward a target-centered bottleneck pose while reasoning about surrounding obstacles. We evaluate ObstaDiff on 61 real-robot greenhouse trials per method (366 executions in total). ObstaDiff achieves 75.41% average task success and 8.20% average obstacle collision rate, outperforming representative imitation-learning baselines and improving generalization in cluttered agricultural scenes.

AI.tldr: ObstaDiff leverages a decomposed diffusion-policy with an obstacle-aware visual encoder to enable obstacle-aware manipulation in cluttered scenes, showing improved success and reduced collisions in greenhouse tasks.
AI.motivation: Imitation learning for robotic manipulation often fails to generalize to cluttered, real-world environments with unstructured obstacles; there is a need for explicit obstacle-aware motion generation.
AI.method: ObstaDiff uses a lightweight obstacle-aware visual encoder to extract a structured target–obstacle–background representation and couples it with a decomposed diffusion-policy that guides the end-effector to a target-centered bottleneck pose while reasoning about obstacles.
AI.result: Evaluated on 61 real-robot greenhouse trials per method (366 executions in total), ObstaDiff achieves 75.41% average task success and 8.20% average obstacle collision rate, outperforming representative imitation-learning baselines and improving generalization in cluttered agricultural scenes.
AI.conclusion: ObstaDiff demonstrates effective obstacle-aware diffusion-based manipulation in cluttered real-world environments, offering improved success and reduced collisions and indicating strong generalization for unstructured settings such as greenhouses.

title: The Truth Was Never Gone: Perfect Aliasing in Compliant-Context Truth Probes
comment: 36 pages, 15 figures. Code and aggregate results: https://github.com/dylanjayabahu/perfect-aliasing
summary: A truth probe fitted where truthful reporting and a task's prescribed action coincide cannot distinguish those targets from its fitting labels alone. We call this failure of semantic identification perfect aliasing. In a controlled binary reporting game, truth and prescribed-action probes fitted on compliant contexts solve the same optimization. On rival contexts their labels are complements, forcing their AUROCs to sum to one; this identity holds across 751 cell-layer pairs to floating-point precision. We separate prescribed output symbols from semantic action using randomized codebooks, then separate truth from prescribed action by fitting on mixed compliant and rival contexts. For a reward-trained Gemma-2-9B policy that answers falsely on all evaluated rival trials, the conventional probe scores $0.006 \pm 0.005$ AUROC across three training seeds, while mixed-fit probes score $1.000$ on the same held-out activations. Mixed fitting uses more training examples and access to labelled rival contexts, so this comparison establishes linear recoverability rather than isolating the benefit of decorrelation. We also show that two compliant-fit probes, both perfect in-distribution, score $0.080$ and $0.986$ on the same rival activations. The findings concern what a probe measures: they do not establish preserved functional belief, causal use of the recovered direction, or a deployable deception detector. Code and aggregate results accompany the paper.

AI.tldr: Probes for truthfulness vs. prescribed action exhibit perfect aliasing in rival contexts; mixing compliant and rival contexts with codebooks enables separating signals, yielding a perfect AUROC on held activations, revealing linear recoverability but not causal beliefs or deployable deception detection.
AI.motivation: Investigate what standard probes actually measure about truthfulness and task adherence, and whether semantic-identification of intent is possible; assess identifiability vs. aliasing in probe measurements.
AI.method: Controlled binary reporting game with compliant and rival contexts; trains truth and prescribed-action probes; uses randomized codebooks to decorrelate outputs; fits probes on mixed compliant/rival data; compares against conventional probes; evaluates on a reward-trained Gemma-2-9B policy across 751 cell-layer pairs.
AI.result: Across rival contexts truth and prescribed-action probes yield complementary labels with AUROC summing to 1.0; mixed-fit probes achieve AUROC of 1.000 on held-out activations, while conventional probes score ~0.006; two compliant-fit probes score ~0.080 and ~0.986 on rival activations; results indicate linear recoverability and decorrelation effects, but do not establish preserved functional belief, causal use, or a deployable deception detector.
AI.conclusion: Probes primarily reveal linear, decorrelated signals rather than causal beliefs; the results caution against interpreting probe success as evidence of secret beliefs or detector of deception; code and aggregate results accompany the paper.

title: How Much Velocity Does Off-Ball Space Value Need? A Broadcast-Viewport Benchmark
comment: 15 pages, 3 figures, 4 tables. Code, logs and data: https://github.com/nowayfootball/offscreen-impute (velocity/)
summary: Velocity-aware pitch control is standard, but under a broadcast viewport half the players are off screen and on-screen velocities come from a drifting calibration. We ask at which layer of broadcast off-ball analysis velocity changes the answer. Inheriting our off-screen imputation protocol (three Metrica matches, 44 m viewport, block-bootstrap CIs), we score four velocity regimes -- none, viewport-legal observed, true-for-visible, true-for-all -- against a velocity-aware ground truth at three layers: imputation, the control surface, and team verdicts. Velocity is nearly useless for imputation (-0.2 pp against a 12--14 pp velocity-free surface MAE), first-order for the surface (-1.5 to -1.8 pp, 11--15% of that MAE), and ten times smaller for verdicts (-0.12 to -0.19 pp). The velocity that matters is the visible channel: perfect occluded-player velocity adds 2--6% of the visible gain, and no last-seen decay policy we tested exceeds that. Omitting velocity blurs the surface (per-frame |e| 2.2--2.6 pp) with small time-averaged bias (per cell <=0.4 pp), whereas imputation error is a structured bias against the defending team's deep zone (5--9 pp). At a fixed velocity window, a noise ladder of eleven jitter settings, including sigma_v-matched pairs, is ordered to first order by one velocity-noise axis sigma_v with break-even ~1 m/s; eleven SoccerNet-GSR clips from one match through our pipeline measure sigma_v=1.65 m/s yet recover 24--36% of the benefit: 43% of the variance is frame-common, which the surface tolerates, and the residual is heavy-tailed and clustered, which Gaussian controls matched on component RMS do not reproduce (+0.03 vs. +0.36). The share of velocity-free error that velocity removes grows with viewport width (7% at 36 m, 21% at 60 m): fix imputation on tight shots, velocity on wide ones. Code and logs are released.

AI.tldr: Velocity-aware analysis yields modest gains: useful mainly for visible channels; imputation dominates errors in off-screen regions; best practice is to fix imputation on tight shots and apply velocity on wide shots; the visible channel is the key source of velocity information.
AI.motivation: Evaluate at which broadcast off-ball analysis layer velocity information meaningfully improves accuracy, across imputation, the control surface, and team verdicts, using an off-screen imputation protocol and velocity regimes.
AI.method: Three Metrica matches with a 44 m viewport; four velocity regimes (none, viewport-legal observed, true-for-visible, true-for-all); evaluation against a velocity-aware ground truth across three layers (imputation, surface, verdicts); block-bootstrap CIs; noise ladder with eleven jitter settings; SoccerNet-GSR clips; metrics include MAE, percent-of-variance, per-frame error, and structured bias analyses.
AI.result: Velocity has minimal impact on imputation (-0.2 percentage points vs a large velocity-free MAE); first-order impact on the control surface (-1.5 to -1.8 pp, 11–15% of MAE); much smaller impact on verdicts (-0.12 to -0.19 pp). The key informative velocity is from the visible channel; perfect occluded-velocity adds 2–6% of the visible gain; no last-seen decay policy beats that. Omitting velocity increases surface error (per-frame |e| 2.2–2.6 pp) but has small time-averaged bias; imputation error shows structured bias toward defending deep zones (5–9 pp). A noise axis sigma_v governs the benefit; break-even ~1 m/s; eleven clips yield 24–36% of the velocity benefit recovered; 43% of variance is frame-common and tolerated by the surface; residual is heavy-tailed and not well captured by Gaussian controls. Velocity-free error reduction grows with viewport width (7% at 36 m, 21% at 60 m). Conclusion: prioritize velocity on wide shots and fix imputation on tight shots; code and logs released.
AI.conclusion: The critical source of velocity information is the visible channel; velocity improves surface performance modestly and verdicts only slightly; for tight shots fix imputation; for wide shots apply velocity; overall, velocity benefits are context-dependent and most pronounced when the viewport includes wide shots.

title: Studying Without a Syllabus: Task-Agnostic Environment Preprocessing
summary: Before an LLM agent tackles tasks in a new environment, it can inspect available corpora and tools and construct reusable resources such as indices, scripts, or procedural guidance. Most automated adaptation methods, however, rely on task examples, trajectories, or evaluation feedback to decide what to build. Existing task-agnostic approaches avoid this supervision but commit in advance to a preparation strategy for a particular type of environment. We study a more open-ended setting: can an agent study an unfamiliar environment without a syllabus, i.e. before test time and without knowledge of the downstream task distribution, and choose how to prepare it? We formalize task-agnostic environment preprocessing, in which a studying system explores an environment under a budget and produces artifacts for a frozen solver. We compare unaided and archive-equipped meta-agents with fixed synthetic-practice and corpus-processing methods across six heterogeneous benchmarks. A meta-agent variant achieves the highest Avg@3 reward on five benchmarks, while fixed corpus processing remains best on the largest corpus benchmark. Larger study budgets do not reliably improve downstream reward. Nevertheless, studied artifacts reduce the test-time sampling needed to reach a given score, demonstrating how reusable preparation can shift computation from repeated test-time attempts to a pre-task study phase.

AI.tldr: A study of task-agnostic environment preprocessing for LLM agents. It investigates how an agent can study an unfamiliar environment without a syllabus or downstream task distribution, and generate reusable artifacts for a frozen solver. Across six benchmarks, a meta-agent variant often achieves the best Avg@3, while fixed corpus processing shines on the largest corpus. Bigger study budgets do not reliably improve downstream reward, but the artifacts reduce the test-time sampling needed to reach target performance, showing a pre-task study phase can shift computation from test-time to preparation.
AI.motivation: To enable robust, task-agnostic preparation for unseen environments by moving the design of preparation actions before test time, without requiring task-specific supervision or knowledge of downstream distributions.
AI.method: Formalize task-agnostic environment preprocessing where a studying system explores an environment under a budget and produces artifacts for a frozen solver. Compare unaided and archive-equipped meta-agents against fixed synthetic-practice and corpus-processing baselines across six heterogeneous benchmarks.
AI.result: A meta-agent variant achieves the highest Avg@3 reward on five benchmarks; fixed corpus processing is best on the largest corpus benchmark. Increasing study budgets does not reliably improve downstream reward. Learned artifacts reduce the amount of test-time sampling needed to reach a given score.
AI.conclusion: Reusable artifacts from pre-task study can shift computation from repeated test-time attempts to a pre-task preparation phase, offering performance gains and sample-efficiency in downstream tasks, though benefits of larger budgets are environment- and method-dependent.

title: Testing Between the Test Cases: Proving End-to-End Steering in Conditions You Never Drove
summary: AI-based automated vehicle testing is challenging because a model that passes every test condition can still fail in the real world. Formal verification offers a way to directly address this gap. On a simulated highway and an arterial road we trained two small end-to-end steering networks each in CARLA, one on clear conditions alone and one on clear, fog, night and low sun. All four models were driven against a 2.19 ft lane-departure budget. Without driving again, we used bound propagation, a formal method that reads the trained weights, to compute how far steering can drift at every disturbance strength between two captured images. One calculation covers more than a campaign could drive: on the arterial it spans 133 poses, where ten intensities each would be 10^133 combinations, in minutes on one GPU. Not only did formal verification find conditions that broke the clear-trained policy without simulation testing, it provided some preliminary evidence for potential failures between the test cases. Our overall conclusion is that formal verification is a viable complement to simulation, and could be adopted as a part of verification and validation for automated driving.

AI.tldr: Formal verification via bound propagation detects steering policy vulnerabilities beyond simulation, showing it can complement simulation in automated driving verification.
AI.motivation: Address the gap where a model passes test scenarios but fails in real-world driving; provide proactive, formal guarantees about model behavior under input perturbations.
AI.method: Two small end-to-end steering networks were trained in CARLA (one on clear conditions; one on clear+fog/night/low sun). They were tested with a 2.19 ft lane-departure budget. Bound propagation reads the trained weights to bound steering drift for disturbances between two captured images; a single calculation spans many poses (e.g., 133) and disturbances, aggregating exponentially many scenarios cheaply (minutes on one GPU).
AI.result: Formal verification identified conditions that broke the clear-trained policy without additional simulation and offered preliminary evidence for potential failures between test cases.
AI.conclusion: Formal verification is a viable complement to simulation and could be adopted as part of the verification and validation process for automated driving.

title: Adaptive Margin Ordinal Loss: Penalizing Center-Class Hedging in Ordinal Classification
summary: Standard cross-entropy loss causes neural networks trained on ordinal classification tasks to hedge predictions toward center classes, a failure mode we term \emph{center-class hedging}. This occurs because predicting the middle class minimizes expected symmetric loss, making it the path of least resistance regardless of the true label. Existing ordinal losses address related problems such as large-error penalization and rank consistency, but none directly suppresses center-class hedging as a function of where the true label lies relative to the ordinal center. We propose the Adaptive Margin Ordinal Loss (AMOL), a multiplicative weight applied to per-class loss terms of the form $m(k,y) = 1 + α\cdot (1 - |k-c|/c) \cdot (|y-c|/c)$, where $c$ is the center class, $k$ is the candidate class, and $y$ is the true label. The weight encodes a joint condition: it is large only when the candidate class is near center and the true label is far from center, collapsing to standard behavior otherwise. We further introduce the Center-Hedging Rate (CHR) as a diagnostic metric that directly quantifies this failure mode. Across four ordinal classification benchmarks and five random seeds, AMOL achieves the best or tied-best Quadratic Weighted Kappa (QWK) on all four datasets compared to cross-entropy, OLL, and SORD baselines. An asymmetric variant (AMOL-asym) eliminates center-class hedging entirely on the Abalone dataset ($\text{CHR} = 0.000 \pm 0.000$ across all five seeds, $n \approx 266$ extreme-class test samples per run), compared to $0.074 \pm 0.005$ for standard cross-entropy.

AI.tldr: Adaptive Margin Ordinal Loss (AMOL) suppresses center-class hedging in ordinal classification via a multiplicative per-class weight dependent on center c, with CHR diagnostic; shows strong QWK and zero CHR asym on Abalone with AMOL-asym.
AI.motivation: Center-class hedging arises when standard cross-entropy biases predictions toward middle classes in ordinal tasks. Existing ordinal losses address related issues but do not directly penalize center bias conditioned on proximity to the ordinal center. A loss that adaptively penalizes near-center predictions when the true label is farther from center is needed.
AI.method: Introduce AMOL: a multiplicative weight m(k,y) = 1 + α*(1 - |k-c|/c) * (|y-c|/c) applied to per-class loss terms; c is the center class, k candidate class, y true label. The weight increases for near-center predictions when the true label is far from center. Also propose AMOL-asym which further reduces center hedging. Introduce Center-Hedging Rate (CHR) as a diagnostic metric. Evaluated on four ordinal benchmarks with five seeds; compared against cross-entropy, OLL, and SORD; primary metric is Quadratic Weighted Kappa (QWK).
AI.result: AMOL achieves the best or tied-best QWK on all four datasets across four baselines. AMOL-asym eliminates center-class hedging (CHR = 0.000 ± 0.000 across five seeds on Abalone, n ≈ 266 extreme-class test samples per run), while CE shows CHR ≈ 0.074 ± 0.005.
AI.conclusion: AMOL effectively mitigates center-class hedging in ordinal classification; the AMOL-asym variant can fully remove the bias in at least one dataset. CHR proves to be a useful diagnostic for this failure mode, and AMOL yields strong performance gains on standard ordinal benchmarks.

title: TrajFusionNet+: Transformer-Based Prediction of Pedestrian Crossing Intention via Fusion of Trajectory Representations and Scene Graphs
comment: This work has been submitted to Signal, Image and Video Processing for possible publication
summary: The pedestrian crossing intention task involves predicting whether pedestrians are likely to cross the road from the point of view of an autonomous vehicle. We introduce TrajFusionNet+, a novel transformer-based model for pedestrian crossing intention prediction. TrajFusionNet+ combines sequential and visual representations of pedestrian trajectory with a graph-based representation of the scene context in order to predict pedestrian crossing intention. The proposed architecture builds upon our previous model, TrajFusionNet, and comprises three branches: a Sequence Attention Module (SAM), which processes a sequential representation of past and predicted pedestrian trajectories; a Visual Attention Module (VAM), which utilizes a visual representation of the pedestrian trajectories by overlaying observed and predicted bounding boxes onto scene images; and a Graph Attention Module (GAM), which extracts pedestrian-centric graphs from segmented scene images and captures the relational dependencies between pedestrians and traffic elements. TrajFusionNet+ achieves improved state-of-the-art performance on the two most widely used pedestrian crossing intention datasets, PIE and JAAD. Furthermore, we introduce a new evaluation protocol in which models are trained jointly on the PIE and JAAD datasets but evaluated separately on each. Under this setting, TrajFusionNet+ demonstrates superior generalization compared to existing approaches.

AI.tldr: TrajFusionNet+ is a transformer-based tri-branch model that fuses sequential trajectory, visual scene overlays, and scene-graph relations to predict pedestrian crossing intentions; it achieves state-of-the-art on PIE and JAAD and generalizes well under a joint training protocol with separate evaluation.
AI.motivation: Accurate pedestrian crossing intention prediction is critical for safe autonomous driving and requires leveraging multiple information sources (past/predicted trajectories, scene visuals, and relational scene context) beyond single-modality cues; previous work (TrajFusionNet) lacked unified multi-branch fusion and cross-dataset generalization.
AI.method: Three-branch architecture: SAM processes sequential past and predicted trajectories; VAM overlays observed/predicted bounding boxes on scene images to extract visual features; GAM constructs pedestrian-centric graphs from segmented scene images to capture relations to traffic elements; transformer-based fusion combines the branches; builds on TrajFusionNet.
AI.result: State-of-the-art performance on PIE and JAAD; new joint-training evaluation protocol on PIE+JAAD with separate evaluation shows TrajFusionNet+ better generalization than prior approaches.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates effective multi-source fusion for pedestrian crossing prediction with improved generalization; the joint training evaluation protocol offers a robust benchmark; suggests potential for deployment in autonomous driving systems.

title: When Validation Stops Learning: Auditing Update Admission for Continual Embodied Agents
summary: Independent evaluation can reject harmful policy updates yet also prevent useful continual learning. We argue that update admission must be assessed through both error control and retained learning opportunities at a stated interaction budget. We identify a concrete failure: a range-based confidence gate cannot certify unchanged old-task behavior within otherwise substantial budgets. A standard paired-binomial construction reduces this burden when outcome disagreements are rare. We also specify certified historical-reference promotion and a round-level missed-opportunity metric. In a constructed one-step pushing diagnostic with 32 seeds, fresh paired checks admit 31.6% of a common update stream at 2,000 episodes per stage, versus zero for the range-based gate; unconditional replay nevertheless learns better in closed-loop runs. A separate learned-dynamics stress test distinguishes model bias from feedback-selection error. The contribution is an admission-audit protocol with analytical and synthetic evidence; physical-robot and VLA validation remain open.

AI.tldr: An admission-audit protocol for evaluating update admission that balances error control with retained learning opportunities, using a paired-binomial approach to overcome range-based gate failures; introduces metrics like certified historical-reference promotion and round-level missed opportunities; empirical results show limited admission under a one-step pushing diagnostic (31.6% vs 0%) with 32 seeds, while unconditional replay can learn better; validation via analytical and synthetic evidence; physical-robot and VLA validation remain open.
AI.motivation: Independent evaluation can reject harmful updates but may hinder useful continual learning; a practical approach is needed to assess updates within a stated interaction budget by accounting both for error control and retained learning opportunities.
AI.method: Propose an admission-audit protocol with analytical and synthetic evaluation; implement a paired-binomial construction to certify updates when disagreement is rare; define certified historical-reference promotion and a round-level missed-opportunity metric; conduct a one-step pushing diagnostic across 32 seeds; compare a range-based confidence gate to the paired-binomial admission checks; include a learned-dynamics stress test to separate model bias from feedback-selection error.
AI.result: Demonstrates a concrete failure of range-based gates to certify unchanged old-task behavior under substantial budgets; the paired-binomial approach reduces admission burden when disagreements are rare, admitting 31.6% of a typical update stream at 2,000 episodes per stage in the diagnostic, whereas the range-based gate admits zero; unconditional replay performs better in closed-loop; separate stress tests distinguish bias from feedback-selection error; evidence is analytical and synthetic, with open validation for physical-robot and VLA.
AI.conclusion: The contribution is an admission-audit protocol supported by analytical and synthetic evidence; open questions remain for physical-robot and VLA validation.

title: LTLDiff: Finite Linear Temporal Logic-Guided Data Generation and Diffusion Policies for Multi-agent Robotic Manipulation
summary: Multi-agent robotic manipulation tasks require coordination among agents to satisfy task-level temporal, logical, and safety constraints. Recently, diffusion policies have been used to perform the task. However, they still suffer from desynchronization, incorrect action ordering, and coordination failures in tasks that require simultaneous or sequential multi-agent interaction. Therefore, LTLDiff is proposed as a framework that combines Finite Linear Temporal Logic (LTLf) specification learning for both the generation of demonstrations and learning via diffusion policies. Each task has a specific LTLf formula that is learned from a set of natural language instructions using a large-scale language model. To enable a fixed-dimensional vector embedding of the learned specification from the language model, LTLf uses an abstract syntax tree representation scheme. This embedding of logic serves as a condition for (i) logic-guided data collection and (ii) diffusion-based policy training, encouraging trajectories that are consistent with the desired ordering and coordination requirements. Experiments on multi-agent LTLDiff manipulation tasks demonstrate improved task success rates compared to the baseline. Together, these contributions demonstrate the effectiveness of LTLDiff for coordinated multi-agent manipulation.

AI.tldr: LTLDiff learns LTLf task specifications from natural language instructions via a large language model, encodes them with an abstract syntax tree for a fixed-dimensional embedding, and conditions diffusion-based policies and data collection to enforce temporal/logical constraints in multi-agent manipulation, improving task success over baselines.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent manipulation requires satisfying task-level temporal, logical, and safety constraints. Diffusion policies alone suffer from desynchronization and poor action ordering when coordinating multiple agents. There is a need to integrate structured, learnable specifications into policy training to enforce coordination.
AI.method: 1) Learn per-task LTLf formulas from natural language instructions using a large-language model. 2) Represent LTLf via an abstract syntax tree and obtain a fixed-dimensional embedding. 3) Use the LTLf embedding as a condition for logic-guided data collection and for diffusion-policy training. 4) Train diffusion policies to generate trajectories consistent with the learned LTLf constraints. 5) Evaluate on multi-agent LTLDiff manipulation tasks.
AI.result: Experiments show improved task success rates of LTLDiff over baseline diffusion-policy approaches in multi-agent manipulation tasks.
AI.conclusion: Combining LTLf specification learning with diffusion-policy training effectively coordinates multi-agent manipulation by enforcing temporal and ordering constraints through logic-guided data collection and policy conditioning.

title: A Bellman Optimality Equation for Plasticity
summary: In continual reinforcement learning, carefully managing the stability-plasticity tradeoff remains a core challenge. Recent work by Abel et al. (2025) formalized this dilemma by defining plasticity as the generalized directed information from an agent's observations to its actions, and empowerment as the generalized directed information from its actions to its observations. This formulation successfully reframes the traditional stability-plasticity tradeoff as an empowerment-plasticity tradeoff. However, while extensive literature exists on optimizing for empowerment, there is currently no research addressing the optimization of plasticity under this new definition. This paper presents preliminary work toward optimizing plasticity within Markov decision processes. We show that there exists a Bellman optimality equation for optimizing plasticity similar to previous work for empowerment.

AI.tldr: Introduces a directed-information framing of stability-plasticity in continual RL, reframes to empowerment-plasticity, and proves a Bellman optimality equation for plasticity optimization in MDPs; purely theoretical, preliminarily establishing foundations with no empirical results yet.
AI.motivation: Address the enduring stability-plasticity tradeoff in continual reinforcement learning by providing a formal, optimizable target for plasticity under a new information-theoretic definition; extend the empowerment optimization literature to plasticity.
AI.method: Define plasticity as generalized directed information from observations to actions; show an analogue of Bellman optimality for plasticity in Markov decision processes, paralleling prior work on empowerment optimization; present foundational theoretical results (no empirical validation reported).
AI.result: Demonstrates existence of a Bellman optimality equation for optimizing plasticity in MDPs, establishing a theoretical basis for future algorithms.
AI.conclusion: Preliminary theoretical contribution establishing a formal optimization framework for plasticity; sets the stage for algorithmic development and empirical evaluation aimed at balancing empowerment-plasticity in continual RL.

title: Overpainting: Localized Context-aware Diffusion Image Editing
summary:
We present "overpainting", an image editing operation which offers both control over the location of the edit and awareness of the previous content in that location. The overpainted area is given by a trimap, where white-annotated pixels must be edited, gray-annotated pixels may be edited, and black-annotated pixels must not be edited. This enables both precise and loose control, depending on user intent.
  We implement overpainting by adapting a pretrained image editing diffusion model using a combination of joint attention and low-rank adaption across input images with attention-dropout to balance the information flow between noise, source and mask images. We present a novel, automated, training data generation pipeline that (1) generates a set of candidate image pairs leveraging existing language-based editing models, (2) carefully curates those pairs, and (3) extracts a trimap from each usable pair. We demonstrate the versatility of our overpainting model on a wide range of editing tasks.

AI.tldr: Introduces overpainting, a trimap-guided image editing operator using a diffusion model; enables precise region edits with awareness of prior content, via joint attention and low-rank adaptation with attention-dropout; includes an automated data-generation pipeline and shows versatility across editing tasks.
AI.motivation: Need for precise, region-aware image edits with clear control over where edits occur, while preserving or acknowledging surrounding content. Existing diffusion-editing approaches lack explicit spatial control and may degrade content fidelity; the paper proposes a controllable, content-aware editing paradigm and automated data synthesis.
AI.method: Repurposes a pretrained diffusion editor by integrating joint attention and low-rank adaptation (LoRA) across input images, with attention-dropout to balance information flow among noise, source, and mask. The edit region is defined by a trimap (white = must edit, gray = may edit, black = must not edit). An automated data pipeline creates training pairs by leveraging language-based editing models, curates them, and extracts trimaps from usable pairs.
AI.result: Demonstrates the model’s versatility across a broad set of editing tasks, achieving controllable edits confined to specified regions while maintaining awareness of the existing content.
AI.conclusion: Proposes overpainting as a controllable, content-aware image-editing operator, supported by a data-generation pipeline and an adaptation strategy for diffusion models, enabling precise, region-specific edits with flexible control.

title: Decoupling Readiness from Release for Tail-Aware Scheduling of Agentic LLM Workflows
summary: Agentic LLM workflows consist of sequences of model turns interleaved with tool interactions, so their end-to-end completion time depends not only on inference speed but also on when ready turns are released. Most runtimes release each turn immediately upon readiness. Under contention, this eager release policy can accumulate released but unfinished work; once submitted, those turns can no longer be reordered by the workflow-level policy, increasing tail latency. We present a tail-risk-aware turn release scheduling method that jointly decides which ready turn to release next and how much released but unfinished work to maintain. The method uses a mean--Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) objective to capture the evolving tail risk of unfinished workflows, incorporates online estimates of turn work when prioritizing ready turns, and adapts the released work budget to observed queue pressure. We evaluate the method using real agent execution traces from software engineering tasks across multiple LLMs and workflow arrival rates. The method performs comparably to eager release under light load and substantially reduces the P95 of workflow flow time under contention, achieving up to a \(3.50\times\) speedup.

AI.tldr: A tail-risk-aware turn release policy for agentic LLM workflows reduces tail latency under contention by jointly selecting the next ready turn to release and how much released but unfinished work to keep, using a mean-CVaR objective and online workload estimates; it matches eager release under light load and yields large P95 reductions (up to 3.5x) under contention.
AI.motivation: Eagerly releasing ready turns in agentic LLM workflows can cause many unfinished, released turns that cannot be reordered, inflating tail latency under contention. A strategy is needed to manage release timing and the amount of in-flight work to control tail risk.
AI.method: Proposes a tail-risk-aware turn release scheduling method that (1) jointly decides which ready turn to release next and how much unfinished work to maintain, (2) optimizes a mean-CVaR objective to capture tail-risk of unfinished workflows, (3) uses online estimates of turn work for prioritization, and (4) adapts the released-work budget based on observed queue pressure. Evaluation uses real agent-execution traces across multiple LLMs and workflow arrival rates.
AI.result: Under light load, performance is comparable to eager release. Under contention, P95 flow time is substantially reduced, with up to a 3.50× speedup in some settings.
AI.conclusion: Tail-risk-aware release scheduling effectively mitigates tail latency in agentic LLM workflows by controlling release decisions and in-flight work, adapting to queue pressure and workload, and delivering significant gains under contention.

title: Gait-Dependent Effects on Quadruped Locomotion for Load-Carrying using Passive Mechanism
summary: Passive mechanical interfaces offer a lightweight alternative to actuated manipulators for quadruped payload carrying, but their impedance directly couples the payload dynamics with the locomotion pattern. This paper analyzes how passive-arm stiffness-damping selection affects payload-carrying locomotion under different gait and payload conditions. We compare damped and underdamped passive-arm impedance configurations in simulation during flat-ground locomotion. For crawl gaits, where the support polygon remains well defined, the results show that underdamped impedance increases passive-joint oscillations and can reduce the ZMP margin with respect to the support polygon. Trot is retained as a dynamic excitation case for the passive arm, but it is not used for direct ZMP-margin stability comparison. The results are summarized in gait-payload-stiffness-damping maps, where ZMP-margin reduction is evaluated for crawl gaits and trot is retained only as a passive-arm excitation case.

AI.tldr: Underdamped vs damped passive-arm impedance in quadruped payload transport: simulation shows underdamped increases joint oscillations and can reduce ZMP margin during crawl gaits; results summarized in gait-payload-stiffness-damping maps; trot used as excitation but not for direct ZMP comparison.
AI.motivation: Understand how passive-arm impedance choices affect payload-carrying stability and locomotion coupling, to inform design of passive interfaces in quadrupeds.
AI.method: Simulation study of a quadruped with a passive arm, comparing damped and underdamped impedance across gait types (crawl, trot), varying payload and stiffness/damping; analyze ZMP margin relative to the support polygon; produce gait-payload-stiffness-damping maps.
AI.result: Underdamped impedance increases passive-joint oscillations and can reduce ZMP margin during crawl gaits; trot included as a dynamic excitation case; ZMP-margin changes summarized in maps.
AI.conclusion: Impedance selection materially affects stability in payload-carrying locomotion; underdamped passive arms may degrade ZMP margin in crawl gaits; the study provides maps to guide impedance tuning, with future work needed for broader gaits, other terrains, and experimental validation.

title: Counterfactual Marginalisation: Framework for Evaluating Robustness to Nuisance Variables
summary: Machine learning models can achieve strong test performance while relying on demographic or acquisition-related shortcuts. We propose counterfactual (CF) marginalisation as a test-time evaluation procedure for assessing robustness of classification models to such variables. Given a CF image generator, we intervene on nuisance parent variables such as age or sex, generate CF versions of each test image, and average predictions over a target intervention distribution. This produces intervention-aware predictions that marginalise demographic effects while preserving patient-specific latent information. We use these predictions to define metrics for CF risk, calibration, stability and worst-case sensitivity. We demonstrate this framework's utility for quantitative robustness evaluation.

AI.tldr: Counterfactual marginalisation for test-time robustness: intervene on nuisance variables (age/sex) via a CF image generator, average predictions over a target distribution to obtain intervention-aware predictions that marginalise demographic effects; define CF risk, calibration, stability, and worst-case sensitivity metrics; demonstrated for quantitative robustness evaluation.
AI.motivation: Many ML models rely on demographic or acquisition-related shortcuts; need a test-time procedure to assess robustness to nuisance variables and ensure predictions rely on patient-specific information.
AI.method: Given a counterfactual image generator, intervene on nuisance parent variables (e.g., age, sex), create counterfactual test images, average predictions over a specified intervention distribution, yielding intervention-aware predictions that remove demographic effects while preserving patient latent content.
AI.result: Introduces metrics for CF risk, calibration, stability, and worst-case sensitivity; demonstrates the framework's utility for quantitative robustness evaluation.
AI.conclusion: CF marginalisation is a practical, model-agnostic approach to evaluate and quantify robustness to demographic shortcuts at test time, enabling more reliable deployment.

title: BodyCam-VQA: Enhanced Body-Worn Camera Video Captioning via Multimodal Reasoning and Probe Question Generation
summary: Police body-worn camera (BWC) footage has emerged as a critical aspect of law enforcement that ensures legal transparency, officer accountability, and the protection of civil rights. However, effectively processing this data remains a significant challenge due to its multimodal video format. BWC videos, in many cases, comprise chaotic scenes with low visual quality, rapid movement/interactions, and high-noise audio that make visual understanding a challenge for even SOTA multimodal models. Current Vision-Language Models (VLMs) frequently overlook critical forensic details, such as the presence of valuable evidence or the latent nuances of suspect-officer interactions, which are vital for fair legal outcomes and civilian/officer safety. To address these limitations, we propose an Adaptive Visual Question Answering (VQA) framework engineered for high-stakes law enforcement. Our framework employs a structured reasoning approach to extract fine-grained visual evidence that traditional captioning systems fail to capture. We experiment with multiple question generation models, including foundation models and fine-tuned open-weight models, to observe performance variation among question generation model implementations. Our results demonstrate that this VQA-driven architecture provides a more reliable, objective, and detailed record of enforcement events, ultimately serving as a powerful tool to protect both law enforcement officers and the public through AI-assisted forensic clarity.

AI.tldr: An Adaptive VQA framework for police body-worn camera footage that uses structured reasoning and multiple question-generation models to extract fine-grained forensic evidence, aiming for improved reliability and objectivity over captioning.
AI.motivation: BWC video is multimodal and often low-quality; traditional vision-language models can miss critical forensic details, potentially affecting legal outcomes. There is a need for a reliable, objective record of enforcement events.
AI.method: Propose an Adaptive VQA architecture with structured reasoning to extract fine-grained evidence. Evaluate multiple question-generation models, including foundation models and fine-tuned open-weight models, to assess performance variation across implementations.
AI.result: The VQA-driven approach yields more reliable, objective, and detailed records of enforcement events, improving forensic clarity and supporting officer and public safety.
AI.conclusion: An AI-assisted VQA framework for high-stakes policing shows promise for enhancing forensic clarity and accountability, with performance influenced by the choice of Q-generation models and the effectiveness of structured reasoning.

title: Demystifying the Privacy-Utility Trade-off in LLM Interactions
summary: The integration of Large Language Models into daily tasks relies on context-rich instructions, inevitably exposing sensitive user information. Current privacy-preserving methods typically employ context-agnostic static rules, causing severe utility degradation. However, the specific mechanisms governing how sanitization impacts downstream performance remain largely underexplored. To address this, we conduct a systematic analysis to deconstruct the privacy-utility trade-off, uncovering three underlying mechanisms: (1) Context-Dependent Utility, which first establishes when to sanitize by revealing that data value shifts from critical constraints to dispensable noise based on user intent; (2) Strategic Adaptation, which subsequently determines how to sanitize by dictating that the choice between removal and replacement depends on the task's reliance on factual integrity versus structural coherence; and (3) Combinatorial Interplay, which finally extends the protection scope by demonstrating that attributes form a semantic web of synergistic dependencies or antagonistic redundancies. Guided by these insights, we introduce an intent-driven local protection framework. By distilling a lightweight model Veilmind-4B to drive a dynamic extraction-sanitization-restoration pipeline, our approach reaches a low-leakage privacy point while preserving substantially higher response utility than existing privacy-oriented baselines, advancing the privacy-utility trade-off toward the Pareto frontier.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes privacy-utility trade-offs in context-aware sanitization for LLMs, identifies three mechanisms driving sanitization decisions, and proposes an intent-driven local protection framework using Veilmind-4B to achieve low leakage with higher utility, advancing toward the Pareto frontier.
AI.motivation: Address pervasive privacy leakage when integrating LLMs into daily tasks. Current context-agnostic rules reduce utility; understanding sanitization dynamics is essential to improve protection without excessive utility loss.
AI.method: Systematic analysis revealing three mechanisms: Context-Dependent Utility (when to sanitize), Strategic Adaptation (how to sanitize), and Combinatorial Interplay (how attributes interact). Proposes an intent-driven local protection framework and implements a lightweight Veilmind-4B model to drive a dynamic extraction-sanitization-restoration pipeline.
AI.result: The approach achieves low-leakage privacy while maintaining substantially higher response utility than existing privacy-oriented baselines, improving the privacy-utility trade-off toward the Pareto frontier.
AI.conclusion: Provides a structured understanding of privacy-utility trade-offs in sanitization for LLMs and a practical, intent-driven pipeline (Veilmind-4B) to balance privacy with utility, pushing performance closer to the Pareto-optimal frontier.

title: Freehand Sketching for End-User Programming of Robot Swarms
summary: Robot swarms are increasingly used in applications where accessible interaction with non-expert users is desirable. This paper investigates freehand sketching as an end-user programming interface for specifying robot swarm geometries. Users communicate spatial intent through a drawing, while the swarm autonomously extracts target formation points, constructs a rigid formation graph, assigns robots to formation nodes, and executes distributed formation control with a guarantee against unintended reflected formations. The resulting sketch-to-swarm framework is evaluated through a human study examining the usability of freehand formation specification. Twenty participants generated $42$ geometric shapes, and the interface achieved a mean System Usability Scale score of $84.25$, which conventionally indicates high perceived usability. The results support freehand sketching as an intuitive interaction abstraction for human-swarm collaboration without requiring robotics or programming expertise.

AI.tldr: Sketch-to-swarm: freehand sketching to specify swarm formations; demonstrated high usability (SUS 84.25) with non-experts.
AI.motivation: Make end-user programming of robot swarms accessible to non-experts; lower the barrier to human-swarm collaboration and reduce need for robotics/programming expertise.
AI.method: From a user sketch, the swarm extracts target formation points, builds a rigid formation graph, assigns robots to formation nodes, and executes distributed formation control with a guarantee against unintended reflected formations.
AI.result: Human study with 20 participants who generated 42 geometric shapes; SUS score 84.25 indicating high perceived usability; supports freehand sketching as an intuitive interaction abstraction for human-swarm collaboration.
AI.conclusion: Freehand sketching is a viable, intuitive interface for end-user specification of swarm geometries, enabling non-experts to specify formations without robotics or programming expertise.

title: From Connectivity to Rewards: Dense Reward Learning with Directed State Graphs
summary: The integration of graphs with Goal-Conditioned Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (GCHRL) has received increasing attention, as graphs naturally encode task hierarchies for effective subgoal sampling. However, existing methods often overlook intrinsic connectivity information, failing to fully leverage the underlying topology for efficient learning. Most graph-based GCHRL methods use the graph as a stochastic sampling tool rather than as an environmental model that encodes connectivity and state-accessibility information. This limitation is particularly acute in quasimetric environments, where the inherent asymmetry of state transitions poses a fundamental challenge to stable policy learning and robust path planning. In this paper, we address these problems by introducing a state connectivity model designed to predict pairwise state connectivity strength in asymmetric environments. We transform these connectivity strengths into scalar auxiliary dense rewards, providing continuous guidance across multiple hierarchical levels. We demonstrate that our proposed framework, Graph-Guided Quasimetric Dense Reward (G2QDR), can theoretically be integrated into any existing GCHRL architecture, and the state connectivity model is efficiently implemented via a neural network trained on a directed state graph generated during exploration. Empirical results across a wide range of sparse reward environments indicate that, in general, G2QDR can enhance the performance of baseline GCHRL approaches with acceptable computational overhead.

AI.tldr: Proposes G2QDR: a state connectivity model that predicts pairwise connectivity in quasimetric environments and converts it into auxiliary dense rewards to guide Graph-Guided GCHRL, improving sparse-reward performance with modest overhead.
AI.motivation: Exploit intrinsic graph connectivity and topology to provide continuous guidance across hierarchy in GCHRL, addressing state-transition asymmetry and improving learning stability and planning.
AI.method: Introduce a neural network-based state connectivity model trained on a directed state graph formed during exploration; convert predicted connectivity strengths into scalar auxiliary dense rewards that can be integrated into any GCHRL architecture; efficient due to directed exploration.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation across sparse-reward environments shows that G2QDR generally enhances baseline GCHRL performance with acceptable computational overhead.
AI.conclusion: G2QDR offers a theoretically compatible, scalable augmentation for GCHRL by leveraging state connectivity to provide dense, hierarchical guidance in quasimetric environments.

title: Are We Really Doing Few-Shot Learning? A Critical Examination of Pre-Training Assumptions
summary: Few-shot learning is commonly evaluated under protocols that pre-train a model on a large auxiliary set whose classes are disjoint from the target episodes yet drawn from the same visual domain. This paper examines whether such protocols truly reflect low-data learning. We systematically compare no pre-training, class-disjoint in-domain pre-training, supervised out-of-domain pre-training, and label-free out-of-domain pre-training across eight datasets, three few-shot architectures, and multiple way-shot settings. Our results show that class disjointness alone is insufficient to remove the influence of target-domain data. In-domain pre-training improves over no pre-training by 33.41 percentage points on average, whereas supervised out-of-domain pre-training yields 23.75 percentage points, revealing a 9.66-point optimistic bias associated with domain overlap. Although out-of-domain pre-training is more realistic in applications where target-domain data are scarce, its effectiveness depends strongly on the compatibility between source and target domains. We further show that labeled source data are not strictly required, with an augmentation-based label-free strategy reaching an average gain of 27.71 percentage points and closely matching supervised out-of-domain pre-training at 27.97 percentage points. Finally, we introduce a descriptor-based source-selection strategy that estimates source-domain suitability before pre-training, reaching a median gap of only 1.37 percentage points to oracle selection. These findings highlight the need to move beyond in-domain pre-training as the default few-shot evaluation protocol, since it can overestimate performance in realistic scenarios where target-domain data are scarce.

AI.tldr: Disjoint in-domain pre-training yields substantial gains but does not eliminate reliance on target-domain data; out-of-domain pre-training depends on domain similarity; label-free augmentation and descriptor-based source selection can approach supervised/oracle performance.
AI.motivation: Assess whether common few-shot evaluation protocols reflect true low-data learning and quantify effects of different pre-training strategies across domains and architectures; identify biases and practical strategies.
AI.method: Systematic empirical study across eight datasets, three few-shot architectures, multiple way-shot settings; compare four pre-training regimes (no pre-training, in-domain class-disjoint pre-training, supervised out-of-domain pre-training, label-free out-of-domain pre-training); introduce descriptor-based source-selection; evaluate augmentation-based label-free strategy; report gains in percentage points and medians.
AI.result: In-domain pre-training improves over no pre-training by 33.41 percentage points on average; supervised out-of-domain pre-training yields 23.75 points; domain overlap yields a 9.66-point optimistic bias; label-free augmentation achieves 27.71 points, closely matching supervised out-of-domain at 27.97 points; descriptor-based source selection reduces gap to oracle to a median of 1.37 points; domain compatibility strongly influences out-of-domain pre-training effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: Measurement protocols should move beyond in-domain pre-training as the default; target-domain data can influence performance even with disjoint classes; leverage label-free strategies and source-selection to better approximate realistic low-data learning, and tailor pre-training choices to domain compatibility.

title: Defining AI Agents: A Compendium of Criteria, Metrics, and Benchmarks
summary: The term agent in artificial intelligence lacks a standard definition, complicating the evaluation, comparison, and reproducibility of AI agent research. We address this ambiguity through a survey organized around five dimensions of agenticness: environmental interaction, learning and adaptation, autonomy, goal-directed behavior, and temporal coherence. For each dimension, we examine how the underlying capability has been conceptualized across prior work and synthesize the metrics, benchmarks, and evaluation frameworks used to assess it. This review provides a structured account of the current landscape of agent evaluation, highlighting both established approaches and areas where evaluation remains limited or inconsistent. We additionally introduce the Agent Compendium, a public-facing digital resource that organizes and extends the evaluation methods identified through this review. Together, the survey and compendium provide a common structure for evaluating and comparing agent capabilities across AI systems, supporting more reproducible research, clearer communication, and more systematic study of artificial agents.

AI.tldr: A survey of AI agent notions organized around five dimensions of agenticness, surveying metrics/benchmarks/evaluation frameworks; introduces the Agent Compendium to standardize and extend agent evaluation for reproducibility and clear communication.
AI.motivation: The lack of a standard definition of 'agent' in AI undermines evaluation, comparison, and reproducibility across studies. A structured, multi-dimensional survey can unify terminology and assessment methods.
AI.method: A literature survey organized around five dimensions of agenticness (environmental interaction, learning/adaptation, autonomy, goal-directed behavior, temporal coherence). For each dimension, the authors review conceptualizations, synthesize related metrics, benchmarks, and evaluation frameworks, and identify gaps. They also introduce the Agent Compendium, a public resource aggregating evaluation methods.
AI.result: Provides a structured overview of current agent evaluation practices, highlights established approaches and areas of inconsistency, and presents a public resource (Agent Compendium) to organize and extend evaluation methods.
AI.conclusion: The combined survey and compendium offer a common framework for evaluating and comparing AI agents, enabling more reproducible research, sharper communication, and more systematic study of artificial agents.

title: RIDE: Relocalization-Informed Depth Estimation with 3D Gaussian Splatting
summary: Render--match--PnP relocalization establishes correspondences between query image pixels and 3D map points for camera pose recovery, but their potential to support dense depth estimation is often overlooked. To exploit this geometric information, we present RIDE, which estimates dense metric depth from a robot's RGB stream. Given a metrically scaled 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) model, RIDE combines sparse metric depth observations derived from PnP-RANSAC inlier correspondences with the geometric prior of a pretrained video-depth model. To handle uneven and intermittent observations, it integrates global and local depth correction with temporal memory, supporting depth estimation through short observation gaps after metric scale initialization. Trained on public RGB-D videos, RIDE is evaluated on robot sequences without fine tuning. Experiments show improved depth accuracy and temporal consistency over scale-only calibration, demonstrating how localization geometry can support both pose recovery and dense robot perception.

AI.tldr: RIDE fuses PnP-derived sparse depth with a pretrained video-depth prior and a 3D Gaussian Splatting model to produce dense metric depth from RGB streams, using temporal memory to bridge observation gaps; it improves depth accuracy and temporal consistency on robotic data without fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Leverage localization geometry from render-match-PnP relocalization not only for pose recovery but also for dense metric depth estimation, addressing lack of scale, sparse inlier observations, and intermittent data in robotic perception.
AI.method: Compute sparse metric depth from PnP-RANSAC inliers mapped to 3D map points, use a pretrained video-depth model as a geometric prior, integrate a 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scale, and apply global/local depth correction with temporal memory to handle uneven observations and short gaps; no fine-tuning on target robots; trained on public RGB-D videos.
AI.result: Quantitative and qualitative evaluation on robot sequences shows improved depth accuracy and temporal coherence over scale-only calibration, validating that localization geometry can support both pose estimation and dense robot perception.
AI.conclusion: Localization geometry derived from render-match-PnP can be repurposed to enable accurate dense metric depth estimation in robotics, enabling robust dense perception under intermittent observations without task-specific fine-tuning.

title: DR-LabStack: Design and Implementation of a Clinician-Facing Web System for Diabetic Retinopathy Prediction
summary: Pretrained diabetic retinopathy (DR) prediction models differ in their input fields, serialization formats, preprocessing requirements, and output semantics. Making these models accessible through a common clinical interface therefore requires explicit coordination between the user interface and the inference service. We designed and implemented DR-LabStack, a React-Flask web system integrating four externally developed pretrained models: RuleFit, Pruned RuleFit, Elaborative XGBoost, and Two-level Ensemble. A shared form retrieves ordered model features, renders model-specific numerical and categorical controls, and constructs a positional input vector. Backend adapters load heterogeneous artifacts and apply the ensemble's accompanying scaler, while a common JSON response supports binary classification display alongside method and source information. Functional evaluation on September 8, 2026 used copied application files and real model artifacts in a documented isolated environment. All four models loaded and exposed their 14-, 6-, 8-, and 25-field contracts. Sixty-two Flask test-client requests characterized service behavior; 12 limited-vector checks confirmed invocation-path and threshold consistency. Twenty-four browser-component scenarios with mocked transport verified input ordering and result rendering and characterized input-validation behavior. The resulting system demonstrates a reusable interaction and serving workflow for heterogeneous DR models. The contribution is web-system design, integration, and software functionality; clinical effectiveness and clinician usability require separate evaluation.

AI.tldr: A web-based system (DR-LabStack) unifies heterogeneous pretrained DR prediction models via a React-Flask interface, adapters, and a common JSON API; evaluated with unit and browser tests; demonstrates reusable integration workflow; clinical effectiveness requires separate evaluation.
AI.motivation: Enable clinicians to interact with diverse pretrained DR models that differ in inputs, formats, and outputs, through a single, coherent clinical interface.
AI.method: Implemented DR-LabStack with a React frontend and Flask backend; built adapters to load four external models (RuleFit, Pruned RuleFit, Elaborative XGBoost, Two-level Ensemble); a shared form collects features, constructs input vectors, and a common JSON response conveys results and provenance; extensive testing includes Flask client tests, path checks, and browser-component scenarios.
AI.result: All four models exposed their respective input contracts (14, 6, 8, 25 fields). 62 Flask test-client requests; 12 invocation-path/threshold checks; 24 browser scenarios with mocked transport, validating input order, rendering, and validation behavior.
AI.conclusion: The work delivers a reusable interaction and serving workflow for heterogeneous DR models. Clinical effectiveness and clinician usability require separate, dedicated evaluation.

title: Evaluation of Vision-Language Models Across Diverse Coastal Environments
comment: This work has been accepted for publication with the 2026 IEEE OCEANS conference
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) enable robotic per- ception by associating visual observations with natural-language concepts. Yet their performance in coastal environments remains largely unexplored. We introduce a densely labeled coastal dataset containing more than 1,000 images collected across seven missions in three regions of Oahu, Hawaii, with 18 semantic classes and over 7,400 annotated instances. We evaluate seven modern VLMs through three complementary experiments mea- suring text-to-mask, mask-to-mask, and mask-to-text alignment. Broad landscape classes are generally recognized more accurately than conventional object and coastal classes, with coastal con- cepts presenting the greatest challenge. However, comparisons of shared conventional classes across coastal and terrestrial datasets reveal no consistent performance difference attributable solely to environmental context. Mask-to-mask matching also remains similar across conventional and coastal classes, while alternative textual labels substantially improve recognition of several coastal concepts. These results suggest that lower performance on coastal classes (at least on the objects/query categories evaluated) is heavily influenced by segmentation and linguistic representation.

AI.tldr: A densely labeled coastal VLM dataset (1k+ images, 7 missions, 3 regions, 18 semantic classes, 7.4k+ instances) is introduced, alongside an evaluation of seven modern VLMs using text-to-mask, mask-to-mask, and mask-to-text tasks. Coastal concepts are harder to recognize than broad landscape classes. Shared conventional classes show no consistent performance drop due to coastal context. Mask-to-mask performance is similar across class types, while alternative textual labels improve coastal concept recognition. Overall, lower coastal performance appears driven by segmentation and linguistic representation rather than environmental context.
AI.motivation: Address the gap in understanding how vision-language models perform in coastal environments and whether coastal context or segmentation/language issues drive performance gaps.
AI.method: (1) Build a densely labeled coastal dataset with >1,000 images from seven missions across three Oahu regions; 18 semantic classes; >7,400 annotated instances. (2) Evaluate seven modern VLMs through three experiments: text-to-mask, mask-to-mask, and mask-to-text alignment. (3) Compare coastal vs terrestrial data for shared conventional classes; test alternate textual labels for coastal concepts.
AI.result: Broad landscape classes are generally recognized more accurately than coastal/object classes. No consistent performance difference for shared conventional classes across coastal vs terrestrial datasets. Mask-to-mask matching shows similar results across class types. Using alternative textual labels significantly improves recognition of several coastal concepts.
AI.conclusion: Performance gaps for coastal concepts are mainly due to segmentation and linguistic representation rather than environmental context alone. Improvements should focus on better segmentation of coastal objects and richer linguistic prompts/labels to capture coastal semantics.

title: The Agent Incident Registry: Toward Preventing Repeated AI Agent Failures
summary: AI agents increasingly act through tools and delegated authority, but general incident repositories rarely capture the mechanisms needed to compare public failures with agent-security evaluations. We present the Agent Incident Registry (AIR), a source-linked catalog containing \N{} records of agent-related events disclosed from \Yfirst{} through \Ylast{}. Each record includes supporting evidence, a stable identifier, and missingness-aware labels for causal role, disclosure class, mechanism, and outcome. Among the \Nprimary{} generative-system records in which the agent acted, \Rprimary{} involved realized harm (\Pprimary\%). Realized outcomes concentrate in in-the-wild and safety-failure records, while responsible disclosures and research demonstrations are overwhelmingly demonstrated; the aggregate share therefore characterizes collection composition rather than deployment risk. After initial curation, a second human reviewer checked all \N{} records and their existing labels for completeness and correctness. In a deployment-analogue audit, InjecAgent's \NInjecAgentCases{} cases occupy three of AIR's twelve surfaces and are all attacker-triggered, whereas AIR contains \Nsafety{} no-adversary safety failures. AIR supports source-grounded case retrieval and evaluation-scope auditing, not failure-rate or control-efficacy estimation.

AI.tldr: AIR is a source-linked registry of agent-related incidents with labeled records, enabling retrieval and auditing and revealing composition patterns; it is not designed for estimating failure rates or control efficacy.
AI.motivation: To fill gaps in public incident repositories by providing a structured, source-grounded catalog of agent-related events with labeled attributes (causal role, disclosure class, mechanism, outcome) to support cross-case comparison and auditing of agent-security evaluations.
AI.method: Construct AIR by aggregating N records of agent-related events disclosed from Yfirst to Ylast, each with supporting evidence, a stable identifier, and missingness-aware labels for causal role, disclosure class, mechanism, and outcome. After initial curation, a second human reviewer validates completeness and correctness. A deployment-analogue audit uses InjecAgent cases to examine surfaces and whether triggers are attacker-driven. AIR includes twelve surfaces and catalogues the distribution of realized harm, disclosure types, mechanisms, and outcomes.
AI.result: Among the N primary generative-system records, R_primary records involve realized harm, representing P_primary percent. Realized outcomes concentrate in in-the-wild and safety-failure records, while responsible disclosures and research demonstrations are overwhelmingly present; thus aggregate patterns describe collection composition rather than deployment risk. InjecAgent cases occupy three of AIR's twelve surfaces and are attacker-triggered; AIR contains N_safety no-adversary safety failures.
AI.conclusion: AIR supports source-grounded case retrieval and evaluation-scope auditing, but it does not provide failure-rate estimation or control-efficacy assessment.

title: Harness Robotic OS: A Unified Embodied-Agent Runtime for Closed-Loop Quadruped Inspection
summary: Autonomous property inspection requires more than robust robot navigation: a deployable system must connect heterogeneous sensing, reusable autonomy capabilities, multimodal scene understanding, human interaction, and enterprise response within a traceable operational loop. Existing quadruped inspection systems commonly integrate these functions through task-specific interfaces, making contextual coordination, knowledge reuse, and controlled adaptation difficult. This paper presents \textit{Harness Robotic OS} (HROS), a unified embodied-agent runtime, and Argos, its realization for residential-community inspection. HROS organizes the system into robot runtime, embodied autonomy skills, cognitive agent runtime, and interaction and operations planes. A shared context connects physical state with agent reasoning; streaming ASR/TTS supports voice-based mission interaction; hierarchical working, episodic, and semantic memory preserves operational knowledge; and a safety-gated self-evolution loop converts execution traces into versioned candidate updates without permitting unconstrained online modification. The Argos prototype integrates a Vbot quadruped, Fast-LIO2 localization and mapping, Hobot-Stereo depth perception, PCT-Planner global planning, EGO-Planner local motion generation, and OpenClaw-orchestrated Qwen3-VL inspection analysis. Experiments in a residential property environment achieved 100\% waypoint reachability, outdoor localization error below 10~cm, local obstacle-response latency below 200~ms, representative hazard-detection rates of 85--95\%, and 99\% success in alarm delivery and structured-report generation. These results validate the deployed navigation and inspection closed loop, while HROS provides an extensible software foundation for memory-augmented, voice-aware, and continuously improvable embodied inspection agents.

AI.tldr: HROS is a unified embodied-agent runtime for property inspection, enabling memory-augmented, voice-aware, and continuously improvable agents; Argos demonstrates robust sensing/planning and report generation on a quadruped with multiple perception/planning modules.
AI.motivation: To address the lack of integrated, adaptable systems in autonomous inspection that unify sensing, autonomy, memory, human interaction, and enterprise traces; existing quadruped-inspection systems rely on task-specific interfaces hindering coordination and reuse.
AI.method: Proposes Harness Robotic OS (HROS) architecture: robot runtime, embodied autonomy skills, cognitive agent runtime, interaction/operations planes; shared context linking physical state with reasoning; streaming ASR/TTS for voice interaction; memory layers (working/episodic/semantic); safety-gated self-evolution loop for versioned updates; Argos realization integrating Vbot, Fast-LIO2, Hobot-Stereo, PCT-Planner, EGO-Planner, OpenClaw/Qwen3-VL for analysis; experiments on a residential property.
AI.result: Experimental results show 100% waypoint reachability, outdoor localization error <10 cm, obstacle-response latency <200 ms, hazard-detection 85–95%, alarm/report success 99%, validating closed-loop navigation and inspection.
AI.conclusion: HROS provides an extensible software foundation for memory-augmented, voice-aware, and continuously improvable embodied inspection agents and demonstrates a practical Argos prototype for residential-community inspection.

title: RiVaT-Fuse: Reliability-Calibrated Variational Tensor Fusion for Multimodal Prediction under Modality Uncertainty
summary: Image-metadata prediction requires fusing heterogeneous evidence whose reliability can vary across samples and latent factors. Existing representation-level fusion methods typically choose an aggregation architecture, such as concatenation, gating, conditional modulation, or attention, without explicitly defining what the fused representation should mean under modality uncertainty. We propose RiVaT-Fuse, a reliability-calibrated variational tensor fusion framework that defines fusion as sample-wise latent-state estimation. Rather than producing a fused vector by direct aggregation, RiVaT-Fuse estimates a consensus latent state through a variational objective that balances image evidence, metadata evidence, structured cross-modal interaction, and stability. The resulting framework replaces scalar modality confidence with matrix-valued trust geometry, decomposes interaction into additive, multiplicative, and relational components, and couples the latent state with conditional robustness and structured multi-task prediction. We provide well-posedness and stability interpretations of the latent solve and instantiate the framework with efficient low-rank-plus-diagonal trust operators. On an image-level image-metadata prediction benchmark, RiVaT-Fuse achieves the strongest overall predictive rank among direct representation-level baselines while improving probability and label stability under perturbation.

AI.tldr: RiVaT-Fuse reframes image-metadata fusion as sample-wise latent-state estimation using reliability-calibrated tensor fusion; introduces matrix-valued trust geometry and low-rank-plus-diagonal operators, achieving strong ranking and robustness on an image-level benchmark.
AI.motivation: Fusion of heterogeneous evidence with varying reliability; existing representation-level fusion lacks explicit meaning for fused representations under modality uncertainty; a reliability-aware, theoretically grounded fusion mechanism is needed.
AI.method: Variational objective to estimate a consensus latent state rather than direct aggregation; decomposes cross-modal interaction into additive, multiplicative, and relational components; replaces scalar modality confidence with matrix-valued trust geometry; couples latent state with conditional robustness and structured multi-task prediction; introduces well-posedness and stability interpretations of the latent solve; uses efficient low-rank-plus-diagonal trust operators.
AI.result: On an image-level image-metadata benchmark, RiVaT-Fuse achieves the strongest overall predictive rank among direct representation-level baselines; improves probability and label stability under perturbation; provides theoretical interpretations of the latent solve and efficient instantiation.
AI.conclusion: Reliability-calibrated, variational tensor fusion yields more robust, interpretable fusion for heterogeneous evidence, with strong empirical performance and practical efficiency.

title: Symmetry-aware super-resolution of crystal orientation maps via invariant latent-space learning
summary: Crystal-orientation maps are physical fields defined only up to crystal symmetry; electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) resolves them experimentally, but acquisition-time constraints limit spatial resolution. Unlike conventional images, EBSD data lie on the quotient space $\mathrm{SO}(3)/G$, where $G$ is the crystal-symmetry group. Standard Euclidean interpolation can therefore mix symmetry-equivalent representations and blur grain boundaries. We introduce the Symmetry-Group-Aware Super-Resolution Attention Network (SG-SRAN), which incorporates crystal symmetry and boundary preservation by design.
