Yet within the range we test, neither worry materializes; what emerges instead is an invariance. Making the split more unequal barely changes the speed of collapse. Destinations move even less: the share and identity knobs shift five-generation endpoints by only a few percent of the drift common to all arms -- the ecosystems collapse to nearly the same place. An extreme share paired with the strongest injected bias still does not guarantee steering, and the topic shifts it does produce leave only a faint trace on the ruler that measures collapse. What sets the speed is who supplies the pool and how readily those suppliers are carried along: with every share held fixed, swapping the members of a K=3 ecosystem changes five-generation drift by 2.8x; a share-weighted index of each member's susceptibility explains the speed differences across nineteen arms with R^2 = 0.68; and replacing half the pool with human text roughly halves drift without changing its course. Within the tested range, concentration sets neither the destination nor the pace of collapse; the pace follows whose text fills the pool.

title: Safety-aware Skill Adaptation for Reinforcement Learning in Dynamic Environments
comment: Accepted for Presentation and Publication at IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems 2026
summary: Skill adaptation frameworks based on reinforcement learning often require restrictive assumptions to maintain stability, such as fixed observations or tightly controlled exploration schedules. In cluttered and dynamic environments, however, unrestricted exploration can lead to unsafe behaviour and unstable learning, particularly when task-relevant observations lie near obstacles or involve moving objects. In this work, we present Dist-GPRL, a distance-aware and safety-guided reinforcement learning framework for structured robot skill adaptation. Building upon Gaussian Process (GP)-based skill parameterisation, our framework sequentially adapts overlapping local windows of sparse trajectory via-points rather than modifying the complete skill at every policy step. Raw policy outputs are correlated through the GP covariance structure, producing temporally coherent trajectory updates while reducing the action-space and credit-assignment difficulties associated with global trajectory adaptation. Safety is incorporated through two complementary forms of guidance. A safe-subspace prior derived from the Hausdorff Approximation Planner (HAP) biases policy exploration toward feasible regions, while dynamically updated distance field clearance and gradient rewards provide local obstacle awareness. A trajectory-kinematics similarity regulariser further preserves the demonstrated velocity and acceleration characteristics during adaptation. We evaluate the framework on two dynamic object-manipulation tasks in simulation and transfer the learned policy to real-world robot execution. Experimental results demonstrate higher task success, lower collision frequency, and more stable learning than the baselines, while preserving the kinematic characteristics of the demonstrated skill.

AI.tldr: A distance-aware, safety-guided GP-based local trajectory adaptation framework that enhances safety, stability, and sim-to-real transfer in cluttered, dynamic environments.
AI.motivation: To overcome stability and safety constraints in RL-based skill adaptation under unrestricted exploration in cluttered/dynamic environments, while preserving demonstrated kinematics and simplifying credit assignment by local, not global, updates.
AI.method: GP-based skill parameterisation; sequential adaptation of overlapping local windows of sparse trajectory via-points; GP covariance enforces temporal coherence; safety via a safe-subspace prior derived from the Hausdorff Approximation Planner (HAP) and distance-field clearance with gradient rewards; trajectory-kinematics similarity regulariser to preserve velocity/acceleration; sim-to-real transfer evaluation.
AI.result: In two dynamic object-manipulation tasks in simulation, the approach yields higher task success, lower collision frequency, and more stable learning than baselines, with successful transfer to a real robot and preservation of demonstrated kinematics.
AI.conclusion: Dist-GPRL provides a scalable, safer, and more stable framework for RL-based skill adaptation by leveraging local GP-based trajectory updates and safety guidance, enabling effective sim-to-real transfer.

title: AUC Maximization from Biased Positive-unlabeled Data with Confidence
summary: Maximizing the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) is a standard approach to imbalanced binary classification. Although positive and negative data are required for maximizing the AUC, negative data are often difficult to collect in some real-world applications due to privacy concerns or the need for specialized expertise to annotate them. Thus, AUC maximization from positive and unlabeled (PU) data has been attracting attention. Existing methods assume that labeled positive data are unbiased samples from the true positive distribution. However, this ideal assumption is often violated in practice. In this paper, we propose a method to maximize the AUC from biased PU data. To address the bias, our key idea is to exploit {\it confidence}, i.e., the probability that an instance is positive, associated with the small number of labeled positive data. We derive an estimator of the AUC risk using biased PU data with confidence, enabling AUC maximization under such bias. We further show that the rewritten AUC risk induces a Bayes-optimal AUC ranking even when the available confidence is any strictly increasing transformation of the true posterior probability. We experimentally show the effectiveness of our method on eight real-world datasets.

AI.tldr: Introduces a method to maximize AUC from biased positive-unlabeled data by leveraging confidence scores for the positives; derives a bias-aware AUC risk estimator, shows Bayes-optimal ranking under any monotone confidence transform, and validates on eight real-world datasets.
AI.motivation: In imbalanced binary classification, obtaining negative examples is hard due to privacy or expertise constraints. PU learning assuming unbiased positives fails in practice. There is a need to account for label bias when maximizing AUC.
AI.method: Develops an estimator of AUC risk using biased PU data with confidence, by rewriting AUC risk and leveraging the confidence associated with labeled positives. Proves the rewritten risk yields Bayes-optimal AUC ranking even when confidence is any strictly increasing transformation of the true posterior. Training uses this risk estimator.
AI.result: The proposed estimator enables AUC maximization under bias and is empirically effective on eight real-world datasets.
AI.conclusion: Bias-aware AUC maximization in PU settings is feasible; the approach achieves Bayes-optimal ranking under monotone confidence transformations and demonstrates practical utility across multiple datasets.

title: Beyond Benchmarks: Using VLMs to Reveal Systematic Classification Failures Under Real World Conditions
comment: To be presented at SPIE Sensors + Imaging, Edinburgh, in September 2026
summary: Verification and validation (V&V) of classification models is crucial to enable a wide range of sensor processing applications. Currently, the V&V process relies on time-consuming manual inspection of erroneous samples to find meaningful patterns. This work explores the use of Vision Language Models (VLMs) to speed up this laborious process. VLMs are trained to embed images into a semantically meaningful vector representation, from which human-interpretable systematic errors can be distilled. Deploying such VLM-based methods in a defence context introduces two major challenges: (1) the defence domain is underrepresented in the training data of VLMs, and (2) surroundings and context are less diverse than for other domains. This study provides an initial assessment of the suitability of VLM-based methods for V&V of defence applications. We propose a VLM-based error slice detection (ESD) method that independently groups and labels systematic errors made by a classification model. We demonstrate that this method is able to identify operationally-relevant artificially added perturbations in a non-military dataset. In a military context, our method clusters and describes images based on their surroundings, but also exhibits overlap between cluster descriptions. We further investigate the difference in embedding variation between our military and non-military dataset, which remains a topic of interest. Although the results do not yet warrant fully automated V&V through VLM-based ESD, they show that VLMs could be used to accelerate V&V processes in the future.

AI.tldr: VLMs are explored to speed up V&V of image classifiers in defense by creating semantic embeddings to detect systematic errors. A VLM-based error slice detection (ESD) method is proposed and evaluated on non-military data and, to a limited extent, military data. Results show potential but not yet fully automated.
AI.motivation: Verification and validation of classification models is time-consuming; existing V&V relies on manual inspection of erroneous samples. VLMs offer semantically meaningful embeddings that could reveal systematic errors, but the defense domain is underrepresented and contexts are less diverse in training data, posing challenges for deployment.
AI.method: Introduce a VLM-based error slice detection (ESD) method that independently groups and labels systematic errors made by a classifier. Evaluate on a non-military dataset with artificially added perturbations. In a military context, cluster images by surroundings and describe them, noting overlap between cluster descriptions. Compare embedding variation between military and non-military datasets to assess domain differences.
AI.result: ESD can identify artificially introduced perturbations in the non-military dataset. In the military context, clustering by surroundings is feasible but cluster descriptions overlap, limiting interpretability. Embedding variation differs between military and non-military data, indicating domain-specific characteristics. Overall, results are promising but not yet sufficient for fully automated V&V.
AI.conclusion: VLM-based ESD shows potential to accelerate V&V workflows for defense applications, but additional work is needed to improve automation, disambiguate cluster descriptions, and address domain-specific embedding behavior before deployment.

title: Autonomous Chemical Mechanistic Discovery through Agentic Reasoning and Validation
comment: This paper has been submitted to Nature Communications
summary: Unraveling reaction mechanisms is central to modern chemistry, yet automating these investigations remains challenging because computational workflows still rely heavily on expert intervention. Here we introduce ARCHE, an autonomous agentic system that integrates a general-purpose reasoning model, a domain-specialized computational chemistry model, and a structured tool registry to transform mechanistic inquiry into a scalable, self-validating process. ARCHE interprets scientific questions, generates and prioritizes mechanistic hypotheses, orchestrates computational workflows, and iteratively refines conclusions based on computed evidence within a closed loop. We validate its capabilities across three increasingly demanding scenarios: reconstructing stereocontrolling transition states and validating the corresponding reaction mechanism in a previously reported asymmetric catalytic reaction; proposing and validating a plausible radical pathway through iterative hypothesis refinement for a recently discovered but unpublished $α$-iodoboronate C-I cleavage reaction; and identifying a chemically interpretable descriptor that governs selectivity in nickel-catalysed migratory cross-coupling reactions. By coupling agentic reasoning with rigorous computational validation, ARCHE advances autonomous mechanistic discovery and establishes a foundation for broader machine-assisted chemical research. The code for ARCHE is publicly available at https://github.com/JetAstra/Arche-Harness.

AI.tldr: ARCHE is an autonomous agentic system that drives automated, self-validating mechanistic chemistry research by coupling reasoning, computational chemistry, and a tool registry.
AI.motivation: Automating mechanistic investigations remains challenging due to reliance on expert intervention; there is a need for scalable, self-correcting, autonomous workflows.
AI.method: ARCHE integrates a general-purpose reasoning model, a domain-specialized computational chemistry model, and a structured tool registry; it interprets questions, generates and prioritizes mechanistic hypotheses, orchestrates computational workflows, and iteratively refines conclusions within a closed loop.
AI.result: Validated across three escalating scenarios: (1) reconstructing stereocontrolling transition states and mechanism in an asymmetric catalytic reaction; (2) proposing and validating a plausible radical pathway for an unpublished α-iodoboronate C–I cleavage reaction; (3) identifying a chemically interpretable descriptor governing selectivity in nickel-catalyzed migratory cross-coupling.
AI.conclusion: ARCHE advances autonomous mechanistic discovery by coupling agentic reasoning with rigorous computational validation and establishes a foundation for broader machine-assisted chemical research; the code is publicly available.

title: FARM: Reading Failure Signals from the Internal Predictive States of a Frozen Robotic World Model
summary: Reliable robot deployment requires online failure monitoring, yet existing monitors mainly derive risk from proxy signals or train dedicated monitoring components. We ask whether the internal predictive states of a frozen pretrained robotic world model already contain directly decodable failure information. Failure-Aware Readout from World Models (FARM) trains only a 33,985-parameter supervised readout over frozen VLA-JEPA predictive states, producing step-wise failure scores and causal trajectory risk. Five-fold out-of-fold evaluation across seven source tasks reaches 85.68/88.59 pooled AUROC/AUPRC, and FARM gives the best Seen performance among 15 matched baselines on the 10-task benchmark. Across four real-robot populations on PIPER X, SO-101, and Franka, fixed-readout transfer and readout-only adaptation test deployment shifts without updating the predictive backbone. FARM also discriminates failures from partial causal histories and adds 0.2256 ms mean CUDA latency once the frozen state is available. These results support frozen predictive world-model states as reusable features for causal, transferable, and low-overhead execution monitoring.

AI.tldr: A tiny readout on frozen world-model states enables reliable, low-overhead failure monitoring with strong cross-task transfer and real-robot validation.
AI.motivation: Reliable online failure monitoring is often achieved via proxies or dedicated monitors; this work asks if internal predictive states from a frozen pretrained world model already encode decodable failure information.
AI.method: Train a 33,985-parameter supervised readout on frozen VLA-JEPA predictive states to output step-wise failure scores and causal trajectory risk. Evaluate with five-fold out-of-fold on seven source tasks; test transfer to real robots with fixed-readout adaptation across multiple platforms.
AI.result: Five-fold out-of-fold evaluation on seven source tasks yields pooled AUROC 85.68 and AUPRC 88.59. Farm achieves the best Seen performance among 15 baselines on a 10-task benchmark. Real-robot validation across PIPER X, SO-101, and Franka shows successful readout-only transfer without backbone updates and a mean CUDA latency of 0.2256 ms once the frozen state is available.
AI.conclusion: Frozen predictive world-model states serve as reusable, causal, transferable, and low-overhead features for execution monitoring.

title: Measuring the Value of World-Model Updates: A Counterfactual Utility Protocol for Continual Adaptation
comment: 13 pages, 2 figures, under review at the CWM workshop
summary: Continual world models must decide whether new data justify changing the model. Fixed replay schedules and prediction-error triggers specify when to update, but neither reveals the value of an individual update: one deployment run cannot show how the same model would have performed at that moment had it held its parameters. We introduce the fork ledger, which branches a deployment stream at pre-registered decision points into matched update and hold continuations under common random numbers. It evaluates both continuations on the same episodes and records $ΔR = R_{\mathrm{update}} - R_{\mathrm{hold}}$. Always applying one fixed update mechanism lowers return on all three simulated control tasks: CartPole ($-144.0$; checkpoint-bootstrap $95\%$ CI $[-185.4,-116.1]$, against a converged return near $650$), Walker ($-82.8$; $[-101.1,-61.7]$) and Cheetah ($-18.6$; $[-29.0,-6.6]$). Divergence is an outcome of applying the update, so the estimand counts every attempted fork; restricted to the $693$ of $720$ that did not collapse, CartPole and Walker are unchanged in sign ($-113.4$ and $-82.1$) and Cheetah becomes unresolved ($-3.9$; $[-17.5,+13.0]$). The task is the unit of inference: each contributes $240$ attempted forks over five pretrained checkpoints crossed with two drift directions. The ledger makes counterfactual utility observable for a fixed mechanism, allowing triggers to be judged by the updates they select rather than by surprise detection alone.

AI.tldr: Fork ledger introduces counterfactual evaluation of updates in continual world models by branching deployment into update and hold continuations under common randomness; across CartPole, Walker, and Cheetah updates under a fixed mechanism reduce returns, with partial forks surviving; enables judging triggers by their selected updates rather than surprise alone.
AI.motivation: Quantify the actual value of model updates during continual learning, accounting for counterfactual outcomes that a single deployment cannot reveal.
AI.method: At predefined decision points, fork the deployment stream into two continuations (update and hold) using common random numbers. Run both on the same episodes, record ΔR = R_update − R_hold. Analyze fixed update mechanisms across multiple tasks, drift directions, and checkpoints; report attempted forks and survival to assess the utility of updates.
AI.result: Fixed-update schemes degrade performance across tasks: CartPole ΔR = −144.0 (CI −185.4 to −116.1), Walker ΔR = −82.8 (CI −101.1 to −61.7), Cheetah ΔR = −18.6 (CI −29.0 to −6.6). Of 720 forks, 693 did not collapse; CartPole and Walker remain negative in sign (−113.4 and −82.1), Cheetah becomes unresolved (−3.9; CI −17.5 to +13.0). Each task contributes 240 attempted forks (five pretrained checkpoints × two drift directions).
AI.conclusion: The fork ledger makes counterfactual utility observable for a fixed mechanism, allowing triggers to be judged by the updates they select rather than by surprise detection alone.

title: ReconPlusGen: Injecting Reconstruction Prior into Multi-view 3D Generation through Noise Inversion and Modulation
summary: Qualitative results and an illustration of our core idea. Top left: reconstruction results on benchmark images. Top right: reconstruction results on real-world images. Bottom: illustration of reconstruction-guided noise initialization and modulation. Given multiple input images, we predict a point cloud in canonical space, deterministically inject the predicted geometry into the diffusion process through noise inversion, and modulate the resulting noise to preserve the generative flexibility required to complete unobserved regions and refine visible geometry.

AI.tldr: A diffusion-based 3D reconstruction framework using canonical-space point clouds as geometry priors, injecting geometry into the diffusion process via noise inversion and modulating noise to preserve generative flexibility for unobserved regions.
AI.motivation: Reconstruct 3D geometry from multiple input images by leveraging diffusion models while retaining the ability to complete unobserved regions and refine observed geometry.
AI.method: Predict a canonical-space point cloud from multiple inputs; deterministically inject the predicted geometry into the diffusion process through noise inversion; modulate the resulting noise to balance fidelity and the ability to complete missing regions.
AI.result: Qualitative results and an illustration of the core idea, including reconstruction results on benchmark images and real-world images, and an illustration of reconstruction-guided noise initialization and modulation.
AI.conclusion: The approach integrates canonical-space geometry with diffusion-based generation to achieve controllable, geometry-consistent reconstructions with the ability to complete missing regions.

title: DRG-MAPPO: Hierarchical Dynamic Role-Graph Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Cooperative Air Combat
summary: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) has emerged as a pivotal paradigm for complex decision-making in autonomous systems and air combat. While MARL has demonstrated significant potential in air combat, achieving sophisticated tactical coordination remains a non-trivial challenge. This difficulty is largely attributed to two primary limitations: (1) the absence of structured relational modeling hinders agents from capturing complex, time-varying interactions among battlefield entities; and (2) conventional flat architectures often lack the capability to explicitly model tactical roles, leading to ambiguous task allocation in highly dynamic environments. To address these challenges, we propose Hierarchical Dynamic Role-Graph Multi-Agent Proximal Policy Optimization (DRG-MAPPO), a novel MARL framework that integrates graph-based relational modeling with dynamic role assignment. Specifically, DRG-MAPPO constructs a graph-based representation of battlefield interactions and leverages graph attention mechanisms to extract critical relational features among allies, enemies, and threats. Subsequently, a high-level policy employs a dynamic role assignment mechanism to determine tactical responsibilities (e.g., ``leader'' and ``supporter''). Conditioned on these roles and encoded graph-relational features, a low-level policy executes discrete maneuver actions, facilitating the joint optimization of tactical strategy and collaborative execution. Furthermore, a target-priority auxiliary task is designed to foster the emergence of behaviors such as focus-fire. Experimental results demonstrate that DRG-MAPPO achieves a state-of-the-art win rate of 87%, suggesting that our framework effectively balances relational modeling, interpretability, and optimization stability for cooperative air combat.

AI.tldr: Hierarchical DRG-MAPPO combines graph-relational modeling with dynamic role assignment to enhance coordination in cooperative air combat; reports high performance.
AI.motivation: Address two key MARL limitations in air combat: (1) lack of structured relational modeling for time-varying battlefield interactions, (2) absence of explicit tactical role modeling in flat architectures, which hinders task allocation and coordination.
AI.method: Construct a graph-based representation of battlefield entities (allies, enemies, threats) and apply graph attention to extract relational features. A high-level policy dynamically assigns roles (e.g., leader, supporter). A low-level policy executes discrete maneuvers conditioned on roles and encoded graph-relational features. A target-priority auxiliary task promotes behaviors like focus-fire.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation shows DRG-MAPPO achieves a state-of-the-art win rate of 87% in cooperative air combat scenarios.
AI.conclusion: The framework effectively balances relational modeling, interpretability, and optimization stability, enabling emergent tactical roles and improved cooperative performance.

title: 3D Euler-Angle Orientation Control for Two-Ray Fading Mitigation in Maritime Air-to-Sea Communications
comment: Accepted to the 2026 IEEE Global Communications Conference, GLOBECOM 2026
summary: Maritime Air-to-Sea links are dominated by a line-of-sight ray and a sea-surface reflected ray whose destructive combination produces deep fades. Existing mitigation strategies optimize Unmanned Aerial Vehicle position or trajectory but leave attitude unexploited. This paper treats the full three dimensional attitude as a physical-layer control variable that shapes the two-ray interference through antenna phase-center displacement. Under small-angle and far-field assumptions, the constructive-interference condition reduces to an affine constraint in the Euler angles and admits a closed-form family of minimum-norm attitude candidates. A differentiable soft-minimum rule yields a smooth reference tracked by a constrained Nonlinear Model Predictive Control controller on a fully-actuated tilting multirotor. The proposed scheme increases cumulative throughput by 11.4% over a pitch-only benchmark and 22.2% over a zero-orientation baseline, while preserving trajectory tracking and respecting actuator limits.

AI.tldr: Attitude as a 3D physical-layer control leverages UAV phase-center shifts to mitigate two-ray A2S fading; yields closed-form minimum-norm attitudes under affine Euler-angle constraints and NP-based control.
AI.motivation: Mitigate destructive two-ray interference in maritime air-to-sea links by exploiting UAV attitude, beyond traditional position/trajectory optimization.
AI.method: Model the two-ray interference with attitude-induced phase-center displacement under small-angle, far-field assumptions. Derive an affine constraint in Euler angles for constructive interference, yielding a closed-form family of minimum-norm attitudes. Use a differentiable soft-minimum rule to select a reference attitude and track it with a constrained nonlinear MPC on a fully-actuated tilting multirotor.
AI.result: Throughput gains of 11.4% over a pitch-only baseline and 22.2% over a zero-orientation baseline, while maintaining trajectory tracking and respecting actuator limits.
AI.conclusion: Attitude-aware control expands the design space for maritime A2S links, enabling notable performance gains via a principled, differentiable, constraint-consistent MPC that exploits phase-center shifts to shape two-ray interference.

title: When More Is Not Better: Component Anti-Synergy in a P300 Speller
summary: P300 brain-computer interface (BCI) spellers can provide hands-free communication for people with severe motor impairments. Modern pipelines combine multiple individually promising components, often assuming that 'more-is-better'. We tested this assumption using a four-component full-factorial experiment varying the inclusion of Euclidean Alignment (EA), xDAWN spatial filtering, subject calibration, and language model priors on a public P300 dataset. Performance was evaluated using accuracy, repetitions, and information transfer rate (ITR) with mixed-effects models. Results show that the value of components is conditional rather than additive. Calibration was the strongest singular contributor, while EA compensated for its absence in zero-calibration settings. Adding independently useful components could also reduce performance, revealing component anti-synergy. Contrary to conventional wisdom, LM support was not universally beneficial: its effect depends strongly on the strength of the underlying EEG pipeline, while results from a larger LM showed a similar pattern. Together, these findings challenge maximal 'all-on' pipeline design and highlight the value of selecting spatial and language-support components according to the quality of available EEG evidence.

AI.tldr: A multi-component P300 BCI speller study shows that more components do not guarantee better performance; calibration is the strongest contributor, EA aids zero-calibration, and language-model priors have conditional benefit tied to EEG pipeline quality, revealing anti-synergy among components and arguing for selective, data-driven pipeline design.
AI.motivation: To test the common assumption that adding more components to P300 BCI pipelines yields higher performance, by systematically evaluating interactions among spatial filtering (xDAWN), alignment (EA), calibration strategy, and language-model priors on a public dataset.
AI.method: Full-factorial 2x2x2x2 design manipulating: Euclidean Alignment (EA vs none), xDAWN spatial filtering (with vs without), subject calibration (calibrated vs zero-calibration), and language model priors (present vs absent). Performance metrics include accuracy, repetition count, and information transfer rate (ITR); analyzed with mixed-effects models across a public P300 dataset.
AI.result: Component value is conditional rather than additive. Calibration dominates as the strongest contributor; EA can compensate for lack of calibration in zero-calibration settings. Adding individually useful components can reduce performance (anti-synergy). Language-model priors are not universally beneficial; their effect depends on the strength of the EEG pipeline, and findings generalize with larger LMs.
AI.conclusion: Selective, data-driven pipeline design is preferable to maximal inclusion of components. Spatial and language-support components should be tailored to the quality of available EEG evidence, rather than assuming all components add value.

title: LAION-Mobile: Evaluating Deepfake Detectors On One Million Smartphone Photos
summary: Most Deepfake detectors report near-perfect AUC scores on their reference benchmarks. However, a recent ICML position paper argues that these evaluations collectively neglect the impact of modern smartphone photography: the widely used on-device neural image-signal processing pipelines (like multi-sensor fusion or noise and motion-blur suppression) increasingly shift the imaging paradigm from simple lens projections towards computational photography. Hence, devices actually generate, rather than record photos. This increases the risk that deepfake detectors may flag ordinary phone photos as fake. Due to the lack of large-scale datasets containing images from modern smartphones, this hypothesis has so far only been tested in small proof-of-concept studies. The aim of this paper is to close this gap. We introduce LAION-Mobile, an open dataset containing about 1 million smartphone images with EXIF metadata distilled from re-LAION-5B. Evaluating twelve state-of-the-art deepfake detectors with their original paper checkpoints on a 9,115-image evaluation sample of this pool (DIRE on 738), we report three key findings: (i) On modern AI content no detector exceeds AUC 0.624, and five of twelve fall below chance. (ii) Real-photo false-alarm rates are an artefact of threshold calibration: thresholds fitted on legacy GAN data make several detectors look deployable (less than 11 percent FPR), yet the same detectors flag 17-91 percent of real photos once the identical criterion is refit on modern content. (iii) Consequently, no detector both beats chance on modern AI content and keeps a deployable real-photo false-alarm rate. Mirroring the device mix of web collections, the corpus probes the first neural-ISP generation (2018-2020); current flagships are essentially absent, leaving the modern-ISP regime as the open gap.

AI.tldr: LAION-Mobile shows deepfake detectors struggle with modern smartphone ISP-produced images; a ~1M-image dataset reveals detectors underperform (max AUC ~0.624; many below chance); threshold calibration on legacy data inflates deployability, but modern content yields high real-photo false alarms. No detector is robust across modern AI content and real-photo criteria yet; the modern-ISP regime is an open gap.
AI.motivation: To test whether state-of-the-art deepfake detectors, trained on legacy AI content, generalize to images produced by contemporary smartphone computational photography pipelines, given the lack of large-scale modern-device datasets.
AI.method: Create LAION-Mobile (~1M smartphone images with distilled EXIF from re-LAION-5B). Evaluate 12 detectors using their original checkpoints on a 9,115-image evaluation sample (DIRE on 738). Assess AUC on modern AI content and real-photo false-alarm rates, including re-fitting thresholds on modern data.
AI.result: On modern AI content, no detector exceeds AUC 0.624; five detectors fall below chance. Thresholds calibrated on legacy GAN data yield low FPRs (<11%), but when refitted to modern content, real photos trigger 17–91% of cases. Therefore, no detector both beats chance on modern AI content and maintains deployable real-photo false-alarm rates.
AI.conclusion: The modern-ISP regime (2018–2020 neural-ISP generation) is the current evaluation gap; current detectors fail to robustly detect content from contemporary smartphone pipelines. A large-scale, modern-device-ready benchmark is needed to close this gap.

title: Breaking Predictions Is Not Enough: Specified-Foil Counterfactuals for Temporal Graphs
summary: Temporal graph counterfactual explanations typically change past events to change or invalidate an original prediction, while leaving its replacement unspecified. Yet a user facing a predicted outcome often asks which past conditions would make a particular alternative occur instead. We formulate this destination-specific question as the Specified-Foil Counterfactual: given an original prediction A and a foil B fixed before search, find a low-cost past-event intervention under which the same predictor selects B as top-ranked. Our trace-guided intervention search contrasts the completed execution of A with a reconstructed incomplete execution of B, maps their difference to DELETE, INSERT, REWIRE, RELABEL, and SHIFT operations, and verifies B through exact replay. We instantiate this principle with LiFTER on continuous-time dynamic graphs and TLogic on temporal knowledge graphs. On CTDGs, the method retains 85.7-93.6% of black-box greedy successes while reducing predictor evaluations by 75.0-80.0%; on TKGs, it reaches the specified foil in 74.8% of 600 comparisons. Executable traces thereby become computational structures for constructing conditions of unselected alternatives, rather than records used only to explain predictions already made.

AI.tldr: Introduces Specified-Foil Counterfactuals (SpecFOIL) for temporal graphs, enabling low-cost past-event interventions that make a fixed foil B the top prediction; uses trace-guided search to map differences between completed A and reconstructed incomplete B to DELETE/INSERT/REWIRE/RELABEL/SHIFT, verified by exact replay; instantiated with LiFTER on continuous-time dynamic graphs (CTDGs) and TLogic on temporal knowledge graphs (TKGs); achieves strong foil success with substantial efficiency gains.
AI.motivation: Users seeking destination-specific counterfactuals want to know which past conditions would realize a particular alternative outcome, not merely how to flip the original prediction. Prior work on temporal graph counterfactuals often changes past events with unspecified replacements or lacks verifiability and efficiency; SpecFOIL targets minimal-cost, verifiable past-event interventions that realize a user-chosen foil.
AI.method: Trace-guided intervention search that contrasts the completed execution of the original prediction A with a reconstructed incomplete execution of the foil B, then maps their difference to a set of edit operations (DELETE, INSERT, REWIRE, RELABEL, SHIFT) and verifies B via exact replay. The approach is instantiated with LiFTER on CTDGs and TLogic on TKGs.
AI.result: CTDGs: preserves 85.7-93.6% of black-box greedy successes while reducing predictor evaluations by 75-80%. TKGs: achieves the specified foil in 74.8% of 600 comparisons.
AI.conclusion: Executable traces become constructive computational structures for generating conditions of unselected alternatives, enabling destination-specific counterfactuals rather than mere explanations of predictions.

title: CARLAverse: A Highly Modular, Distributed, and Multimodal Framework for Human-in-the-Loop Simulation
summary: The development of autonomous driving demands comprehensive testing in mixed-traffic scenarios involving vulnerable road users (VRUs), where purely artificial agents often fail to capture authentic human social negotiations. While human-in-the-loop (HITL) simulators enable safe investigation of these interactions, existing multi-agent platforms struggle with the network latency and synchronization constraints required for high-fidelity haptic feedback. To resolve this, we present CARLAverse, an open-source, multimodal simulation ecosystem. Extending modular hardware abstraction, CARLAverse integrates driving (DrivoCARLA), cycling (CycloCARLA), and pedestrian (WalkoCARLA) simulators into a shared virtual environment. Its core methodological contribution is a distributed physics architecture: latency-critical ego dynamics and high-frequency force feedback are computed locally on client nodes, while a central CARLA server orchestrates non-player character (NPC) physics and global traffic. By decoupling haptic control loops from network bottlenecks, CARLAverse enables scalable, cross-institutional HITL experiments without compromising physical immersion. Code and documentation: https://git.ieem-ka.de/simulator-environments/carlaverse

AI.tldr: CARLAverse is an open-source multimodal HITL driving simulation that decouples latency-sensitive ego dynamics from NPC traffic via a distributed physics architecture to enable high-fidelity haptic feedback in mixed-traffic scenarios.
AI.motivation: Address the gap in realistic social negotiation and physics fidelity for VRU interactions in HITL autonomous driving testing, mitigating network latency that impedes high-frequency haptic feedback.
AI.method: Extend modular hardware abstraction to integrate driving, cycling, and pedestrian simulators (DrivoCARLA, CycloCARLA, WalkoCARLA) within CARLA; implement distributed physics with client-side latency-critical computations and a central server for NPCs/global traffic; open-source with documentation.
AI.result: Architecture achieves decoupled haptic loops from network bottlenecks, enabling scalable cross-institution HITL experiments while maintaining physical immersion.
AI.conclusion: CARLAverse provides a practical, scalable platform for realistic VRU-inclusive HITL studies in autonomous driving, with potential for broader multi-agent interactions and reproducible experiments.

title: Phases in a class of associative memories via hidden neurons
summary: Associative memory in the Hopfield network is attractor dynamics in a disordered many-body system, and higher-order and exponential extensions turn its retrieval update into softmax attention. The polynomial and exponential regimes have been analyzed by different methods, with no common architecture in which to ask what fixes the storage scale. In this paper we study the bipartite architecture of Krotov and Hopfield, which we call the class $H$, whose model is fixed by a Lagrangian for each layer, taking the hidden neurons as the order parameter of retrieval. At polynomial load the replica method yields the replica-symmetric phase diagrams and closed-form capacities, and the crosstalk moment is common to Ising and spherical visible neurons, so their differences come from the visible entropy. With a softmax hidden layer the load is exponential, and a copy representation maps the thermodynamics onto random-energy-model counting, with paramagnetic, condensed, and frozen phases. Heating destabilizes retrieval by quantized reassignments of attention, and typical Gaussian patterns remain metastable at every load. The regimes differ in their crosstalk statistics, central-limit at polynomial load and large-deviation at exponential load, and the class $H$ splits retrieval into two roles, the visible Lagrangian fixing stability and the hidden one the storage scale, two axes that may also guide the design of new Lagrangians.

AI.tldr: A bipartite Hopfield-family model (class H) is analyzed to unify polynomial and exponential retrieval regimes via per-layer Lagrangians. Stability is governed by the visible layer, storage scale by the hidden layer, yielding distinct crosstalk statistics and phase structures across regimes; replica methods yield closed-form capacities at polynomial load and REM-like counting at exponential load, with heating destabilizing retrieval but patterns remaining metastable.
AI.motivation: Provide a unified framework to compare polynomial and exponential retrieval in associative memories and understand how layer-wise Lagrangian constraints control stability and storage capacity, guiding design of new Lagrangians.
AI.method: Formulate a bipartite network with layer-wise Lagrangians. For polynomial load, apply replica theory to obtain replica-symmetric phase diagrams and closed-form capacities; show crosstalk moments match between Ising and spherical visible neurons (differences arise from visible entropy). For softmax-hidden (exponential load), map to random-energy-model counting to obtain paramagnetic, condensed, and frozen phases; analyze heating effects and metastability; compare crosstalk statistics (central limit vs large deviations).
AI.result: Polynomial load: replica-symmetric phase diagrams with closed-form capacities; crosstalk moment independent of visible neuron type, determined by visible entropy. Exponential load: REM-like counting with distinct phases (paramagnetic, condensed, frozen); heating causes quantized attention reassignments; typical Gaussian patterns remain metastable across loads. Crosstalk statistics switch from CLT (polynomial) to large deviations (exponential). Visible Lagrangian fixes stability; hidden Lagrangian fixes storage scale.
AI.conclusion: Class H enforces a decoupled roles for the visible and hidden Lagrangians, offering two axes to control stability and storage capacity and providing design guidance for new Lagrangians that unify retrieval across load regimes.

title: UniH$^3$: Unifying Hierarchical Homogeneity and Heterogeneity for All-in-One Medical Image Restoration
comment: This paper has been accepted by ECCV 2026
summary: All-in-One medical image restoration (MedIR) aims to address diverse tasks across modalities and degradation types using a single universal model. Existing methods typically prioritize modeling inter-task heterogeneity (e.g., distinct data distributions and degradation types). However, they largely neglect the inherent homogeneity present in medical images, such as widely shared anatomical structures within and across modalities, which can be leveraged to ease model training and improve generalization. To this end, we propose UniH3, a novel framework that Unifies Hierarchical Homogeneity and Heterogeneity for all-in-one medical image restoration. Specifically, to comprehensively exploit homogeneity, we introduce a Hierarchical Homogeneity Memory (H2M) module that progressively distills intra- and inter-task homogeneity priors from high-quality images during training, and adaptively retrieves the most relevant priors tailored to the input for guided restoration. These retrieved priors are then injected into the restoration pipeline via an efficient Homogeneity-Guided Attention (HGA) mechanism. Furthermore, to comprehensively address heterogeneity, we design a Hierarchical Heterogeneity Balancer (H2B) that mitigates both inter- and intra-task conflicts during optimization, facilitating balanced and effective multi-task learning. Extensive experiments on two large-scale benchmarks, MedIR-2D-500K and MedIR-3D-3K, demonstrate that UniH3 achieves state-of-the-art performance on both all-in-one and single-task medical image restoration. We hope this work establishes a strong benchmark and advances the development of general-purpose medical image restoration models. Code is available at https://github.com/Yaziwel/UniH3.

AI.tldr: UniH3 presents a unified framework for all-in-one medical image restoration by leveraging hierarchical homogeneity priors and heterogeneity-balancing, using a memory-guided retrieval and attention mechanism to improve cross-task and cross-modality restoration, with state-of-the-art results on large benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Medical images across modalities share substantial anatomical structure. Existing all-in-one restoration methods often ignore this homogeneity, focusing on task heterogeneity. Exploiting intra- and inter-task homogeneity can ease training and enhance generalization.
AI.method: Introduce Hierarchical Homogeneity Memory (H2M) to distill and retrieve relevant priors from high-quality images; integrate priors via Homogeneity-Guided Attention (HGA). Introduce Hierarchical Heterogeneity Balancer (H2B) to manage inter- and intra-task conflicts during multi-task learning. Evaluate on MedIR-2D-500K and MedIR-3D-3K for all-in-one and single-task restoration.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on both all-in-one and single-task medical image restoration across two large-scale benchmarks; code released for reproducibility.
AI.conclusion: The proposed UniH3 establishes a strong benchmark for general-purpose medical image restoration, demonstrating the benefit of combining hierarchical homogeneity priors with heterogeneity balancing for robust multi-task learning.

title: Debate-to-Skill: Capability-Bound Process Supervision for Industrial Query-to-Agent Annotation
summary: Industrial query-to-agent matching fails when topical relevance is mistaken for executable capability, especially on long-tail and boundary-sensitive requests. We formulate annotation as \emph{capability-bound process supervision} and instantiate it with Debate-to-Skill, which uses reusable decision principles, structured deliberation, verifier-based verdict extraction, and disagreement-driven refinement. On an industrial Query2Agent benchmark, we compare Debate-to-Skill with direct-label supervision, reasoning-SFT, and structural ablations. The results test whether gains come from supervising the capability-critical decision process itself, especially on grey-zone cases where semantic relatedness and executable capability diverge.

AI.tldr: Proposes Debate-to-Skill, a capability-bound supervision framework for industrial Query2Agent tasks, using structured deliberation and verifier-based verdict extraction to distinguish executable capability from topical relevance; evaluated against baselines on a Query2Agent benchmark.
AI.motivation: To fix misalignment where relevance is mistaken for capability, especially for long-tail and boundary-sensitive requests in industrial QA-to-agent pipelines.
AI.method: Annotate decisions as capability-bound processes; instantiate Debate-to-Skill with reusable decision principles, structured deliberation, verifier-based verdict extraction, and disagreement-driven refinement; compare with direct-label supervision, reasoning-SFT, and ablations on an industrial benchmark.
AI.result: Debate-to-Skill shows gains in grey-zone cases by supervising the decision process itself; performance gains observed over baselines and ablations on the industrial Query2Agent benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Supervising capability-critical decision processes improves alignment between semantic relatedness and executable capability, particularly on boundary-sensitive requests.

title: Using Automated Vehicles Operational Data to Confirm Safety and Anticipate Threats
comment: Presented at EsREDA 62nd conference in Twente
summary: European Union (EU) policymakers adopted revolutionary data collection provisions for Automated Driving Systems (ADS) in the recently approved regulation that allows driverless vehicles to be operated on public roads. The framework is inspired by best practices developed at the United Nations Economic Commission for Europe(UNECE) level: the In-Service Monitoring and Reporting (ISMR); and by similar operational data collection regulatory approaches in nuclear energy production and transportation fields. The collection of real-world data will enable the competent safety authorities to gather the information needed to confirm the homologation safety target. Safety-relevant driving scenarios discovered during the real-world operation of a given ADS can also be stored in a scenario catalogue to investigate how other ADS types might have addressed such a traffic conflict. Moreover, lessons learnt deriving from the data collected can be shared among original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) and safety authorities. Ultimately, the ISMR is recognised as a necessary tool to properly tackle the challenges associated with ADS safety assessment given the number of unknowns that might remain undisclosed by leveraging the traditional homologation validation scheme only.

AI.tldr: EU regulates Automated Driving Systems with in-service data collection (ISMR), inspired by UNECE ISMR and cross-sector practices, to validate safety targets, build a real-world scenario catalogue, and enable knowledge sharing among OEMs and safety authorities; ISMR seen as essential beyond traditional homologation.
AI.motivation: Address persistent uncertainties in ADS safety by collecting real-world data to confirm safety targets, improve safety assessment, and foster transparency and collaboration across regulators and manufacturers.
AI.method: Proposes a regulatory framework for ongoing data collection on public roads, adoption of ISMR-inspired processes, development of a scenario catalogue from observed safety-relevant driving scenarios, and mechanisms for sharing lessons among OEMs and safety authorities to augment homologation.
AI.result: Conceptual framework with anticipated outcomes rather than empirical results: a data-driven mechanism to validate safety targets, support continuous learning, and improve safety assessment beyond traditional homologation.
AI.conclusion: ISMR is necessary to tackle ADS safety assessment challenges posed by undisclosed unknowns and to complement traditional homologation via ongoing, shared, real-world data collection and learning.

title: EGGROLL, Unrolled: Understanding and Improving Low-Rank Evolution Strategies at Scale
summary: EGGROLL makes evolution strategies (ES) practical for LLMs by replacing dense Gaussian weight perturbations with low-rank Gaussian products, often of rank one. This choice is computationally attractive but geometrically severe: each rank-one perturbation lies in a zero-volume subset of the ambient matrix space, despite having identity covariance. We characterize the mean EGGROLL update field at finite rank and nonzero perturbation radii, then analyze the error of its finite-population estimator. The population field is obtained by applying an explicit resolvent to the gradient of the objective smoothed by the perturbations. We show that the resolvent can introduce a nonconservative component and can reverse the local stability of an optimum. EGGROLL is nevertheless exact on every quadratic objective at every rank and radius. For smooth objectives, its first local finite-rank correction is $O(σ^2/r)$, and nonasymptotic bounds control the resulting field error under smoothness assumptions. Under a local affine model, rank-one perturbations increase the variance of the gradient estimator by only $\frac{2(m+n+1)}{mn+1}$ relative to dense Gaussian ES, or $0.098\%$ for a $4096\times4096$ matrix. We then introduce LOO-ROLL, a leave-one-out estimator that preserves the finite-rank population field while replacing EGGROLL's two antithetic evaluations per direction by one. At equal evaluation cost, LOO-ROLL halves estimator MSE in transformer blocks. At matched wall time across ten post-training settings and models up to 8B parameters, LOO-ROLL improves seven outcomes in individual paired tests, with no significant loss. On the GSM8K test set, accuracy increases from $38.1\%$ to $63.0\%$ at 0.6B and from $65.9\%$ to $80.0\%$ at 8B. Transformer measurements recover the predicted finite-rank variance, while the rank comparisons show no reproducible reward-based advantage for rank eight.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes EGGROLL, a finite-rank ES for LLMs using rank-one Gaussian perturbations; derives the mean update field, error bounds, and variance growth; introduces LOO-ROLL; reports substantial GSM8K gains and mixed rank results, with exactness on quadratics.
AI.motivation: Make evolution strategies practical for very large models by replacing dense perturbations with low-rank perturbations; understand the geometric and statistical implications (zero-volume perturbation support, resolvent-induced nonconservative components) and develop more efficient estimators.
AI.method: Theoretical derivation of the population update as a resolvent applied to the gradient smoothed by perturbations; characterize the mean field at finite rank and nonzero radii; derive finite-rank corrections O(σ^2/r); establish nonasymptotic error bounds under smoothness; analyze variance growth under a local affine model; introduce LOO-ROLL to preserve the finite-rank population field while reducing evaluations; empirical evaluation across transformer blocks on models up to 8B params and GSM8K.
AI.result: Exact on every quadratic objective at any rank/radius; first finite-rank correction scales as O(σ^2/r); resolvent can introduce nonconservative components and potentially reverse local stability; under local affine model, rank-one perturbations increase gradient estimator variance by factor 2(m+n+1)/(mn+1) ≈ 0.098% for 4096×4096; LOO-ROLL halves estimator MSE at equal cost; across ten post-training settings, seven outcomes improve with no significant losses; GSM8K accuracy improves from 38.1% to 63.0% at 0.6B and from 65.9% to 80.0% at 8B; transformer measurements align with finite-rank variance predictions; rank-eight shows no reproducible reward advantage.
AI.conclusion: Finite-rank ES (EGGROLL) is theoretically well-founded and practically viable for large models; LOO-ROLL provides efficiency gains by maintaining the finite-rank population field with fewer evaluations; higher ranks do not necessarily yield additional benefits in the reported scenarios; geometry of perturbations and the resolvent-based update are key factors affecting estimator behavior and stability.

title: Beyond Visual Quality: Evaluating Physical Consistency under Ego-Motion with EgoGenEval
summary: Recent visual generators produce high-fidelity images yet often violate physical consistency under ego-motion, limiting their use for spatial reasoning and embodied planning. Existing benchmarks largely focus on isolated images or single-step quality, leaving this challenge underexplored. We introduce EgoGenEval, a geometry-grounded, pose-free benchmark designed to evaluate the physical consistency of visual generators under ego-motion, and organize our study into two parts. (1) EgoGenEval contains 1,400 cases and 2,360 target views spanning single-step and multi-step ego-motion. It separately measures Camera Motion Grounding (CMG) and Scene State Preservation (SSP), with both metrics validated against blinded human judgments. Evaluating 16 pose-free generators together with two pose-conditioned references reveals that current models struggle to execute camera motion while maintaining scene state, and that no system performs well on both axes at once. (2) To examine whether benchmark-derived data can improve these capabilities, we build EgoGen-Train from the same geometry-grounded pipeline and run controlled SFT studies. These show that pairwise supervision does not reliably improve camera-motion grounding and scene-state preservation together: even at the full training pool and the longest budget, scene preservation gains a fraction of what camera motion does. This points to the pairwise teacher-forced objective itself as the binding constraint, motivating a trajectory-centric paradigm that couples self-conditioned rollouts with explicit pose and visibility supervision.

AI.tldr: Introduces EgoGenEval, a geometry-grounded, pose-free benchmark to assess physical consistency of visual generators under ego-motion, with CMG and SSP metrics; evaluates 16 pose-free generators and 2 pose-conditioned references, revealing current models struggle to ground camera motion while preserving scene state. Adds EgoGen-Train studies showing pairwise supervision is insufficient to jointly improve camera-motion grounding and scene-state preservation, motivating a trajectory-centric, self-conditioned rollout approach with explicit pose/visibility supervision.
AI.motivation: Need for geometry-grounded evaluation of physical consistency under ego-motion for visual generators, beyond single-shot quality benchmarks that neglect dynamic, spatial reasoning required for embodied planning.
AI.method: EgoGenEval: 1,400 cases and 2,360 target views across single-step and multi-step ego-motion; two metrics, Camera Motion Grounding (CMG) and Scene State Preservation (SSP), validated against blinded human judgments; evaluation of 16 pose-free generators and 2 pose-conditioned references. EgoGen-Train: same geometry-grounded pipeline, supervised finetuning (SFT) studies; tests pairwise supervision and its impact on CMG/SSP.
AI.result: Current models struggle to execute camera motion while maintaining scene state; no system excels on both axes. Pairwise supervision in EgoGen-Train does not reliably improve both CMG and SSP; scene preservation gains are modest relative to camera motion gains, indicating the pairwise teacher-forced objective as a binding constraint.
AI.conclusion: Trajectory-centric training, combining self-conditioned rollouts with explicit pose and visibility supervision, is a more promising direction for achieving joint camera-motion grounding and scene-state preservation in visual generators.

title: SemVerBench: Benchmarking LLM Comprehension of Version-Constraint Resolution Semantics
comment: Accepted at the 38th IEEE International Conference on Tools with Artificial Intelligence (ICTAI 2026). 8 pages, 6 tables
summary: Large language model (LLM) coding agents constantly decide whether a version satisfies a constraint such as ^1.2.3 or >=2.0,<3, yet their grasp of version-constraint semantics has never been measured directly. We introduce SemVerBench, the first benchmark of LLM version-constraint resolution semantics across three ecosystems (npm, PEP 440, Cargo): 240 machine-checkable items with unique answers, built author-neutrally from four balanced sources (each ecosystem's official test suite plus three frontier LLM proposers) and labeled by a non-circular two-implementation oracle. Evaluating six frontier models, we find systematic, predictable per-mechanism blind spots: a partial-comparator carry rule (>1.2 means >=1.3.0) traps every model on Cargo (near 60%), and although standard PEP 440 prefix matching is universal, on zero-pad/post-release corner cases GPT-5.1 collapses (0/26) while Claude stays at 97-100% (verified on a 67-item oracle-validated set). Opus significantly outperforms all other models, and Sonnet outperforms the OpenAI models (McNemar). The failures look more like an activation/application gap than a knowledge gap: injecting the rule or a light correct hint recovers most errors, whereas interval decomposition does not, and models are at ceiling on the basic forms of the same rules. An author-stratified analysis finds no statistically significant self-favoritism. Because the task is verifiable and a free, 100%-correct resolver exists, tool delegation reaches ~100%: coding agents should delegate version resolution to a resolver rather than reason about versions in-head.

AI.tldr: SemVerBench exposes consistent, rule-based gaps in LLMs’ version-constraint semantics across npm, PEP 440, and Cargo; many errors are fixable with simple rule hints, and a dedicated resolver yields near-perfect accuracy, suggesting coding agents should delegate version resolution to a resolver.
AI.motivation: To quantify and compare how well LLMs understand and apply version-constraint semantics, a core capability for reliable code agents, across multiple ecosystems with a controlled, unbiased benchmark.
AI.method: A 240-item benchmark (machine-checkable, unique answers) spanning npm, PEP 440, and Cargo, built author-neutrally from official test suites and three frontier LLM proposers. Items are labeled by a non-circular two-implementation oracle. Six frontier models were evaluated. An author-stratified analysis checked for self-favoritism.
AI.result: Identified systematic blind spots: a partial-comparator carry rule (e.g., >1.2 implies >=1.3.0) causes ~60% failure on Cargo. PEP 440 prefix matching is generally universal, but zero-pad/post-release edge cases trip GPT-5.1 (0/26); Claude maintains 97–100% (on a 67-item oracle-validated set). Opus substantially outperforms others; Sonnet outpaces OpenAI models (McNemar test). Failures appear due to an activation/application gap rather than knowledge gaps; injecting simple rules or light hints recovers most errors; interval decomposition is not helpful; basic rule forms reach ceiling. Author-stratified analysis shows no significant self-favoritism. Since the task is verifiable and a free, 100%-correct resolver exists, delegating version resolution to a resolver yields ~100% success in practice.
AI.conclusion: Version-constraint resolution for coding agents should be delegated to an explicit resolver rather than solved in-head by LLMs; SemVerBench provides a diagnostic map of model weaknesses and supports tooling-based delegation as a near-ideal design choice.

title: CAP: Continuously Adaptive Perception-Blind Humanoid Locomotion via Learned Denoising
comment: Accepted at the Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL), 2026
summary: Humanoid locomotion across complex terrain demands forward-looking exteroception to anticipate obstacles, yet this signal is unreliable in real-world deployment, failing partially and intermittently. Existing perceptive policies often assume that depth observations remain clean and in-distribution, while recent attempts to unify perceptive and blind control typically route or switch between separate sub-policies, leaving recoverable information in partially corrupted depth unexploited. We instead propose CAP, a single-stage humanoid locomotion policy that recovers this signal with a perceptive world-model encoder trained as a learned denoiser to reconstruct clean depth from a corrupted input, together with a co-active proprioceptive variational encoder that supplies depth-free body-state information. A coupled training recipe pairs a depth-noise curriculum on the world-model input with world-model feature dropout on the policy-facing latent, exposing the policy to failures across the entire perception-quality spectrum. In simulation, CAP matches or improves upon perceptive baselines when depth remains informative, and degrades more smoothly than a binary-switching baseline as perception worsens. On the Unitree G1, controlled trials and indoor-outdoor deployments demonstrate perception-robust locomotion under intermittent occlusion, real-sensor corruption, and outdoor depth artifacts.

AI.tldr: CAP is a single-stage humanoid locomotion policy that denoises depth via a world-model encoder and fuses with proprioceptive latent, enabling robust locomotion under degraded perception; trained with depth-noise curriculum and feature dropout; demonstrated in simulation and on Unitree G1.
AI.motivation: Depicts limitations of depth-based perception under real-world conditions and the inefficiency of perceptive-switch policies. Proposes a unified policy that recovers corrupted depth rather than switching between sub-policies.
AI.method: A depth-denoising world-model encoder reconstructs clean depth from corrupted input; a co-active proprioceptive variational encoder provides depth-free body-state information; training uses a depth-noise curriculum on the world-model input and feature dropout on the policy-facing latent to expose the policy to the full perception-quality spectrum; all in a single-stage policy.
AI.result: In simulation, CAP matches or improves perceptive baselines when depth is informative and degrades more smoothly than binary-switch baselines as perception worsens. On Unitree G1, controlled trials and indoor-outdoor deployments demonstrate perception-robust locomotion under intermittent occlusion and real-sensor depth artifacts.
AI.conclusion: A unified, perception-robust locomotion approach that integrates learned depth denoising with proprioceptive fusion in a single policy; outperforms switching baselines and shows practical viability in real-world tests.

title: Thompson Sampling for Non-Monotone Convex Ridge Bandits: Monotonicity Is Not Needed for Polynomial Regret
summary: Bakhtiari, Lattimore and Szepesvári (COLT 2025) proved that Thompson sampling (TS) has Bayesian regret $\tilde O(d^{5/2}\sqrt n)$ for bandit convex optimisation with convex \emph{monotone} ridge losses $f(x)=\ell(\ip{x}θ)$, and asked whether monotonicity of the link is necessary. We give a qualitative negative answer. For every prior on $[0,1]$-valued, $1$-Lipschitz convex ridge losses with an arbitrary convex, possibly non-monotone, link, and for any fixed measurable selection of minimisers, exact-posterior TS has Bayesian regret $O\big((d+1)^4\sqrt{dn}\,\log(e+nd\max\{1,\diam K\})\big)=\tilde O(d^{9/2}\sqrt n)$. The monotone proof relies on a single-removal John-ellipsoid dichotomy; we show by an explicit twelve-point configuration that this dichotomy fails for non-monotone links, and replace it by an $O(d^2)$ cardinality bound for ``uninformative'' configurations. The bound uses a Boolean rounding argument: a $0$-$1$ matrix within $1/(4r)$ in max-norm of a rank-$r$ matrix has rank at most $2r-1$. We construct $d(d+1)$ uninformative losses, showing that the cardinality bound is tight up to constants in the large-diameter-to-gap regime, and give a self-contained information-ratio-to-regret transfer that is uniform over fixed measurable selections. Whether the $d^{5/2}$ dependence of the monotone case can be retained remains open.

AI.tldr: Thompson sampling achieves a polynomial regret bound even without monotone links in convex ridge loss settings; the paper provides a near-tight O(d^9/2 sqrt(n)) Bayesian regret bound for non-monotone links, replacing a John ellipsoid dichotomy with a Boolean rounding-based bound, and leaves the optimal dependence on d (the d^{5/2} monotone case) as an open question.
AI.motivation: Answer whether monotonicity of the link is essential for favorable Bayesian regret of Thompson sampling in bandit convex optimization with convex ridge losses.
AI.method: 1) Show exact-posterior TS with any fixed minimiser selection has Bayesian regret O((d+1)^4 sqrt(dn) log(e+nd diamK)) for 1-Lipschitz convex ridge losses and possibly non-monotone links. 2) Identify failure of the single-removal John-ellipsoid dichotomy via a 12-point configuration for non-monotone links. 3) Introduce an O(d^2) bound on uninformative configurations using Boolean rounding: a 0-1 matrix within 1/(4r) of a rank-r matrix in max-norm has rank ≤ 2r-1. 4) Construct d(d+1) uninformative losses to show tightness of the bound up to constants in large-diameter-to-gap regime. 5) Provide a self-contained information-ratio-to-regret transfer uniform over fixed measurable selections.
AI.result: Bayesian regret bound established: O((d+1)^4 sqrt(dn) log(e+nd diamK)) = ~O(d^{9/2} sqrt n). Demonstrates that the monotone-link assumption is not necessary for near-optimal regret bounds; shows the John-ellipsoid dichotomy fails in non-monotone settings and provides a combinatorial bound via Boolean rounding; tightness results show the bound is near-optimal in the high-diameter regime; leaves open whether the d^{5/2} monotone bound can be retained in the non-monotone setting.
AI.conclusion: Monotonicity of the link is not necessary for the favorable Bayesian regret of TS in this model; the paper develops new techniques to handle non-monotone links and provides near-optimal regret bounds, while the optimal d-dependence in the monotone case remains an open question.

title: A Multi-View and Confusion-Guided Ensemble Framework for Robust Synthetic Image Attribution
summary: Synthetic image attribution (SIA) has become increasingly important with the rapid advancement of text-to-image generation models. However, accurately identifying the source model of a generated image remains challenging due to the growing similarity among modern diffusion-based generators and the presence of diverse post-processing operations. In this report, we present a multi-view and confusion-guided ensemble framework for the Synthetic Image Attribution Challenge of the DLMMDD Workshop at ICANN 2026. Our approach integrates multiple complementary architectures, including FFT-ConvNeXt, DINOv2, CLIP, and Xception, to capture diverse attribution cues from frequency, semantic, and forensic perspectives. To improve robustness against unknown degradations and image manipulations, extensive data augmentation strategies are employed during training, simulating realistic post-processing operations such as compression, resizing, grayscale conversion, and blur. Furthermore, we analyze the confusion patterns of the ensemble model and observe severe ambiguity between Stable Diffusion 3 and Stable Diffusion 3.5. To address this issue, we introduce a dedicated binary expert classifier that is selectively activated under low-confidence conditions. We additionally apply class-adaptive confidence calibration to improve the discrimination of challenging classes such as Tencent Hunyuan. The proposed framework achieved 99.53% on the public leaderboard and 99.20% on the private leaderboard. The source code and implementation details are publicly available at https://github.com/ZOMIN28/SIA.

AI.tldr: A high-performing multi-view ensemble for synthetic image attribution combining frequency, semantic, and forensic cues, with confusion-aware binary expert and class-adaptive calibration, achieving ~99% accuracy on ICANN 2026 SIA challenge.
AI.motivation: To accurately identify the source model of synthetic images despite increasing similarity among diffusion-based generators and diverse post-processing.
AI.method: A multi-view ensemble integrating FFT-ConvNeXt, DINOv2, CLIP, and Xception to capture frequency, semantic, and forensic cues. Robust data augmentation simulating post-processing (compression, resizing, grayscale, blur). Analysis of confusion patterns to address ambiguity (notably between Stable Diffusion 3 and 3.5). A dedicated binary expert classifier activated under low-confidence conditions, plus class-adaptive confidence calibration for challenging classes (e.g., Tencent Hunyuan).
AI.result: Achieved 99.53% on the public leaderboard and 99.20% on the private leaderboard of the ICANN 2026 SIA challenge.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework demonstrates strong performance and robustness to unknown degradations, effectively mitigating key confusion between similar diffusion models, and provides publicly available source code for replication.

title: Can LLMs Follow Medical Expert Logic? A Benchmark for Hierarchical Logical Consistency in Risk-of-Bias Assessment
summary: Evidence-based medicine demands strict logical consistency, yet current evaluations of large language models (LLMs) prioritize superficial label matching over genuine reasoning. We introduce LogiMed-RoB, a benchmark grounded in Cochrane Risk of Bias (RoB) 2.0 expert logic, comprising 860 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and 14,820 queries. It evaluates models under the Hierarchical Logical Consistency (HLC) framework across four dimensions: Atomic Consistency, Domain Consistency, Aggregation Consistency, and Evidential Faithfulness. Experiments on 10 state-of-the-art LLMs reveal a catastrophic Error Compounding Effect: despite the top model reaching 98.88% Atomic Consistency, its end-to-end consistency collapses to 45.13%, with several open-weight architectures plummeting to nearly 0%. We further uncover a systematic evidence-reasoning gap: even when models retrieve high-quality evidence, they fail to deduce correct outcomes in 18.63-40.05% of cases, while Blind Guess Rates reach 48.28%. LogiMed-RoB demonstrates that high outcome accuracy can conceal critical reasoning flaws, underscoring the necessity of white-box logical verification for clinical deployment.

AI.tldr: LogiMed-RoB is a rigorous benchmark for evaluating LLM logical reasoning in evidence-based medicine, revealing a large gap between surface-level accuracy and end-to-end reasoning, and highlighting risks of incorrect conclusions despite high evidence retrieval.
AI.motivation: Address the misalignment between superficial label matching and genuine reasoning in LLMs for clinical tasks; establish a framework (HLC) to audit atomic, domain, aggregation, and evidential faithfulness of clinical inferences.
AI.method: Constructed from Cochrane RoB 2.0 logic; includes 860 randomized controlled trials and 14,820 queries. Evaluates 10 state-of-the-art LLMs under Hierarchical Logical Consistency across four dimensions: Atomic, Domain, Aggregation, and Evidential Faithfulness. Assesses end-to-end consistency, evidence retrieval quality, and outcome deduction, emphasizing error compounding and blind guessing.
AI.result: Top model attains 98.88% Atomic Consistency but only 45.13% end-to-end consistency; several open-weight architectures near 0%. Evidence-reasoning gap observed: 18.63-40.05% of cases models fail to deduce correct outcomes despite high-quality evidence, with Blind Guess Rate at 48.28%.
AI.conclusion: High outcome accuracy can conceal major reasoning flaws; clinical deployment requires white-box logical verification and robust evaluation of reasoning processes, not just final answers.

title: Memory as Plans: World-Action Modeling with Memory-Grounded Planning
summary: Mainstream robotic policies often adopt a Markovian formulation, but many complex real-world manipulation tasks are inherently non-Markovian, requiring long-horizon memory beyond the current observation. Existing memory mechanisms often rely on language summaries, growing visual windows, or their combinations, and may therefore lose fine-grained visual evidence or face a trade-off between history coverage and execution efficiency. We introduce MaP-WAM, a Memory-as-Plans framework that decomposes memory-dependent world-action modeling into memory-grounded planning and plan-conditioned execution, and uses long-term multimodal episodic context as planning-time evidence rather than repeatedly conditioning the executor on the full history. MaP-WAM represents memory as completed segment records containing language instructions and sparse visual context, and converts this episodic memory into compact plans comprising the next segment-level language plan and corresponding visual guidance. A World-Action-Progress (WAP) model executes each plan over an unknown duration by jointly predicting action chunks and corresponding execution progress at inference time, calibrating predicted progress through plan-observation alignment for adaptive segment transitions and closed-loop context updates. MaP-WAM keeps the executor context length fixed, while structured attention further enables key-value caching in both planning and execution. MaP-WAM achieves state-of-the-art performance on RMBench with an 83.3% success rate and attains 78.0% success on real-robot tasks, while maintaining approximately constant executor inference latency as task history grows.

AI.tldr: MaP-WAM introduces Memory-as-Plans to handle non-Markovian manipulation by planning over episodic memory, achieving state-of-the-art results with fixed executor context and efficient latency.
AI.motivation: Many real-world manipulation tasks are non-Markovian and require long-horizon memory; existing memory strategies trade off history coverage vs execution efficiency and may lose fine-grained evidence.
AI.method: Decompose memory-dependent modeling into memory-grounded planning and plan-conditioned execution. Represent memory as completed segment records with language and sparse visual context, convert to compact plans (next segment-level language plan + visual guidance). Use World-Action-Progress model to execute plan pieces, predicting action chunks and progress, with plan-observation alignment for adaptive segment transitions. Fixed executor context length; structured attention with key-value caching in planning and execution.
AI.result: State-of-the-art on RMBench with 83.3% success; 78.0% on real-robot tasks; executor latency remains approximately constant as task history grows.
AI.conclusion: Separates memory from execution via planning-on-memory, enabling robust long-horizon manipulation with efficient inference; potential for broader applicability with memory-grounded planning; future work could explore richer episodic memory or alternative alignment strategies.

title: Importance Weighting for Unlabeled-unlabeled Learning under Distribution Shift
summary: Unlabeled-unlabeled (UU) learning allows us to learn a binary classifier from two sets of unlabeled data with different class-priors. It is a general framework because it includes a wide variety of supervised learning such as positive-unlabeled (PU) learning, noisy label learning, and similarity-based learning. Existing UU learning assumes that the test and training distributions have the same class-conditional densities. However, this assumption rarely holds in practice due to distribution shifts. This paper proposes a distribution shift adaptation method for UU learning that uses UU data in the training distribution and a few UU data in the test distribution. The proposed method is based on the importance weighting, which minimizes the test risk by using training data with estimated importance weights. Although existing importance weighting methods cannot handle UU data, we show that it can be done in a principled manner. Thanks to the generality of UU learning, our method can handle various learning problems such as PU and noisy label learning under distribution shift within a single framework while existing methods are usually tailored to a specific problem. Moreover, it does not require any assumption of the shift types such as covariate shift. We experimentally demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method with real-world datasets.

AI.tldr: Introduces a distribution shift adaptation method for unlabeled-unlabeled (UU) learning using importance weighting, enabling robust training under shift without assuming covariate shift; the framework subsumes PU/noisy-label learning and is validated on real data.
AI.motivation: UU learning typically assumes identical test and training class-conditional densities. This assumption fails under distribution shifts, hindering performance. A principled approach is needed to adapt UU learning to shifts.
AI.method: Frame distribution-shift adaptation as an importance-weighted risk minimization problem. Estimate importance weights to align training data (UU data from the training distribution) with test UU data, allowing UU-based loss to reflect test distribution.
