title: Reification as a Transferable Vocabulary: Zero-Shot Link Prediction with Vanilla GNNs
summary: Knowledge graph foundation models such as ULTRA achieve zero-shot link prediction on unseen graphs through dedicated architectures that hard-code a transfer mechanism. In this work we move that mechanism out of the architecture and into the representation, by \emph{reifying} the input graph: every fact becomes a node, connected to its subject, object, and relation type through a fixed vocabulary of six meta-relations, with relation types as anonymous shared nodes rather than model parameters. On this representation, five textbook GNNs (GAT, GINE with sum and with mean+max aggregation, GraphSAGE, R-GCN), each trained on a single knowledge graph of 4,245 triples for 30 minutes on one NVIDIA A100, transfer zero-shot to 40 inductive link-prediction benchmarks. The best of them, an off-the-shelf GAT, matches ULTRA, a dedicated foundation model pretrained on three graphs, across ULTRA's own evaluation suite. The same fixed vocabulary extends to relational databases, a row becoming an entity and a foreign-key column a relation type; a preliminary probe on two unseen databases, with no cell values, schema text or in-context labels, shows a model of this family pretrained on three knowledge graphs ranking foreign-key targets far above random-initialization and degree controls. We release the code, the checkpoints, and the evaluation pipeline for all 40 benchmarks.

AI.tldr: Graph reification: turn facts into nodes connected by six meta-relations, enabling standard GNNs to transfer zero-shot to unseen graphs; best GAT matches ULTRA on its own suite; extends to relational databases; code and data released.
AI.motivation: Reduce reliance on architecture-specific transfer mechanisms by bringing transfer into the representation. Demonstrate that simple, well-known GNNs can generalize across unseen graphs when the input is reified as a fixed-structure heterogeneous graph.
AI.method: Reify each factual triple as a node and connect to subject, object, and relation type via a fixed vocabulary of six meta-relations; treat relation types as anonymous shared nodes; train five textbook GNNs (GAT, GINE with sum, GINE with mean+max, GraphSAGE, R-GCN) on a single KG with 4,245 triples for 30 minutes on an NVIDIA A100; evaluate zero-shot on 40 inductive link-prediction benchmarks; extend approach to relational databases via a similar reification (rows as entities, foreign-key columns as relation types) with two unseen databases in a preliminary probe; pretrained on three knowledge graphs; compare to ULTRA.
AI.result: The approach yields zero-shot transfer to 40 inductive benchmarks for several GNNs; the best single model (off-the-shelf GAT) matches ULTRA on ULTRA’s evaluation suite; preliminary database experiments show the representation generalizes to foreign-key prediction; authors release code, checkpoints, and evaluation pipeline.
AI.conclusion: Reifying input graphs into a fixed, small set of meta-relations allows standard GNNs to achieve strong zero-shot transfer without architecture-level transfer mechanisms, with potential applicability to relational databases; enables reproducibility through open-source release.

title: Pre- and Post-Treatment Brain Metastases Segmentation Using nnU-Net with Post-Processing for BraTS 2026
summary: Brain metastases exhibit high inter-lesion variability in size, enhancement pattern, and post-treatment appearance, making volumetric segmentation of both pre- and post-treatment cases the central challenge of the BraTS 2026 Task 1 (Brain Metastases). We build a pragmatic pipeline on a 5-fold nnU-Net ResEnc-L ensemble, in which each fold is trained independently for 1,000 epochs with the standard Dice + cross-entropy loss on 1,296 four-modality training cases. This ensemble is followed by a rule-based post-processing cascade tuned for the lesion-wise Dice similarity coefficient (LW-DSC), a detection-oriented metric that behaves very differently from the traditional global Dice. The final pipeline reaches an LW-DSC of 0.733 / 0.751 / 0.713 / 0.549 on the enhancing tumour (ET), tumour core (TC), whole tumour (WT), and resection cavity (RC) sub-regions on the official validation leaderboard. Rather than trusting these leaderboard gains, we audit every post-processing stage with a five-fold out-of-fold (OOF) analysis with no model-training leakage over all 1,296 training cases, scored with the official BraTS evaluation code (BraTS_evaluation): it confirms two stages as robust, per-fold-consistent improvements while the third improves only the leaderboard and does not reproduce out-of-fold. We further provide a mechanistic analysis of the LW-DSC metric that explains why recall-recovering post-processing carries low risk whereas component deletion does not, and we report thirteen negative results spanning loss engineering, alternative backbones, and inference-time settings, several of which run counter to widely held intuitions. Source code is released under Apache-2.0 at https://github.com/hornbeamliu/brats2026-met.

AI.tldr: A practical ensemble-based pipeline for BraTS 2026 Task 1 Brain Metastases using a 5-fold nnU-Net ResEnc-L with a rule-based, LW-DSC-tuned post-processing cascade; validated by five-fold out-of-fold audit; notable robust stages, several negative results, and public Apache-2.0 code release.
AI.motivation: Tackle high inter-lesion variability and post-treatment appearance in brain metastases by combining a strong multi-fold segmentation model with lesion-centric, post-processing optimization guided by LW-DSC, and validate reliability with strict OOF auditing.
AI.method: Train a 5-fold nnU-Net ResEnc-L ensemble on 1,296 four-modality training cases for 1,000 epochs per fold using Dice+cross-entropy. Apply a rule-based post-processing cascade optimized for the lesion-wise Dice (LW-DSC). Evaluate on official BraTS validation, reporting ET/TC/WT/RC LW-DSC; perform five-fold out-of-fold analysis with no training leakage; analyze LW-DSC behavior; report 13 negative results; release source code under Apache-2.0.
AI.result: LW-DSC scores on ET/TC/WT/RC: 0.733 / 0.751 / 0.713 / 0.549 on the validation leaderboard. Two post-processing stages show per-fold robust improvements in OOF; a third stage improves only leaderboard scores and not OOF. Mechanistic LW-DSC analysis explains recall-recovery vs. component deletion risks. Thirteen negative results across loss engineering, backbones, and inference settings. Source code released (Apache-2.0).
AI.conclusion: The work emphasizes rigorous validation of post-processing through out-of-fold auditing, demonstrates the reliability of recall-enhancing steps over riskier deletions under LW-DSC, and contributes reproducible results and public code for community adoption, while noting limitations in RC performance and certain post-processing stages.

title: LLMs as Post-hoc Auditors of Physiological Plausibility in Symbolic Regression: A Clinician-Evaluated Case Study
summary: Genetic Programming and its variants, such as grammatical evolution, are widely used in Symbolic Regression to derive mathematical expressions from multivariate data. In addition to predictive accuracy, models are appreciated for their potential to provide interpretability, offering explicit equations that relate input variables to outcomes. However, achieving interpretability and plausibility remains challenging, as evolved models may be complex or scientifically inconsistent. In this study, we explore whether Large Language Models, can assist in improving the explainability of Symbolic Regression models generated by evolutionary computation methods. Building upon our previous work on estimating body fat percentage using grammar-based Genetic Programming , we investigate the use of LLMs as post-processing tools to analyze and rank evolved expressions according to their interpretability and medical plausibility. Four symbolic expressions are analysed by three LLMs over three repeated runs, and the resulting interpretations and rankings are assessed by a panel of three clinicians. Across the three LLMs, comparative model-ranking outputs received more favorable clinician assessments than isolated term-level interpretations. However, the LLMs also produced physiologically and mathematically questionable explanations, indicating that they are better suited to comparative auditing under expert oversight than to autonomous validation.\blfootnote{The present work is an extended version of a paper submitted into a journal.

AI.tldr: LLMs can aid post-hoc auditing of symbolic regression expressions by ranking and interpreting them for interpretability and medical plausibility, but they may generate physiologically or mathematically questionable explanations; best used for comparative auditing under expert oversight rather than autonomous validation.
AI.motivation: Address the interpretability and plausibility gap in grammar-based symbolic regression (GP/SR) by leveraging large language models to analyze and rank evolved expressions for interpretability and medical plausibility; extend prior work on body fat estimation with grammar-based GP.
AI.method: Four evolved symbolic expressions (from grammar-based GP) were analyzed by three different LLMs across three repeated runs. A panel of three clinicians assessed both term-level interpretations and model rankings produced by the LLMs, focusing on interpretability and medical plausibility.
AI.result: LLM-derived comparative model rankings were judged more favorable by clinicians than isolated term-level explanations across the three LLMs. However, LLMs also produced explanations that were physiologically and mathematically questionable, indicating limitations for autonomous validation and suggesting LLMs are better suited for comparative auditing with expert oversight.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can aid in the post-hoc auditing of SR models to improve explainability through comparative analysis, but they should not be trusted for autonomous validation; expert oversight is essential. This work extends prior body fat estimation GP studies and emphasizes the potential and limits of LLM-assisted interpretability in symbolic regression.

title: Local Robustness Quantification for Naive Bayes Classifiers and Generative Forests: a General Approach
summary: We provide methods for calculating the robustness of the predictions of two types of generative classifiers whose underlying distribution is a Probabilistic Graphical Model (PGM): naive Bayes classifiers and generative forests (a probabilistic extension of random forests). Following the paradigm of robustness quantification, we define the robustness of a prediction as the extent to which the distribution of the classifier can be perturbed without changing this prediction. We consider perturbations obtained by varying the local models of the PGMs within general neighborhoods and focus in particular on epsilon-contamination, total variation distance and chi-squared divergence balls. We test our methods on benchmark datasets, demonstrate that the robustness value of a prediction serves as an indicator for its trustworthiness and compare our approach with other such indicators.

AI.tldr: A framework to quantify the prediction robustness of naive Bayes and generative forests under local distribution perturbations of their PGMs, using epsilon-contamination, total variation, and chi-squared divergence neighborhoods; robustness scores correlate with trustworthiness and are compared to other indicators on benchmark datasets.
AI.motivation: Quantify trustworthiness of generative classifier predictions by measuring how sensitive predictions are to local changes in the underlying probabilistic models.
AI.method: Define robustness as the maximum perturbation that does not change the predicted class. Perturb local models within specified neighborhoods (epsilon-contamination, TV distance, chi-squared divergence). Apply to naive Bayes and generative forests and compute per-prediction robustness values.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on benchmark data shows the robustness value is a useful indicator of prediction trustworthiness and is favorably compared to other indicators.
AI.conclusion: Provides a principled, neighborhood-based robustness framework for generative classifiers (NB and generative forests), enabling trustworthiness assessment and potential extensions to other PGMs.

title: FreeFlow: A Bias-free Hierarchical Transformer for Optical Flow Estimation
summary: Optical flow methods typically rely on task-specific inductive biases, such as correlation volumes, feature warping, and iterative refinement, among others, to reach high accuracy. While effective, such biases constrain the model to predefined heuristics, which can limit its expressivity and lead to more complex pipelines and additional computational cost. We present FreeFlow, a hierarchical transformer built without any flow-specific components, using instead a single feed-forward encoder--decoder. FreeFlow combines three attention variants: window attention for local processing, shifted-window attention for cross-window information exchange, and a global attention operating at a reduced resolution. The resulting architecture scales naturally with model capacity, enabling a consistent accuracy gain from small to large variants. Despite the absence of standard inductive biases, FreeFlow achieves state-of-the-art results on major benchmarks, including Sintel (0.68/1.48 EPE on Clean/Final), KITTI-2015 (3.23 Fl-all), and Spring (3.192 1px), while remaining memory efficient at 1080p inference.

AI.tldr: FreeFlow is a flow estimation model using a hierarchical transformer that abandons flow-specific inductive biases in favor of a single encoder–decoder and three attention variants (window, shifted-window, and global at reduced resolution); it achieves state-of-the-art accuracy with efficient 1080p inference.
AI.motivation: To remove hand-crafted, task-specific inductive biases in optical-flow models to improve expressivity, simplify design, and potentially reduce computational cost.
AI.method: A single feed-forward encoder–decoder that integrates three attention variants: window attention for local processing, shifted-window attention for cross-window information exchange, and global attention operating at reduced resolution; no flow-specific components.
AI.result: State-of-the-art performance on Sintel (0.68/1.48 EPE Clean/Final), KITTI-2015 (3.23 Fl-all), and Spring (3.192 1px); remains memory-efficient at 1080p inference.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates that a transformer-based architecture without flow-specific inductive biases can achieve competitive to state-of-the-art optical-flow accuracy with scalable capacity and efficiency.

title: Calibration-Aware Uncertainty Cascades for Efficient Heterogeneous Model Collaboration
comment: 13 pages, 6 figures, 6 tables, including appendix. Under review
summary: Heterogeneous model collaboration seeks to exploit the complementary strengths of different models to balance predictive performance and inference cost. Existing approaches typically rely either on trained routers, which tie routing decisions to a fixed task and model pool, or on raw-confidence cascades, whose thresholds lack consistent reliability semantics across heterogeneous models. Consequently, these approaches adapt poorly to changing model pools and deployment budgets. We propose Calibration-Aware Uncertainty Cascades (CAUC), a simple post-hoc framework that independently calibrates each model's confidence and selects deployment policies using validation data. The resulting calibrated confidence scores establish a common reliability scale for accepting an early prediction, invoking a stronger model, or selectively combining model outputs. This unified decision criterion decouples deployment policies from any particular model pool or operating budget. We further show theoretically that calibration gives confidence thresholds an explicit selective-risk interpretation, whereas uncalibrated scores offer no comparable reliability guarantee. Extensive experiments demonstrate that, across six language benchmarks, CAUC achieves an average relative accuracy improvement of 1.9% over strong-model-only inference while avoiding approximately 47% of strong-model calls. On image classification benchmarks, it maintains or improves predictive performance while reducing measured GFLOPs by up to 57%.

AI.tldr: Calibration-Aware Uncertainty Cascades (CAUC) post-hoc calibrates each model’s confidence to create a common reliability scale, enabling budget-aware heterogeneous model cascades with decoupled deployment policies and shown improvements in language and vision benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing heterogeneous-model approaches rely on fixed routers or raw-confidence cascades that lack reliable reliability semantics and adapt poorly to changing model pools and budgets. A post-hoc, calibration-based approach can provide a stable, model-pool-agnostic decision framework.
AI.method: Calibrate each model’s confidence independently on validation data, then use a unified decision criterion to decide—early exit with current model, invoke a stronger model, or combine outputs—based on calibrated scores. This decouples policy from the specific pool/budget and establishes a reliable thresholding semantics.
AI.result: On six language benchmarks, CAUC yields ~1.9% relative accuracy improvement over strong-model-only inference while avoiding ~47% of strong-model calls. On image classification, it preserves or improves accuracy while reducing GFLOPs by up to 57%.
AI.conclusion: Calibration provides explicit selective-risk interpretation for thresholds; the approach is robust to changes in model pools and budgets and offers practical post-hoc deployment benefits without retraining routing mechanisms.

title: Prevalence Determines Precision:Silent Contamination in Detector-Defined Datasets
summary: Many ML datasets are constructed by running a detector, heuristic, or model over candidate pools; accepted items become labels. Dataset precision is then governed by true-positive prevalence in each pool via Bayes, not solely by detector quality. Using one instrument and period, we hold a detector-defined event dataset plus an independent official index labeling every detected item as real or phantom. One detector, three pools yield phantom rates 81.7%, 9.0%, and 0.0%. Transferring precision from the two high-rate pools to the low-rate pool predicts 0.955 versus measured 0.183, a +422% error; the Bayes expression predicts all three within 3.3%. The detected response curve is an exact convex combination of a true-event and a phantom component (residual 1.1e-16), with phantoms outnumbering true events 473 to 308, so contamination is a second signal with detector-inherited shape, not additive noise. Contamination direction depends on the estimator: on identical windows one statistic is diluted and another inflated because its denominator is also contaminated. A common normalization turns the estimator into a mean of ratios whose expectation need not exist; on the same 335 events it returns 0.40 where the well-defined estimator returns 0.10.

AI.tldr: Dataset construction by detector over pools yields misestimated precision due to phantom contamination; Bayes-based precision depends on prevalence, and normalization can produce biased ratio estimators.
AI.motivation: Examine how detector-derived labels and separate official indices affect precision, showing phantom contamination and estimator biases.
AI.method: One detector, three pools; compare Bayes predictions to measurements; decompose detected response into true-event and phantom components; analyze effect of contamination direction depending on estimator; evaluate normalization-induced bias on 335 events.
AI.result: Phantoms dominate in some pools; simple transfer of precision from high-rate pools to low-rate pool fails by large margin; Bayes yields accurate predictions (within a few percent) for all pools; detected response is a convex combination of true-event and phantom signals; phantoms outnumber true events 473:308; contamination acts as a second signal; estimator choice changes dilution/inflation; normalization yields a non-existent mean for a ratio estimator (0.40 vs 0.10).
AI.conclusion: Contamination is structured and inseparable from the signal; Bayes-based correction is necessary; beware of ratio estimators with contaminated denominators; normalization can induce bias; a proper model of prevalence and contamination improves dataset precision estimation.

title: Recursive Code World Models: Building Complex Worlds through Recursive Scene Programs
summary: Code world models represent worlds as executable programs, but this representation alone does not determine how to construct a complex world. We introduce Recursive Code World Models (RCWM), a framework for reconstructing complex 3D worlds in code from a single reference image. RCWM couples a Recursive Scene Program (RSP) representation with a construction solver that recursively calls itself. An RSP represents the executable world as compositional scene code, while each solver call follows the same complete process: establish the whole, recursively reconstruct unresolved parts, and revisit the whole to refine their composition. This global-local-global recursion gives fine-scale structures their own perception-and-editing loops while preserving scene-wide geometry and relationships. Reference-aligned views propagate a shared camera projection across levels, while parent revisitation addresses boundaries, spatial relations, and shared errors that emerge after local refinement. A vision-language coding agent directly compares reference images with scene renders to guide refinement, recursive descent, and return. Across complex scenes, RCWM outperforms prior code-based image-to-scene reconstruction methods. Ablation studies further support the benefits of recursive construction and suggest that deeper calls can improve finer-scale reconstruction. RCWM provides a recursive construction principle for building complex executable worlds from visual evidence.

AI.tldr: RCWM introduces a recursive, code-based framework to reconstruct complex 3D worlds from a single image using a Recursive Scene Program (RSP) and a construction solver that recurses globally and locally, guided by vision-language comparisons of reference images to renders; it outperforms prior methods, with ablations suggesting deeper recursion improves finer-scale reconstruction.
AI.motivation: To build executable, stable 3D world representations from visual evidence, addressing limitations of existing code-based image-to-scene methods in capturing global geometry and fine-scale details through iterative, recursive refinement.
AI.method: RCWM couples a compositional Recursive Scene Program (RSP) with a construction solver that repeatedly: (i) establishes the whole scene, (ii) recursively reconstructs unresolved parts, and (iii) revisits the whole to refine composition. It enforces reference-aligned views with a shared camera projection, uses parent revisitation to fix boundaries and relations, and employs a vision-language coding agent that compares reference images with rendered scenes to guide refinement, recursive descent, and return.
AI.result: Across complex scenes, RCWM outperforms prior code-based image-to-scene reconstruction methods. Ablation studies support the benefits of recursive construction, with deeper calls improving finer-scale reconstruction.
AI.conclusion: RCWM provides a recursive construction principle for building complex executable worlds from visual evidence, demonstrating the value of recursive, global-local-global refinement in code-based scene reconstruction.

title: RouteRepair: Instance-Level Failure Diagnosis and Targeted Repair in LLM-Based Automated Heuristic Design for Routing Optimization
summary: Efficient routing optimization is essential to freight transportation, urban logistics, and shared mobility, where high-quality heuristics are often required under limited computational budgets. Recent large language model (LLM)-based automated heuristic design methods can generate effective routing rules, but aggregate evaluation may mask recurrent failures on particular instance structures. To address this limitation, this study develops RouteRepair, which diagnoses parent-specific weaknesses from instance-level performance and applies targeted modifications to the corresponding heuristic components while protecting behavior that already performs well. Routing evidence, solver behavior, and program context are combined to define bounded repair objectives, and each intervention is validated through matched parent-child evaluation of failure recovery and collateral degradation. Experiments on the traveling salesman problem (TSP) and capacitated vehicle routing problem (CVRP) span constructive search, guided local search, and ant colony optimization. RouteRepair-GLS reduces the mean TSP optimality gap from 1.7476% to 0.7587%, while the constructive CVRP heuristic lowers average route cost by 1.91% relative to the savings heuristic; the generated ACO priors also outperform matched hand-designed priors. These results show that failure-aware, evidence-constrained refinement can improve routing heuristics on difficult instances while preserving performance on cases they already solve well.

AI.tldr: RouteRepair introduces failure-aware, bounded repair of LLM-designed routing heuristics; it identifies instance-level weaknesses, makes targeted modifications to heuristic components, and preserves strong behavior; shows sizable improvements on TSP and CVRP.
AI.motivation: Aggregate evaluation of LLM-derived routing heuristics can mask systematic weaknesses tied to particular instance structures. There is a need for failure-aware, evidence-constrained refinement to improve performance under limited compute budgets.
AI.method: RouteRepair diagnoses parent-specific weaknesses from per-instance performance and applies targeted, bounded modifications to the corresponding heuristic components while protecting well-performing behavior. It combines routing evidence, solver behavior, and program context to define repair objectives, and validates each intervention via matched parent-child evaluation of failure recovery and collateral degradation. Evaluations span constructive search, guided local search, and ant colony optimization for TSP and CVRP.
AI.result: For TSP, mean optimality gap reduced from 1.7476% to 0.7587%. For CVRP, the constructive heuristic lowers average route cost by 1.91% relative to the savings heuristic. Generated ACO priors outperform matched hand-designed priors.
AI.conclusion: Failure-aware, evidence-constrained refinement can improve routing heuristics on difficult instances while preserving performance on cases they already solve well.

title: Combining Synthetic and Real Data for Low-Resource Historical OCR: A Manchu Case Study
summary: Manchu, now critically endangered, was one of the principal languages of the Qing empire (1636-1912), and its extensive archival record is increasingly digitized but remains difficult to search and analyze at scale. Previous work showed that vision-language models (VLMs) trained only on synthetic Manchu word images can reach 87.4% word accuracy on real Qing manuscripts and prints, leaving a substantial synthetic-to-real gap. This study examines how synthetic and real historical training data should be combined for low-resource OCR. Using 60,000 synthetic and 20,306 real historical word images, we evaluate three pretrained VLMs and a compact convolutional recurrent neural network (CRNN) under four regimes: synthetic-only, real-only, joint synthetic-real, and sequential synthetic-to-real training, following a common checkpoint-selection and archival evaluation protocol. Introducing real training images raises the leading configurations to between 95.09% and 96.28% word accuracy, while no synthetic-only configuration exceeds 87.92%. Synthetic supplementation substantially improves all three VLMs, whereas its marginal effect for the CRNN is sensitive to the training objective. Joint and sequential training yield broadly similar archival accuracy under the tested practical pipelines. A compact CRNN also reaches the leading performance range once real images are available, showing that model scale alone does not determine recognition accuracy. Finally, complementary errors among strong recognizers allow voting to raise accuracy to 98.27% without additional training, while an eighteenth-century Manchu dictionary provides a principled rule for adjudicating disagreements.

AI.tldr: Real data is crucial for high-accuracy Manchu OCR; combining synthetic and real data yields strong gains, with joint/sequential training offering similar benefits, and ensemble voting pushing accuracy to ~98% aided by an archival dictionary.
AI.motivation: Address the low-resource OCR challenge for Manchu and the synthetic-to-real gap, enabling scalable search and analysis of Qing-era archives.
AI.method: Use 60,000 synthetic and 20,306 real historical word images to evaluate three pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) and a compact CRNN under four regimes: synthetic-only, real-only, joint synthetic-real, and sequential synthetic-to-real training. Follow a common checkpoint-selection and archival evaluation protocol. Assess performance and employ voting among models, with an eighteenth-century Manchu dictionary to adjudicate disagreements.
AI.result: Real training raises leading configurations to 95.09%–96.28% word accuracy; synthetic-only configurations stay below 87.92%. Synthetic supplementation benefits all three VLMs; CRNN benefits variably. Joint and sequential training yield broadly similar archival accuracy. A compact CRNN reaches the leading range when real data are available. Complementary errors across strong recognizers enable voting to reach 98.27% accuracy, with the dictionary guiding disagreement resolution.
AI.conclusion: Model scale alone does not determine performance; leveraging complementary strengths through joint/sequential training and ensemble voting can achieve high accuracy in low-resource Manchu OCR, and archival lexicography can provide principled adjudication of disagreements.

title: UBone3D: Physics-Rectified Conditional Flow Matching for Anatomical 3D Shape Completion from Ultrasound
comment: Accepted to ECCV 2026. Camera-ready Author Version
summary: Three-dimensional ultrasound (US) is a safe, radiation-free complementary modality to CT and X-rays for longitudinal monitoring, yet its segmentation-derived partial point clouds are extremely artifact-laden. Consequently, it is challenging to recover a clean and complete anatomical structure from such US point clouds. In this paper, we present UBone3D, a novel framework based on physics-rectified conditional flow matching (CFM) that performs point cloud completion directly from partial US observations. UBone3D models deterministic physics artifacts (e.g., surface thickening, streaking, dropouts) via a simulated physics proxy, and introduces test-time physics rectification to steer the shape completion. At inference, the completion is jointly steered by two decoupled forces: (1) anatomical plausibility enforced by a CT-trained generative shape prior, BoneFM, and (2) physics consistency enforced by USimNet in the ultrasound formation space. Extensive experiments on simulated and in-vivo data demonstrate significant improvements in reconstruction accuracy and anatomical fidelity over existing baselines.

AI.tldr: UBone3D introduces physics-rectified conditional flow matching to complete partial 3D ultrasound point clouds by combining a CT-trained anatomical prior (BoneFM) with a physics proxy (USimNet) for test-time rectification, achieving improved anatomical fidelity and reconstruction accuracy.
AI.motivation: 3D ultrasound point clouds are heavily artifact-laden and incomplete, making clean anatomical surface recovery difficult. A data-driven completion is augmented by physics-informed priors to ensure anatomical plausibility and physics consistency.
AI.method: The framework uses two decoupled forces at inference: (i) BoneFM, a CT-trained generative shape prior enforcing anatomical plausibility, and (ii) USimNet, a physics-consistency module in the ultrasound formation space. A simulated physics proxy models US artifacts (surface thickening, streaking, dropouts) and test-time physics rectification guides the completion via physics-aware conditional flow matching (CFM). The completion is performed directly from partial US observations.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on simulated and in-vivo data show significant improvements in reconstruction accuracy and anatomical fidelity over existing baselines.
AI.conclusion: UBone3D presents a novel, physics-informed point-cloud completion approach for ultrasound data by coupling a CT-derived anatomical prior with a physics-consistent ultrasound formation proxy, enabling more accurate and plausible reconstructions and potential clinical utility.

title: Flexible and Interpretable Accent Distance Measurements
summary: Determining the differences between two speakers' accents is a fundamental task in linguistics and speech technology research. The methodology used to measure these differences depends on the specific research area. A phonetics researcher may demonstrate accent variation by comparing vowel formants in paired recordings of individual words. These results will be interpretable, but the recordings will be time-consuming to collect and may not be representative of connected speech. Accented Text-to-Speech (TTS) research has pushed towards using accent embeddings derived from accent classification tasks. These embeddings can be produced from any speech recording, but are not readily interpretable. In this paper, we demonstrate that articulatory representations created through articulatory inversion can be used as an interpretable basis for accent comparison and that optimal transport provides a framework for accent comparison across arbitrary recording types.

AI.tldr: Articulatory inversion-based articulatory features, combined with optimal transport, enable interpretable and cross-domain accent comparison.
AI.motivation: Current accent analysis faces a trade-off: phonetics-based formant analyses are interpretable but time-consuming and not representative of connected speech, while accent embeddings from classification are scalable but opaque. A unified, interpretable, cross-recording-type framework is needed.
AI.method: Use articulatory inversion to obtain articulatory representations as an interpretable basis for accent differences; apply optimal transport to compare accents across arbitrary recording types (word-level, connected speech, TTS, etc.).
AI.result: The paper demonstrates that articulatory representations can serve as an interpretable basis for accent comparison and that optimal transport provides a framework for cross-domain accent comparison across diverse recording types.
AI.conclusion: Articulatory-inversion-based articulatory features analyzed with optimal transport offer a generalizable and interpretable approach to accent difference assessment across different recording modalities.

title: DeFiFlowBench: Benchmarking and Improving Safe Executability in Natural-Language DeFi Workflow Synthesis
summary: A structurally valid DeFi workflow can still authorize a costly trade. We introduce DeFiFlowBench, a benchmark of 207 team-authored prompts for natural-language DeFi workflow synthesis. It measures graph coverage, configuration completeness, and declared safety predicates, then tests supported trade configurations on a local EVM. Direct, constrained, and few-shot prompting produce 14-19 unsafe held-out executions per configuration under a fixed 5% price-impact cap. A slippage bound derived from a quote does not prevent the price impact of the order itself. We propose Koan-Safe, which combines a prompt-only intent parser, a replaceable generator, and structural repair with default safety parameters. On 75 held-out workflow prompts, its hybrid variant scores 0.67 on the static safety proxy, compared with 0.33 for the best baseline. Koan-Safe records no unsafe executions on the saved benchmark outputs. A matched-candidate ablation produces 14-17 unsafe executions when enforcement is disabled. Additional tests expose the limits of default injection: permissive existing thresholds can still authorize unsafe trades. A separately evaluated policy cap addresses this failure on a 36-case diagnostic grid. These results support explicit trade protections and execution-based evaluation, while distinguishing declared safety from a general guarantee.

AI.tldr: Benchmark and analysis framework for natural-language DeFi workflow synthesis; DeFiFlowBench with 207 prompts; Koan-Safe safety system; evaluation shows trade protections but limitations of static predicates; policy cap mitigates; emphasizes execution-based evaluation.
AI.motivation: Addresses risk that structurally valid DeFi workflows can authorize unsafe trades; need explicit, execution-aware safety evaluation for NL prompts used to synthesize DeFi operations.
AI.method: Construct DeFiFlowBench; test prompts; measure graph coverage, configuration completeness, safety predicates; test on local EVM; compare prompting strategies (direct, constrained, few-shot); propose Koan-Safe with prompt-only intent parser, replaceable generator, and structural repair; perform held-out evaluations, ablations, and a policy cap analysis.
AI.result: Direct, constrained, and few-shot prompts yield 14–19 unsafe held-out executions per configuration under a fixed 5% price-impact cap. Slippage bound from a quote does not prevent order price impact. Koan-Safe’s hybrid variant scores 0.67 on the static safety proxy vs 0.33 for best baseline; no unsafe executions on saved benchmark outputs; matched-candidate ablation yields 14–17 unsafe when enforcement is disabled; permissive thresholds can still authorize unsafe trades; policy cap addresses this in a 36-case diagnostic grid.
AI.conclusion: Results support explicit trade protections and execution-based evaluation; safety is distinct from declared safety; Koan-Safe provides a pathway toward safer NL-to-DeFi workflow synthesis, though evaluation highlights limits of default thresholds and static checks.

title: Harnessing Intrinsic Subject-Aware Attention for Controllable Multi-Subject Video Generation
summary: Multi-subject video generation faces two key challenges: uncontrollable fidelity strength and potential semantic drift. We address these by analyzing the internal mechanisms of Diffusion Transformers (DiTs). We found that certain attention blocks naturally form an Intrinsic Spatial Grounding Map (ISGM) that precisely locates reference subjects. Building on this insight, we propose Dual-phase Intrinsic Attention Leveraging (DIAL), a framework that uses these internal signals for both training and inference. In low-noise stages, we use ISGM to guide the attention mechanism, allowing precise control over fidelity strength during inference without retraining. In high-noise stages, we use these same maps to automatically build preference pairs at no additional cost for Reinforcement Learning (RL). This RL procedure effectively anchors the model's attention to reference subjects and mitigates semantic drift. Extensive experiments show that DIAL significantly outperforms baseline models on the OpenS2V-Eval benchmark, consistently improving identity consistency and enabling controllable fidelity strength.

AI.tldr: DIAL uses intrinsic signals from Diffusion Transformers to control fidelity and prevent semantic drift in multi-subject video generation. It leverages ISGM to guide attention in low-noise stages for controllable fidelity without retraining and to generate RL preference pairs in high-noise stages to anchor attention to reference subjects, improving identity consistency on OpenS2V-Eval.
AI.motivation: Address two key issues in multi-subject video generation: uncontrollable fidelity strength and semantic drift. The authors exploit intrinsic attention signals (ISGM) within Diffusion Transformers to ground reference subjects without needing retraining.
AI.method: Propose Dual-phase Intrinsic Attention Leveraging (DIAL). In low-noise stages, use ISGM to guide attention for controllable fidelity at inference. In high-noise stages, construct preference pairs from ISGM to train RL, anchoring attention to reference subjects and mitigating semantic drift.
AI.result: DIAL significantly outperforms baselines on the OpenS2V-Eval benchmark, with consistent gains in identity consistency and enabling controllable fidelity strength.
AI.conclusion: DIAL demonstrates that internal Diffusion Transformer signals (ISGM) can be exploited for both training and inference to control fidelity and reduce semantic drift without retraining, achieving robust multi-subject video generation.

title: The Convention Gap: Towards Measuring Implicit Communication in Cooperative AI Evaluation
summary: Cooperative AI agents are evaluated against other AIs, yet human cooperation relies on implicit conventions---shared protocols for reading meaning beyond the literal message---which AI-AI benchmarks may not capture. We propose the \emph{convention gap}, the difference between the failure probability predicted from the literal content of communication and the observed failure rate, as a metric of implicit communication. In the card game Hanabi, the finite deck and deterministic hint constraints make this posterior exactly computable. We replayed about 101,000 play actions from three public datasets of human-human (hanab.live), AI-AI (HOAD), and human-AI (HanabiData) games. The gap was +26.2 percentage points (pp) in human pairs, $-$0.7~pp in AI pairs, and +16.4~pp in human-AI pairs, and was concentrated on plays of cards that had received no hints (+46~pp in human pairs). Within human-AI play, the literal information available to humans was similar across the three AI partners (mean predicted failure 38--41\%), but human failure rates ranged from 14.4\% to 34.4\% and the gap from +24.1 to +6.2~pp; the partner eliciting the largest gap produced the fewest human failures. Game score carried different information: it depended on each corpus's roster composition, whereas the gap separated human from AI play at the agent level. As a known-answer check, Off-Belief Learning agents, whose convention content is controlled by construction, gave a gap of +1.6~pp at the convention-free level, rising monotonically to +21.7~pp. These results suggest that convention compatibility, rather than AI-AI performance, may predict an AI's effectiveness with human partners.

AI.tldr: Introduces the "convention gap" as a metric for implicit communication in Hanabi; finds humans rely on conventions more than AI and that convention compatibility better predicts AI performance with humans than raw AI–AI metrics.
AI.motivation: To quantify implicit communication in human–AI collaboration beyond literal content, addressing a gap that standard AI–AI benchmarks may miss.
AI.method: Compute the convention gap exactly in Hanabi (finite deck, deterministic hints). Analyze about 101,000 play actions from three public datasets: human–human, AI–AI, and human–AI. Compare predicted failure from literal content to observed failure; examine plays with no hints; use Off‑Belief Learning agents with controlled convention content as a baseline across levels of convention dependency.
AI.result: Gaps: +26.2 pp (human–human), −0.7 pp (AI–AI), +16.4 pp (human–AI). No-hint plays show a large gap (+46 pp). Predicted literal failure (38–41%) similar across AI partners, yet human failure rates vary (14.4%–34.4%), with the largest gap partner yielding fewest human failures. Score depends on roster, but the gap distinguishes human vs AI at the agent level. Off‑Belief Learning: gap 1.6 pp at convention‑free level rising to 21.7 pp, validating a predictable convention effect.
AI.conclusion: Convention compatibility—not purely raw AI performance—may predict how effectively an AI collaborates with humans. Designing agents that align with human conventions could improve joint outcomes; the convention gap provides a measurable target for evaluating such alignment.

title: Generalized Score Matching for Parameter Estimation on Convex Domains
summary: Maximum likelihood (ML) estimation is a principled and statistically efficient approach for learning probabilistic models. However, for unnormalized models, ML estimation requires evaluating the partition function and differentiating through it, which may not always be tractable. Score matching provides a practically viable alternative that circumvents this obstacle by fitting the score in a way that eliminates dependence on the normalizing constant. We derive the generalized score matching objective on a convex subset of $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ constructively starting from Minimum Probability Flow (MPF) learning, and show how classical score matching as well as domain-adapted variants for non-negative data arise naturally within the proposed framework. We show that the resulting objective is a {\it proper local scoring rule} of second-order, which provides the theoretical guarantee that the true density is recovered when the objective is minimized. Furthermore, for a model belonging to the exponential family, we establish convexity of the objective together with consistency of the finite-sample estimator under standard regularity conditions. Our derivation sheds new light on the scope and applicability of generalized score matching in various problem settings. We compare generalized score matching-based estimators on constrained domains, where the partition function is analytically intractable. We provide experimental results on parameter estimation for model densities belonging to the exponential family defined over convex subsets of $\mathbb{R}^{d}$, and a generative modeling use-case to demonstrate broader applicability of the proposed generalized score matching framework.

AI.tldr: A generalized score-matching objective derived from MPF for densities on convex domains, yielding a second-order local scoring rule with convexity for exponential-family models, consistency guarantees, and demonstrated on constrained domains and a generative modeling task.
AI.motivation: Unnormalized models require partition function evaluation in maximum likelihood, which is often intractable. Score matching offers a tractable alternative that eliminates the normalizing constant. The work extends score matching via Minimum Probability Flow (MPF) to constrained domains and connects classical score matching variants within a unified framework.
AI.method: Derive a generalized score-matching objective from MPF on convex subsets of R^d. Show that classical score matching and domain-adapted variants arise naturally within the framework. Prove the objective is a second-order proper local scoring rule. For exponential-family models, establish convexity and consistency of the finite-sample estimator. Demonstrate on constrained domains with intractable partition functions and a generative-modeling use-case.
AI.result: The proposed objective recovers the true density when minimized. For exponential-family models, the objective is convex and the estimator is consistent under standard regularity. Experimental results validate parameter estimation for densities on convex subsets and illustrate broader applicability through a generative modeling task.
AI.conclusion: Generalized score matching extends applicability of score-based estimation to constrained domains and other settings with intractable partition functions, providing theoretical guarantees (second-order local scoring rule, convexity, consistency) and practical demonstrations via constrained-domain experiments and a generative modeling use-case.

title: Prototype Matters: Modality-unified Prototype Self-distillation for Unsupervised Visible-infrared Person Re-identification
summary: Estimating reliable cross-modality association is crucial to unsupervised visible-infrared person re-ID. While optimal transport is shown to be a practical solution for cross-modality association, it suffers from the rigidness of hard label assignment without considering the impact of cluster noise. Moreover, enforcing only cross-modality contrast is also suboptimal, as it fails to jointly optimize the similarity relation within and across modality. In this paper, we propose a novel framework for cross-modality learning by well exploitation of prototypes: First, instead of contrasting with cross-modality prototypes, we show that modality-unified prototypical contrast facilitates better modality invariance by jointly and simultaneously optimizing similarity relation within and across-modality. Taking self-prototype as a steady teacher, we further refine the instance-prototype online relation through prototype-guided self-distillation. The two components are optimized in a unified framework, leading to a simple yet effective model. On standard VI-ReID benchmarks, we perform extensive comparison and analysis, validating the effectiveness of our proposed method. Code is available at: https://github.com/Terminator8758/PoSeD.

AI.tldr: A simple, prototype-based framework (PoSeD) for unsupervised visible–infrared person re-ID that jointly optimizes intra- and inter-modality similarities via modality-unified prototypical contrast and prototype-guided self-distillation, outperforming hard-label OT and cross-modality-only approaches.
AI.motivation: Cross-modality association is critical for VI-ReID. OT's hard label assignments and focusing solely on cross-modality contrast neglect the intra-modality structure and noise in clusters.
AI.method: Introduce modality-unified prototypical contrast using self-prototypes as a steady teacher, and refine instance–prototype relations through prototype-guided self-distillation. Two components are integrated in a unified framework to learn modality-invariant representations.
AI.result: Validated on standard VI-ReID benchmarks with extensive comparisons, demonstrating effectiveness of the proposed approach; code available at the referenced repository.
AI.conclusion: Prototype-based, self-distillation-driven cross-modality learning effectively models both intra- and inter-modality similarities, offering a simple yet effective solution for unsupervised VI-ReID.

title: Published Unlearning Numbers Move Per Checkpoint, and Not Because the Removed Data Survives: An Audit of 263 Released Batch-Normalized Checkpoints
comment: 38 pages, 4 figures, 26 tables. Independent of and concurrent with arXiv:2609.08901 (posted 8 Sep 2026): the instrument and protocol here were pre-registered on 29 Aug 2026; dated provenance in Appendix S
summary: An unlearning audit reads its verdict off numbers that an unlearned model and its retrained reference each publish, and both also ship batch-normalization statistics that no gradient step wrote and no release records. Refitting them on kept data at bit-identical weights moves 47 of 221 released checkpoints past the spread their own release's seeds show, several inside a method whose average does not move: what moves is the checkpoint's property, not its method's. What does the moving is not the removed data surviving in the state: exchanging kept records for removed ones inside a fixed fitting pool moves a published cell by almost nothing, while how far a checkpoint's shipped state has drifted from any refit does track it. The consequence for a published decision is real but narrow: twelve verdicts cross, four clear a measured recalibration budget, two clear it on every replicate, and a population we trained and sited near its own criterion yields none. A release should therefore name the fitting convention beside the number, on the batch-normalized vision models where this channel exists.

AI.tldr: An unlearning audit reveals that information about unlearning leaks through released checkpoints and batch-norm statistics, with drift largely tied to the checkpoint state rather than the unlearned data, suggesting that releases should explicitly name the fitting convention used for batch-norm vision models.
AI.motivation: To understand whether removal of training data genuinely unlearns a model and how signals such as batch-norm statistics and published seeds reflect this, across many released checkpoints.
AI.method: Compare an unlearned model to a retrained reference with bit-identical weights; inspect batch-normalization statistics and seeds; refit kept data at identical weights; evaluate 221 released checkpoints and how their properties drift under data removal; exchange kept versus removed data within a fixed pool; assess how far shipped states drift from refits.
AI.result: Across releases, 12 verdicts cross, 4 show a measurable recalibration budget, 2 show a recalibration on every replicate; no verdicts for a population near its criterion. Drift is tied to the checkpoint’s property, not the method. Replacing kept with removed data moves a published cell by almost nothing; the distance from the refit tracks the drift of the shipped state. A released decision has a real but narrow impact.
AI.conclusion: To improve transparency, a release should name the fitting convention beside the release number for batch-norm vision models where this channel exists.

title: Particle GFlowNets: Rethinking Generative Marginalization Models
summary: Generative Marginalization Models (MaMs) have been recently introduced as efficient neural sampling models for any-order autoregressive modelling of discrete distributions. By learning both the marginal and conditional probabilities of a persistent-block Gibbs sampler, MaMs enable fast posterior evaluation with a single neural network forward pass. While prior work has considered MaMs to be distinct from Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets), a well-established paradigm for inference in discrete stochastic models, we show that they are equivalent. Then, we also extend MaMs' sampling strategy to non-autoregressive generative processes. In particular, we describe an automatic criterion for full-state rejuvenation of the Gibbs sampler, derived from the Gelman-Rubin statistic, which plays a key role in speeding up learning convergence. Our experiments show that our method, called Particle GFlowNets, markedly accelerates training in large combinatorial spaces.

AI.tldr: MaMs are equivalent to GFlowNets and extend to non-autoregressive sampling; they introduce a Gelman-Rubin-based full-state rejuvenation criterion, enabling Particle GFlowNets to accelerate training in large combinatorial spaces.
AI.motivation: To achieve efficient sampling for discrete distributions and unify MaMs with GFlowNets, while speeding up convergence and enabling non-autoregressive generation in large combinatorial spaces.
AI.method: Prove the equivalence between Generative Marginalization Models (MaMs) and Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets); extend MaMs to non-autoregressive processes; derive an automatic Gelman-Rubin-based criterion for full-state rejuvenation of the Gibbs sampler; implement Particle GFlowNets to accelerate training.
AI.result: MaMs and GFlowNets are equivalent; the Gelman-Rubin rejuvenation criterion improves convergence; Particle GFlowNets markedly accelerate training in large combinatorial spaces.
AI.conclusion: Unifies MaMs with GFlowNets, broadens sampling strategies to non-autoregressive processes, and provides a practical rejuvenation mechanism that enhances training efficiency in high-dimensional discrete spaces.

title: LoopVAE: Recurrent Depth Across Scales for Visual Tokenization
summary: Hierarchical visual tokenizers typically allocate different processing blocks to different spatial scales. We ask how much of this computation can use the same parameters. LoopVAE reuses a scale- and loop-conditioned core within and across scales, while keeping resolution-changing transitions independent. A four-block core executes 28 block applications per encoder or decoder. On ImageNet-256, the 29M-parameter convolutional model reaches 0.28 rFID and 32.54 dB PSNR under an approximately 30-epoch two-stage training budget, using approximately 65% fewer parameters than the 84M reference VAEs. A non-adversarial Transformer ablation with the same execution graph finds competitive PSNR and SSIM under global sharing, although unshared blocks improve LPIPS. Targeted loop interventions show that completing the trained recurrence improves reconstruction and that even small feature updates can have substantial downstream effects. Truncation also exposes output-range errors, distinguishing useful recurrent computation from reliable early exit. Runtime profiling reveals the execution tradeoff: fewer stored weights require more arithmetic and longer runtime in the tested configurations. With convolutional and Transformer operators and single- or multi-resolution latent interfaces, LoopVAE establishes recurrent depth across scales as a parameter-sharing design axis for visual tokenization.

AI.tldr: LoopVAE shares a scale- and loop-conditioned core across multiple scales in hierarchical visual tokenizers, enabling parameter sharing that reduces parameters by roughly 65% while maintaining competitive reconstruction metrics.
AI.motivation: Reduce parameter count and storage in hierarchical visual tokenizers without sacrificing performance; explore parameter-sharing across scales and the impact of recurrence depth.
AI.method: Proposes a four-block core that is reused within and across scales with scale- and loop-conditioning; employs both convolutional and Transformer operators, and single- or multi-resolution latent interfaces; two-stage training on ImageNet-256 (~30 epochs); includes ablations comparing global sharing vs unshared blocks, targeted loop interventions, truncation analysis, and runtime profiling.
AI.result: A 29M-parameter conv model achieves 0.28 rFID and 32.54 dB PSNR on ImageNet-256; ~65% fewer parameters than an 84M reference VAE; Transformer ablation with the same graph yields competitive PSNR/SSIM under global sharing, while unshared blocks improve LPIPS; recurrence completion improves reconstruction; small feature updates can have large downstream effects; truncation exposes output-range errors; fewer stored weights increases arithmetic and runtime; LoopVAE demonstrates recurrent depth across scales as a parameter-sharing design axis.
AI.conclusion: Recurrent depth across scales with parameter sharing is a viable design axis for visual tokenization, yielding parameter efficiency and flexible performance across convolutional and Transformer operators and multi-/single-resolution interfaces.

title: From Document Silos to Process Intelligence: A Multi-Layer Knowledge Graph for CMC Process Development
summary: Chemistry, Manufacturing and Controls (CMC) process development generates an enormous body of technical information across a multi-stage, knowledge-intensive continuum from drug discovery to commercial manufacturing. This knowledge is traditionally fragmented across functions and heterogeneous formats, causing traceability gaps and significant knowledge-management costs during technology transfer and regulatory filing. We present a modular agentic-AI platform that converts a heterogeneous corpus of process-development documents into a queryable, dual-layer knowledge graph. A base knowledge layer builds a lexical graph with a Document-Section-Chunk hierarchy through lossless ingestion of digital, scanned, handwritten, and multilingual documents, while an intelligence layer extracts ontology-aligned entities and bridges cross-document concepts through a provenance-anchored domain graph. LLM agents operate across both layers, selecting the retrieval path best suited to each question. We evaluate the lexical layer with a novel three-tier protocol measuring the deployment-fidelity of a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system on proprietary data, demonstrated on 505 questions curated from 38 development reports of a Sanofi small-molecule program. Tier-1 multiple-choice accuracy of 95% signals strong platform reliability; the stricter Tier-2 LLM-judge pass rate of 85%, which degrades on comparative and corpus-wide questions, reveals a failure taxonomy that Tier-1 accuracy alone fails to capture. A router agent selects between layers according to question type. We anticipate this protocol will enable future designers of agentic platforms to assess their systems against nonpublic databases, and that graph-based architectures will see broader adoption in pharma as a means of transforming fragmented document repositories into structured process intelligence.

AI.tldr: A modular agentic-AI platform converts heterogeneous CMC process-development documents into a dual-layer knowledge graph (lexical and ontology/provenance) to enable queryable process intelligence; evaluated on 505 questions from 38 Sanofi development reports with Tier-1 accuracy 95% and Tier-2 pass rate 85%; a router selects retrieval Layer; aims to reduce traceability gaps and streamline tech transfer/regulatory filing.
AI.motivation: Fragmented, heterogeneous process-development documentation causes traceability gaps and high knowledge-management costs during technology transfer and regulatory filing in pharma; a structured, queryable representation is needed to integrate diverse formats (digital, scanned, handwritten, multilingual).
AI.method: Introduce a base lexical layer with a Document-Section-Chunk hierarchy built via lossless ingestion of diverse documents; an intelligence layer extracts ontology-aligned entities and links cross-document concepts within a provenance-anchored domain graph. LLM agents operate across both layers; a router selects the optimal retrieval path per question. Evaluation uses a novel three-tier protocol (Tier-1 MCQ accuracy; Tier-2 LLM-judge pass rate) on 505 questions drawn from 38 Sanofi small-molecule development reports.
AI.result: Tier-1 accuracy: 95% indicating high deployment fidelity; Tier-2 LLM-judge pass rate: 85%, revealing a failure taxonomy not captured by Tier-1 alone; the router-layer selection adapts retrieval path by question type; findings support robustness of the platform on proprietary data and identify where performance gaps arise.
AI.conclusion: The proposed three-tier evaluation protocol provides a practical framework for assessing agentic platforms against nonpublic pharma data; graph-based architectures show promise for transforming fragmented document repositories into structured process intelligence, enabling more reliable technology transfer and regulatory filing.

title: A Dataset and Model for Imputing Water Surface Elevation on a Large and Extremely Sparse Spatiotemporal Graph
summary: Continuous monitoring of water surface elevation across river networks is critical for flood forecasting, water resource management, and understanding the global water cycle. Yet, the scarcity of in situ gauges across much of the globe constrains the development of reliable modeling frameworks. Satellite altimetry has the potential to alleviate this problem but its use is currently hindered by sparse temporal coverage. To this end, we introduce AmazonSWE, a dataset for training and evaluating large-scale spatiotemporal graph imputation methods that integrates processed satellite altimetry measurements from a range of sources, including the recent wide-swath SWOT sensor. The dataset covers over 19K river sections and 10 years (2016-2026) in the Amazon river basin, with in situ gauges held out for evaluation. Besides contributing a novel real-world use case with the potential for societal impact, AmazonSWE introduces significant technical challenges: with fewer than 1% of sections observed per day, the dataset is far sparser than existing imputation benchmarks, and its directed acyclic river topology is both structurally different from and larger than graphs in existing datasets. We show that prior spatiotemporal graph imputation methods are not adapted to this topology, scale and sparsity, and propose a simple bidirectional selective state space model that outperforms them by sampling connected subgraphs and flattening space and time into a single token sequence with topology-aware positional encodings. Compared to the state-of-the-art published method for SWOT-based WSE densification, which integrates statistics with physical modeling, our model reduces RMSE against in situ gauges by 18-39%, while producing predictions for every river section rather than only those with sufficient nearby satellite coverage.

AI.tldr: AmazonSWE: a large-scale, sparsity-aware river water surface elevation dataset designed for spatiotemporal graph imputation; introduces a bidirectional selective state-space model with topology-aware encodings; achieves 18–39% RMSE improvement over SWOT-based densification and predicts WSE for all river sections.
AI.motivation: Global water infrastructure is limited by sparse in situ gauges and limited temporal satellite coverage. A real-world, large-scale benchmark is needed to train and evaluate imputation methods that can handle directed, acyclic river topologies and extreme sparsity.
AI.method: Dataset construction over 19k river sections in the Amazon basin with 10 years of data (2016–2026); integrates multiple satellite altimetry sources including SWOT; gauges held out for evaluation. Model development: bidirectional selective state-space model that samples connected subgraphs, flattens space–time into a single token sequence, and uses topology-aware positional encodings to capture the directed acyclic river topology.
AI.result: The proposed model outperforms existing approaches on SWOT-based WSE densification, reducing RMSE against in situ gauges by 18–39% and providing predictions for every river section (not limited to areas with nearby satellite coverage).
AI.conclusion: AmazonSWE represents a significant real-world benchmark for spatiotemporal imputation in river networks, highlighting the benefits of topology-aware modeling under extreme data sparsity and enabling comprehensive river-wide WSE predictions.

title: Learning Interaction between Image and Layout Priors for Joint Image-Layout Generation in Design Templates
comment: Main paper with supplementary material. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
summary:
In this paper, we address the problem of graphic design template creation, which generates a background image and a layout of foreground elements over the background to form a harmonious composition from an input text.
  Prior work on graphic design generation mostly adopts a sequential paradigm, where design elements are generated sequentially. We argue that such a sequential scheme falls short of faithfully capturing the dependency between the background and layout (and thus the joint image-layout distribution), which limits the quality of generated design templates.
  To overcome this limitation, we propose a model, InterIL, which jointly generates the two modalities, background image and layout, in a single generative process. The novel design of our joint model connects the backbones of pretrained image and layout diffusion models with a learnable communication module to explicitly model bidirectional image-layout interaction. During training, the image and layout backbones are frozen to maintain and leverage the vast pretrained single-modality prior knowledge, while only the communication module is updated, so that the model can focus on learning image-layout interaction and thereby better capture the joint image-layout distribution for improved composition harmony.
  Our model has no design-specific inductive bias, which allows it to better preserve the original characteristics of realistic designs. We further introduce a test-time guidance strategy to enable users to impose their specific preferences on generated results.
  Our experiments show that, compared with prior approaches, our model can generate significantly better results in terms of image, layout and image-layout harmonization, producing outputs closer to real samples. We also demonstrate the flexibility of our model in enforcing user preferences at inference without retraining.

AI.tldr: A joint diffusion-based model, InterIL, generates background images and foreground layouts simultaneously to better capture their dependencies and improve design template harmony, using frozen pretrained backbones with a learnable communication module and test-time guidance.
AI.motivation: Sequential generation of background and layout fails to capture inter-modal dependencies, limiting the fidelity of the joint image-layout distribution and compositional harmony.
AI.method: InterIL jointly generates image and layout via a bidirectionally communicating module that interfaces frozen pretrained image and layout diffusion backbones; only the communication module is trainable; test-time guidance is introduced to accommodate user preferences.
AI.result: Outperforms prior sequential approaches in image quality, layout quality, and image-layout harmonization; outputs are closer to real samples; demonstrates flexible user preference control at inference without retraining.
AI.conclusion: Joint modeling with a learnable communication mechanism preserves real design characteristics, avoids inductive bias, and more faithfully models the joint image-layout distribution, enabling effective and user-controllable template generation.

title: ActMap: Single-Pass Uncertainty Quantification from Generation-Time Activation Maps
comment: 13 pages, 4 figures, 10 tables. Includes technical appendix
summary:
Practical uncertainty quantification (UQ) for large language models must decide,
  from a single generation, whether a specific answer should be trusted. Existing
  methods either sample multiple generations, read only output-token probabilities,
  or reduce the model's internal computation to a single hidden state. We introduce
  ActMap, a white-box representation that compresses the generation-time hidden-
  state trajectory (every layer, every generated token) into a fixed $12 \times 32
  \times 128$ tensor of temporal-statistic channels that preserves structure across
  transformer depth and pooled hidden coordinates. The map is captured during the
  generation pass with no measurable overhead, has a fixed shape across model
  depths and hidden sizes, and occupies 96 KiB: a compact artifact that can be
  retained for audit-relevant generations and probed directly, with occlusion
  analysis localizing the classifier's signal to mid-depth regions of the map. A
  lightweight classifier, instantiated as a compact Vision Transformer, reads an
  estimated correctness probability from each map in a fraction of a millisecond;
  capacity-matched MLPs perform comparably, indicating the representation itself
  carries the result. Trained and evaluated in-domain on short-answer QA, direct-
  answer math, and summarization factuality with three instruction-tuned 7-8B
  models, ActMap consistently outperforms sampling, token-probability, attention,
  and embedding baselines, and matches ACT-ViT, a detector trained on dense
  activation tensors $67 \times$ larger, at essentially the same mean AUROC with
  lower calibration error on ten of twelve pairs. The resulting score supports
  abstention, routing, and selective verification from a single generation, making
  it a practical primitive for scalable oversight of deployed models.

AI.tldr: ActMap offers a compact, white-box representation of generation-time hidden states (12x32x128) enabling single-generation uncertainty quantification with a tiny classifier, outperforming several baselines and matching dense-activation detectors at similar AUROC with lower calibration error.
AI.motivation: Need practical, scalable uncertainty quantification (UQ) for LLMs from a single generation, avoiding multiple generations or opaque token-probability signals.
AI.method: Compress the generation-time hidden-state trajectory (all layers, all tokens) into a fixed 12x32x128 tensor, one per generation, capture it with no measurable overhead, and use a lightweight classifier (compact Vision Transformer) to estimate correctness probability. Occlusion analysis localizes signal to mid-depth regions. Evaluate with 7–8B instruction-tuned models on short-answer QA, math, and summarization factuality; compare to baselines (sampling, token probabilities, attention, embedding) and ACT-ViT.
AI.result: ActMap consistently outperforms the baselines and matches ACT-ViT on mean AUROC across tasks, with lower calibration error on 10 of 12 task-model pairs. The representation preserves structure across depth, enables rapid inference (< fraction of a millisecond per map), and provides a compact 96 KiB artifact suitable for audit-relevant generations. It supports abstention, routing, and selective verification.
AI.conclusion: ActMap provides a practical, low-overhead primitive for scalable oversight of deployed LLMs, enabling single-generation UQ with auditable, interpretable signals localized to mid-depth generation dynamics; further work could extend to broader models and tasks and explore robustness across domains.

title: LoaDiff: Conditional Generation of Electricity Consumption Time Series for Energy Analytics
comment: 10 pages, 5 figures. This paper appeared in IEEE ICDM 2026
summary: The energy transition is reshaping residential electricity consumption through the increasing adoption of distributed generation, electrified appliances, and demand-response programs. Understanding these evolving behaviors requires access to granular smart-meter data for applications such as load forecasting, appliance detection, and demand-side flexibility analysis. However, such data are subject to strict access restrictions and data-protection regulations. Thus, realistic synthetic alternatives are necessary. In this paper, we introduce LoaDiff, a diffusion-based generative model for year-long, sub-hourly smart-meter load curves. LoaDiff supports flexible conditioning on static household attributes, such as appliance ownership, and dynamic contextual variables, including calendar information and outdoor temperature. We evaluate the model against multiple generative baselines on three residential electricity-consumption datasets. Our experiments assess four complementary dimensions: fidelity and diversity, training-record memorization risk, downstream utility for load forecasting and appliance detection, and conditional controllability under alternative temperature conditions. The results show that LoaDiff generates realistic and diverse load profiles, achieves a favorable trade-off between generation quality and limited evidence of memorization, preserves information useful for downstream energy applications, and responds coherently to changes in conditioning variables.

AI.tldr: LoaDiff is a diffusion-based model that generates year-long, sub-hourly smart-meter load profiles with flexible conditioning, enabling privacy-safe synthetic data for load forecasting, appliance detection, and demand-side analysis.
AI.motivation: Access restrictions and data-protection regulations limit real smart-meter data; realistic synthetic alternatives are needed for downstream energy analytics.
AI.method: LoaDiff uses a diffusion-based generative framework conditioned on static household attributes (e.g., appliance ownership) and dynamic contextual variables (calendar info and outdoor temperature). It is evaluated against baselines on three residential datasets, examining fidelity/diversity, memorization risk, downstream utility, and controllability under temperature changes.
AI.result: LoaDiff produces realistic and diverse load profiles, offers a favorable trade-off between generation quality and memorization risk, preserves information useful for downstream tasks like load forecasting and appliance detection, and responds coherently to changes in conditioning variables.
AI.conclusion: LoaDiff provides realistic, controllable synthetic load data suitable for privacy-preserving applications, with strong performance across fidelity, diversity, memorization, and downstream utility.

title: World in World: Explore the World with World Models
summary: Autoregressive video world models enable interactive, long-horizon exploration, but flexible control remains challenging. Exploring a source video from new viewpoints requires the generated rollout to remain synchronised with the recorded event, place observed content in the requested view, plausibly complete newly exposed regions, and recover previously generated appearance on revisits. Existing methods typically address these requirements through task-specific modules or additional training. We present World in World, a training-free inference-time interface that converts heterogeneous control evidence into camera- and time-labelled clean visual states, which are read through the native self attention of a frozen causal video model. The evidence comprises source-video observations, target-view scene projections, geometry renderings that guide completion of newly exposed subject regions, and retrieved generated states beyond the rolling cache. Each evidence source carries token-level support and its own availability schedule. A correspondence router combines persistent point identities with geometry to establish token correspondences, guiding supported queries towards matching source-video tokens. Evidence-wise attention CFG (EWA) then independently regulates each auxiliary channel's additional contribution using attention responses from the same denoising forward pass. The shared interface supports camera-controlled rerendering, long-horizon revisiting, and human-motion transfer with the same frozen backbone. We evaluate World in World on camera-controlled video rerendering under diverse viewpoint changes, assessing perceptual quality, temporal consistency, and camera-following accuracy.

AI.tldr: A training-free, inference-time interface augments a frozen autoregressive video model with heterogeneous control signals to enable camera-aware rerendering and long-horizon planning without additional training.
AI.motivation: To achieve synchronized, view-consistent video rollouts and content completion across viewpoint changes using a single frozen backbone, avoiding task-specific modules and extra training.
AI.method: World in World integrates multiple evidence sources (source video observations, target-view projections, geometry renderings guiding completion of newly exposed regions, and retrieved past states) with token-level support and availability schedules. A correspondence router aligns tokens using persistent point identities and geometry; Evidence-wise Attention CFG (EWA) weights auxiliary channels independently based on attention responses from the same denoising forward pass, all through the frozen model's self-attention.
AI.result: Evaluations focus on camera-controlled video rerendering across diverse viewpoint changes, assessing perceptual quality, temporal consistency, and camera-following accuracy; the approach aims to improve synchronization and robustness without retraining.
