AI.conclusion: The interface provides a versatile, training-free mechanism to perform camera-controlled rerendering, long-horizon revisits, and human-motion transfer using a single frozen backbone, reducing reliance on task-specific modules and additional training.

title: Extending SMT Solving with Non-Ground Clause Learning
summary: Quantifier instantiation is currently the main approach to non-ground SMT solving: solvers generate ground instances and solve the resulting ground SMT problems with CDCL(T)-style reasoning. When a conflict is found, conflict analysis learns only a ground clause, even though the conflict comes from instances of non-ground clauses. Yet non-ground reasoning can give exponentially shorter proofs than purely ground reasoning. We propose a calculus that consists of ground instantiations, CDCL(T)-style rules, and non-ground conflict analysis. The solver reasons on ground instances, but the resolution steps of conflict analysis are performed on their original non-ground clauses. This produces learned clauses that are typically more general than the ground conflict. With a suitable strategy, the learned clauses are even non-redundant. We also show how chronological backtracking can be included in SMT solving. Our calculus gives a common setting for CDCL(T)-style SMT solving, a range of instantiation-based procedures, and non-ground clause learning, and we prove that it simulates CDCL, SCL(FOL), SCL(T), and even Resolution.

AI.tldr: A unified calculus for SMT solving that integrates ground instantiations with non-ground conflict analysis, enabling generalized clause learning and proving simulations of CDCL, SCL(FOL), SCL(T), and Resolution.
AI.motivation: Current SMT practice uses ground instantiations with CDCL(T) but learns only ground clauses; non-ground reasoning can yield shorter proofs. There is a need to combine ground instantiation with non-ground analysis to obtain more general learned clauses and better backtracking behavior.
AI.method: Introduce a calculus combining ground instantiations, CDCL(T)-style inference rules, and non-ground conflict analysis. Conflicts are analyzed on non-ground clauses even though the solver reasons on ground instances, producing more general learned clauses. Provide strategies to ensure non-redundant learning and incorporate chronological backtracking.
AI.result: The calculus offers a common setting for CDCL(T)-style SMT solving, various instantiation-based procedures, and non-ground clause learning, and it is proven to simulate CDCL, SCL(FOL), SCL(T), and Resolution.
AI.conclusion: This framework unifies multiple SMT proving approaches, enabling more powerful reasoning through general, non-redundant clause learning and integrating chronological backtracking, with theoretical simulations to established proof systems.

title: RDDMPI: Residual Denoising Diffusion Model for Probabilistic Multivariate Time Series Imputation
summary: Multivariate time series imputation (MTSI) aims to recover missing values in temporal data composed of multiple interdependent variables. This problem is central to real-world applications such as healthcare monitoring, traffic networks, and energy systems. Recent diffusion-based approaches have shown strong potential for probabilistic imputation by learning to generate missing values through iterative denoising. However, most existing approaches perform diffusion directly in the original data space, requiring the denoising network to simultaneously capture global structure, temporal dynamics, and stochastic variability. This makes the generative task unnecessarily complex, especially when modern deterministic imputers can already provide accurate initial reconstructions. To address this limitation, we propose RDDMPI, a conditional residual diffusion framework that operates directly in residual space. Instead of modeling the full missing signal directly, we reformulate probabilistic imputation as a baseline-residual decomposition, where a pretrained model captures the dominant signal and a diffusion process models the residual uncertainty. To better exploit deterministic guidance, \model{} conditions the reverse denoising process on both the baseline-completed signal and its latent representation, while a reliability-aware conditioning mechanism adaptively controls the influence of baseline information during residual generation. This formulation simplifies the diffusion learning objective, enabling it to focus on structured correction terms rather than reconstructing the full signal. Experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that RDDMPI consistently improves both reconstruction accuracy and uncertainty quantification.

AI.tldr: A residual-space conditional diffusion framework for multivariate time series imputation that uses a baseline-imputer and a reliability-guided residual generator to improve reconstruction and uncertainty quantification.
AI.motivation: To simplify diffusion-based probabilistic imputation by decoupling the dominant signal (captured by a pretrained baseline imputer) from uncertain residuals, thereby easing the learning task and improving calibration.
AI.method: Reformulate imputation as baseline–residual decomposition. The diffusion process operates on the residuals in the space around a baseline completion. The reverse denoising is conditioned on both the baseline-imputed signal and its latent representation, with a reliability-aware mechanism that adaptively scales the influence of the baseline during residual generation.
AI.result: Empirical results on multiple benchmarks show consistent improvements in reconstruction accuracy and uncertainty quantification compared to baseline diffusion methods and possibly non-diffusion imputers.
AI.conclusion: Operating in residual space with baseline guidance simplifies the diffusion objective and yields better probabilistic imputations by focusing on structured corrections rather than full signal reconstruction.

title: A Comparative Evaluation of Pre-trained Convolutional Neural Networks for Melanoma Detection
summary: Early diagnosis of melanoma is critical for improving patient survival rates. However, accurately distinguishing melanoma from other skin lesions remains a significant clinical challenge due to the high visual similarity among lesion types and variability in image acquisition conditions. Artificial intelligence, particularly machine learning, has emerged as a promising tool to support dermatological diagnosis by automating feature extraction from medical images. Among the available approaches, convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have demonstrated strong performance in image classification tasks, making them well-suited for analyzing both dermatoscopic and histopathological images, given their ability to capture hierarchical visual patterns relevant to lesion characterization. Nevertheless, despite numerous pre-trained CNN architectures having been proposed, selecting the most appropriate one for a given imaging modality remains an open challenge. In this study, we evaluate pre-trained convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for skin lesion classification using dermatoscopic and histopathological image datasets. Experiments were conducted on the HAM10000, ISIC 2018, and CR-AI4SkIN datasets, evaluating the ResNet50, VGG16, VGG19, MobileNet, and InceptionV3 architectures under the same training protocol. The experimental evaluation showed that the models achieved accuracies ranging from 71% (InceptionV3 on ISIC 2018) to 84% (ResNet50 on HAM10000) on dermatoscopic images. For histopathological images, accuracies ranged from 72% (VGG19) to 83% (ResNet50) on the CR-AI4SkIN dataset. The results demonstrate that model performance differs between dermatoscopic and histopathological image modalities, showing that architectures exhibiting similar performance on dermatoscopic images exhibit different performance on histopathological data.

AI.tldr: Pre-trained CNNs show modality-dependent performance for skin lesion classification: Dermatoscopic data favored ResNet50 (HAM10000) and had up to 84% accuracy, while histopathology favored ResNet50 up to 83% on CR-AI4SkIN. Architectures with similar dermatoscopic performance diverged on histopathology, indicating modality-specific model selection and the importance of dataset-specific evaluation.
AI.motivation: Early melanoma diagnosis is challenging due to visual similarity among lesion types and variable imaging conditions. The study aims to identify which pre-trained CNNs best classify skin lesions across dermatoscopic and histopathological images.
AI.method: Compared five pre-trained CNNs (ResNet50, VGG16, VGG19, MobileNet, InceptionV3) on three datasets (HAM10000, ISIC 2018, CR-AI4SkIN) using a unified training protocol, reporting accuracy for each modality.
AI.result: Dermatoscopic accuracies ranged 71–84%; histopathological accuracies ranged 72–83%. ResNet50 often achieved top performance on HAM10000 and CR-AI4SkIN; InceptionV3 performed worst on ISIC 2018 among the tested models.
AI.conclusion: Model performance is modality-dependent; there is no single architecture optimal for both dermatoscopic and histopathological images. Architecture comparability on one modality does not guarantee similar performance on another; tailored evaluation and possible modality-specific models are recommended.

title: Lightweight LiDAR-Based Cone Detection Framework Using Random Forest for Formula Student Driverless
comment: 9 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables. Accepted at the 5th International Conference on Cognitive Mobility (CogMob 2026)
summary: Reliable, low-latency perception is crucial for Formula Student Driverless vehicles, yet many existing pipelines rely on deep learning and multi-sensor fusion, often requiring GPU acceleration. This paper presents a lightweight LiDAR-only perception pipeline tailored for CPU execution, combining ground removal, IMU-based motion compensation, DBSCAN clustering, and geometric feature-based Random Forest classification. Feature importance analysis reduced the model input from 12 to 7 features while preserving performance. Evaluated on 2,371 labeled clusters collected from real FSD events, the pipeline achieves an F1-score of 98.33% and an end-to-end runtime of 3.13 ms on CPU-only hardware. The released dataset, labeling tool, and trained models provide a practical and reproducible baseline for other resource-constrained autonomous racing teams.

AI.tldr: Lightweight LiDAR-only, CPU-only perception for autonomous racing achieving high accuracy and ultra-low latency, with released dataset and models.
AI.motivation: Autonomous racing needs low-latency perception on resource-constrained hardware; many pipelines rely on DL and GPUs, which is impractical for Formula Student vehicles.
AI.method: A CPU-friendly pipeline: ground removal, IMU-based motion compensation, DBSCAN clustering, and geometric feature-based Random Forest classification; feature importance analysis reduced input from 12 to 7 features.
AI.result: Evaluated on 2,371 labeled clusters from real FSD events; F1-score 98.33% and end-to-end runtime 3.13 ms on CPU-only hardware.
AI.conclusion: Dataset, labeling tool, and trained models are released, providing a practical and reproducible baseline for resource-constrained autonomous racing teams.

title: Musec: MomentUm SpEctral Clipping for Stable Muon-type Training
summary: Muon has emerged as a highly effective optimizer for large language model training, often achieving superior convergence and performance compared with the widely adopted Adam and AdamW optimizers. Nevertheless, Muon is prone to training instability due to its spectral flattening, manifested by loss spikes and unbounded growth of model weights. Existing approaches primarily rely on weight or attention-logit clipping, which require architecture-specific modifications and do not directly address instability across all model components. We propose MomentUm SpEctral Clipping (Musec), which replaces Muon's spectral flattening with spectral clipping: rather than setting all singular values of the momentum matrix to approximately one, Musec clips singular values that exceed a threshold while preserving the underlying spectral structure of the momentum. Our strategy provides an optimizer-level, architecture-agnostic mechanism for stabilizing Muon training. We further develop Soft Musec, an efficient implementation that uses a smooth spectral saturation function approximated by coupled Newton-Schulz iterations. Theoretically, we establish convergence guarantees for Musec in nonconvex nonsmooth stochastic optimization. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first convergence guarantee for Muon-type methods in the nonconvex nonsmooth setting. We provide empirical studies to show that Soft Musec consistently improves training stability over existing Muon variants across a wide range of learning rates and model sizes. Notably, Soft Musec remains stable in settings where existing Muon variants diverge, while matching their performance under well-tuned configurations.

AI.tldr: Musec introduces spectral clipping for Muon optimizer to stabilize training; provides convergence guarantees in nonconvex nonsmooth settings; Soft Musec is an efficient variant; empirically improves stability across learning rates and model sizes and remains stable where Muon variants diverge.
AI.motivation: Muon's spectral flattening causes instability (loss spikes, unbounded weights). Existing clipping methods are architecture-specific and don't address all components. There is a need for optimizer-level, architecture-agnostic stabilization with theoretical guarantees.
AI.method: Replace Muon's spectral flattening with spectral clipping: clip singular values of the momentum matrix that exceed a threshold, preserving the spectral structure. Soft Musec uses a smooth spectral saturation function implemented via coupled Newton-Schulz iterations.
AI.result: Theoretical convergence guarantees for Musec in nonconvex nonsmooth stochastic optimization; first such guarantee for Muon-type methods. Empirical results show Soft Musec improves training stability across learning rates and model sizes; stable where other Muon variants diverge and matches performance under well-tuned configurations.
AI.conclusion: Musec provides architecture-agnostic stabilization for Muon; Soft Musec offers an efficient, convergent, robust training improvement; promising for robust optimization in large-scale models.

title: Learn the Solid, Not the File: Canonical Inputs for Neural Networks on CAD Boundary Representations
summary:
Boundary representation (B-rep) is the standard format used by modern CAD systems for parametric 3D models. It turns out, the exact same solid can be represented by different B-reps: for example, two engineers using different operations, a geometry kernel rebuilding the file, and an export setting repartitioning faces will lead to different B-reps even though the underlying solid remains the same.
  We show that existing B-rep encoders are not robust to variation in the B-rep with the same solid on perturbations applied to standard benchmarks, naturally occurring variations inherent to CAD software, and differences in how designers model the same part via a human dataset we created in FreeCAD. The performance of popular B-rep encoders often collapses catastrophically.
  We propose the canonical region graph, an input representation whose nodes, features and coordinate frame are derived from the solid itself and show theoretical invariance guarantees on repartitioning and rigid motions. It matches the strongest baseline on standard benchmarks, and is stable under every perturbation we test.

AI.tldr: Canonical region graph (CRG) is proposed as a robust, invariant input representation for boundary representations (B-reps) in CAD, addressing non-robustness to repartitioning, perturbations, and modeling variations; CRG derived from the solid with invariance guarantees under repartitioning and rigid motions, matches strong baselines on benchmarks and is stable under tested perturbations.
AI.motivation: B-rep is widely used in parametric CAD, but the same solid can yield different B-reps due to modeling pipelines and operations, causing encoders to fail under variations. A robust representation is needed for reliable encoding and downstream tasks.
AI.method: Define the canonical region graph (CRG) from the solid itself, with nodes, features, and coordinate frames derived intrinsically. Prove theoretical invariance to face repartitioning and rigid motions. Empirically compare CRG to strong B-rep encoders on standard benchmarks and perturbation-rich data, including a human-made FreeCAD dataset.
AI.result: CRG achieves performance on standard benchmarks comparable to the best baselines and remains stable under all perturbations tested in the study, whereas existing B-rep encoders degrade catastrophically under variations.
AI.conclusion: CRG provides a robust, invariant input representation for B-rep encoding, addressing variability across representations and perturbations. This improves reliability for CAD workflows and paves the way for further exploration of intrinsic geometric representations.

title: Prompt Revision as a Source of Cultural Bias in Text-to-Image Systems
summary: Commercial text-to-image systems silently revise user prompts before generating images, a step users typically cannot disable or even see. Yet, existing audits of cultural bias examine only the final images and treat generation as a single pipeline, so they cannot tell where the bias originates. We introduce WORLDVIEW, a multilingual benchmark of 8,960 prompts across 15 languages and 31 language-context pairings. Using it, we audit the revision layer in three systems (DALL-E-3, Imagen-4, GPT-Image-1.5) through a three-step analysis of how heavily it marks each cultural context, whether it flattens that context into a narrow vocabulary, and whether that vocabulary is stereotypical. Relative to a no-context English baseline, the US is the least-marked context, while non-Western and non-Anglophone contexts are marked far more heavily, flattened into narrow vocabularies applied across topically diverse prompts, and reduced to recognizable cultural stereotypes. Comparing images from original versus revised prompts on models without a revision layer, we identify the layer itself as a previously undocumented, causal source of this stereotyping. To locate cultural bias, and fix it, we must audit the system as deployed, not the model alone.

AI.tldr: WORLDVIEW reveals that the prompt revision layer in commercial text-to-image systems systematically encodes cultural contexts, disproportionately marking non-Western contexts, flattening them into narrow vocabularies, and mapping them to stereotypes; the revision layer is a causal source of bias; auditing deployed systems is essential.
AI.motivation: Audits of cultural bias often focus on final images and treat generation as a single pipeline, obscuring where bias originates. This work targets the prompt revision layer that users cannot disable or view.
AI.method: Introduce WORLDVIEW, a multilingual benchmark of 8,960 prompts across 15 languages and 31 language-context pairings. Conduct a three-step analysis on DALL-E-3, Imagen-4, GPT-Image-1.5: (1) how heavily each context is marked, (2) whether the context is flattened to a narrow vocabulary, (3) whether that vocabulary is stereotypical. Compare results to a no-context English baseline. Examine images from original vs revised prompts on models without a revision layer to identify the revision layer as a causal source of stereotyping.
AI.result: Relative to English baseline, the US is the least-marked context; non-Western and non-Anglophone contexts are marked more heavily, flattened into narrow vocabularies, and mapped to recognizable cultural stereotypes across diverse prompts. The revision layer is shown to be a causal source of stereotyping. Auditing deployed systems, not models alone, is necessary to locate and fix cultural bias.
AI.conclusion: Bias in cultural context arises in the deployed prompt revision layer; to locate and fix it, audits must target the entire deployment pipeline, not just the underlying models.

title: Learnware and AI Model Management System
summary: The transition from file storage to database management systems transformed stored data into managed resources. AI now faces an analogous transition from AI model storage to AI model management. Existing model pools essentially serve as \textit{AI model storage systems}. What is needed instead are \textit{AI model management systems} that enable models trained by different developers, for different tasks, with different data, and under different objectives to be identified, reused, and even assembled to address future user tasks. Because AI model developers are generally unwilling to share their training data, such systems should operate without accessing the training data of model developers and, ideally, without accessing raw data of future users. This requirement poses a fundamental challenge: the functionality of a modern AI model may not be fully understood even by the developer who trained it. How, then, can a system identify which models are useful for a given user task, let alone assemble models developed independently for different purposes? At first glance, this objective may appear unattainable. It becomes possible, however, by upgrading the basic unit of management from a machine learning model to a \textit{learnware}. \textit{Learnware = Model + Specification}. The specification, whose assignment transforms a trained model into a learnware, is generated with the help of a machine learning process without disclosing the training data of the developer and has a theoretically established data-preservation property. The \textit{Learnware Dock System (LDS)} provides a path toward powerful AI model management systems. Because specifications are generated according to a published reference and are comparable across models, they can also serve as an AI model \textit{collaboration protocol} through which independently developed models, including intelligent agents, can collaborate.

AI.tldr: Proposes Learnware: a unit combining a trained model with a specification to enable privacy-preserving, model-level management and collaboration; introduces Learnware Dock System (LDS) and a collaboration protocol for cross-developer model reuse.
AI.motivation: Replace model storage with active model management; enable discovery, reuse, and assembly of models from diverse developers for new tasks while respecting data privacy; handle models whose behavior may not be fully understood by developers.
AI.method: Define learnware as (Model + Specification); generate the specification via a machine learning process that does not disclose training data and has a data-preservation property; propose the Learnware Dock System (LDS) as the management framework; establish that specifications are comparable via a published reference and can serve as a collaboration protocol.
AI.result: Outlines a theoretical framework for learnware and LDS; introduces data-preserving specifications, enables cross-model comparability, and proposes a protocol for collaboration among independently developed models and intelligent agents.
AI.conclusion: Learnware and the LDS framework offer a viable path toward scalable, privacy-preserving AI model management and collaborative reuse/assembly of models from multiple developers.

title: OmniKVQuant: KV Cache Quantization for Omni-LLMs
summary: As Omni-modal large language models (Omni-LLMs) take in audio, video and text together, their KV cache memory cost grows. KV cache quantization is the de facto approach in text-only LLMs, but its application to Omni-LLMs remains unexplored. In this paper, we analyze how TurboQuant, a representative rotation-based KV cache quantization method, behaves on multimodal caches and identify two critical issues: temporal key drift and heterogeneous value geometry. To address these, we propose OmniKVQuant, a training-free framework that (i) sets the key quantization range over each short window of the input stream; and (ii) rotates values separately per modality. On Qwen2.5-Omni and Qwen3-Omni, OmniKVQuant enables 2-bit KV caches while substantially preserving performance across seven audio-visual benchmarks. We further provide a fused Triton decode kernel that unpacks the 2-bit cache during attention, so no dense FP16 cache is ever built. Code: https://github.com/kaistmm/OmniKVQuant

AI.tldr: OmniKVQuant is a training-free framework for 2-bit KV cache quantization in Omni-modal LLMs that mitigates temporal key drift and heterogeneous value geometry by per-window key range quantization and per-modality value rotation, with a fused kernel for efficient unpacking; validated on Qwen2.5-Omni and Qwen3-Omni across seven audio-visual benchmarks.
AI.motivation: KV cache memory growth in Omni-LLMs with multimodal inputs; existing rotation-based quantization (e.g., TurboQuant) struggles with multimodal caches due to temporal drift and value-geometry heterogeneity; a training-free, hardware-efficient solution is needed.
AI.method: Quantization range for keys is set over each short input window; values are rotated separately per modality; training-free framework; includes a fused Triton kernel to unpack the 2-bit cache during attention, avoiding creation of a dense FP16 cache.
AI.result: Achieves 2-bit KV caches on Qwen2.5-Omni and Qwen3-Omni with substantial performance preservation across seven audio-visual benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: OmniKVQuant enables efficient, training-free 2-bit KV cache quantization for Omni-modal LLMs with minimal performance loss and practical runtime efficiency; code is available at the linked GitHub repository.

title: Characterizing Job Power Elasticity for Power-Flexible AI Training
summary:
Large language model (LLM) training is among the fastest-growing sources of electricity demand in modern data centers, and power availability is a primary bottleneck to continued AI infrastructure growth. Making the power consumption of these workloads flexible could unlock additional power for AI growth, limit increases in electricity prices, and improve the utilization of existing grid infrastructure. However, to realize this flexibility, we must first understand how the performance of training workloads changes when GPU power is reduced.
  This paper presents the first systematic characterization of \emph{job power elasticity} (the sensitivity of throughput to power reductions) in LLM training. To quantify elasticity, we introduce the \emph{Power Flexibility Index (PFI)}, a normalized metric that quantifies the performance cost of power reductions and provides a control primitive for SLA-aware power flexibility.
  We collect data from 131 LLM training runs on H200 (plus 24 H200 validation runs and 34 matched H100 runs), including both dense and mixture-of-experts models, pretraining and fine-tuning tasks, and up to 32 GPUs. We find that LLM training jobs exhibit substantial but variable power elasticity, and we identify telemetry signals that predict PFI at runtime. Finally, we demonstrate that PFI-aware power allocation maximizes total tokens/second throughput under power constraints. Under a 30\% power reduction, PFI-aware power allocation recovers ~1.5k tokens/s per job, 63\% of the performance gap between an equal-weight allocation and an oracle with perfect information. Our results establish power elasticity as a measurable property of training jobs and provide a foundation for power-aware, grid-responsive AI infrastructure.

AI.tldr: First systematic study of power elasticity in LLM training; introduces Power Flexibility Index (PFI) to quantify throughput loss under reduced GPU power; shows power-aware allocation improves tokens/second under power limits (e.g., 30% power reduction recovers ~1.5k tokens/s per job, 63% of the gap to an oracle).
AI.motivation: LLM training consumes substantial electricity; enabling flexible power usage could unlock growth, reduce costs, and improve grid utilization; need to quantify performance impact of power reductions.
AI.method: Empirical characterization across 131 LLM training runs on Nvidia H200 (plus 24 validation and 34 H100 matches), including dense and mixture-of-experts models, pretraining and fine-tuning, up to 32 GPUs. Introduces Power Flexibility Index (PFI), identifies telemetry signals predicting PFI, and demonstrates PFI-aware power allocation.
AI.result: LLM training exhibits substantial but variable power elasticity. Telemetry signals can predict PFI at runtime. PFI-aware allocation maximizes total tokens/second under power constraints; under 30% power reduction, observed recovery of ~1.5k tokens/s per job and 63% of the performance gap relative to an oracle.
AI.conclusion: Power elasticity is a measurable property of LLM training jobs and provides a foundation for power-aware, grid-responsive AI infrastructure.

title: Why Does Post-Training Quantization Work?
summary: Post-training quantization compresses large language models (LLMs) by storing their weights at reduced precision, and each quantized weight introduces an error into the hidden states. Naively, these errors should accumulate with depth and corrupt next-token prediction; randomly initialized models accumulate these discrepancies rapidly, whereas quantized pretrained models accumulate much less hidden-state error and largely maintain downstream task performance, even though they were never trained with quantization noise. This raises the question we address: why does post-training quantization work? Comparing full-precision and quantized forward passes, we identify two mechanisms that characterize pretrained quantization robustness. First, the error a layer newly introduces tends to oppose the error it inherits from the layer's input. The two cancel partially such that the discrepancy between full-precision and quantized passes grows slowly. This counteracting residual interaction develops during pretraining. Our quantitative analysis identifies it as a major factor slowing hidden-error growth. Second, LM-head geometry preferentially preserves the scores and probabilities of high-ranked tokens, which typically represent the model's most confident predictions. Together, these mechanisms explain why quantization error that passes through numerous layers can still produce only small output changes, and we verify the findings across models and quantization settings.

AI.tldr: Post-training quantization robustness in pretrained LLMs arises from two main mechanisms: (1) a residual error interaction where the new layer's error tends to oppose the inherited error, slowing overall error growth; (2) LM-head geometry that preserves scores for high-ranked tokens, keeping predictions stable. Together they explain why quantization errors barely affect downstream outputs despite deep propagation, as demonstrated across models and quantization settings.
AI.motivation: Understand why PTQ works for pretrained LLMs and why randomly initialized networks degrade quickly, by identifying the mechanisms that slow hidden-state error growth.
AI.method: Comparative analysis of full-precision and quantized forward passes; quantitative analysis of residual interactions between layer errors; examination of LM-head geometry; empirical verification across multiple models and quantization configurations.
AI.result: Two mechanisms identified: anti-correlated residual interactions between new and inherited errors slow hidden-error growth; LM-head geometry concentrates accuracy on high-ranked tokens, preserving predictions; findings validated across models and quantization settings.
AI.conclusion: Together, these mechanisms explain robust performance of pretrained quantized models and why deep quantization errors do not substantially alter outputs; pretraining shapes mechanisms that counteract quantization-induced perturbations.

title: MMGait: Benchmarking and Unifying Gait Recognition across Heterogeneous Modalities
summary: Gait recognition is commonly studied using RGB videos or their derived silhouettes and poses. Yet human walking produces heterogeneous photometric, geometric, and motion cues that cannot be systematically examined with RGB-centered benchmarks. We present MMGait, a large-scale multi-sensor benchmark that brings visible, infrared, depth, LiDAR, and radar observations into sequence-level correspondence. It provides diverse modalities spanning appearance, contours, geometry, motion, and body structure. Under a shared impostor-augmented protocol, we evaluate single-modal recognition, cross-modal recognition via directed retrieval, and multi-modal recognition using task-specific experts. Across settings, modality rankings vary with probe conditions, cross-modal alignment remains difficult, and fusion often provides complementary gains. This analysis exposes a scalability problem: individual modalities, modality pairs, and fusion configurations are typically handled by separately trained experts. We formulate Omni-Modal Gait Recognition, which unifies single-modal, cross-modal, and multi-modal recognition within a shared identity space. OmniGait++ uses modality-specific front ends followed by a shared identity encoder to preserve modality-dependent cues while learning comparable identity descriptors. An anchor-guided fusion module aggregates modality subsets of varying size without frame-level synchronization. A jointly trained checkpoint covers all three recognition settings and accommodates modality subsets of different compositions and cardinalities. Experiments show OmniGait++ remains competitive with task-specific experts in many shared settings and extends to higher-cardinality fusion unavailable to fixed-pair models. The results establish MMGait as a common testbed for heterogeneous gait sensing and demonstrate the feasibility of unified recognition under varying modality availability.

AI.tldr: Introduces MMGait, a large-scale multi-sensor gait benchmark across RGB, infrared, depth, LiDAR, and radar, with a unified OmniGait++ framework that learns across single-, cross-, and multi-modal recognition in a shared identity space.
AI.motivation: Address the fragmentation of gait benchmarks and methods that rely on RGB-only data by creating a heterogeneous, sequence-aligned benchmark and a unified recognition framework that can leverage multiple sensing modalities.
AI.method: MMGait provides sequence-level correspondences across multiple modalities (visible, IR, depth, LiDAR, radar) and an impostor-augmented protocol for evaluation. OmniGait++ uses modality-specific front ends feeding into a shared identity encoder, an anchor-guided fusion module, and a jointly trained checkpoint covering single-, cross-, and multi-modal recognition, enabling modality subsets of varying composition without frame-level synchronization.
AI.result: Experiments show modality rankings depend on probe conditions; cross-modal alignment remains challenging; fusion offers complementary gains. OmniGait++ is competitive with task-specific experts in many settings and scales to high-cardinality fusion not feasible for fixed-pair models, establishing MMGait as a versatile testbed for heterogeneous gait sensing.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates the feasibility of unified gait recognition across heterogeneous modalities and presents a scalable, unified framework (OmniGait++) that remains competitive with specialized solutions while accommodating varying modality availability and large-scale multi-sensor data.

title: Enabling Knowledge Graph Understanding at Scale with the EXplore Your Graphs ENgine (EXYGEN)
summary: We present EXYGEN (EXplore Your Graphs ENgine), a framework for knowledge graph (KG) understanding that enables conversational access to KGs at scale. We address two questions in sequence. First, how effectively can LLMs perform text-to-SPARQL generation given only automatically derived structured metadata and small graph samples, rather than task-specific fine-tuning? We integrate VoID descriptions and ShEx schemas into a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline and ablate KG-derived context on the SciQA benchmark. Our best configuration -- combining ShEx schemas, retrieved triples, and example question-query pairs -- reaches an exact match of 0.419 on execution results without any LLM fine-tuning. We further find that lexical metrics such as F1 poorly predict query correctness, and that larger general-purpose LLMs can outperform smaller code-specialized ones once given sufficient context. Second, we ask how to generate the structured metadata that this method relies on from very large KGs, where KG metadata generation becomes computationally intractable. We introduce a predicate-coverage-aware parallel graph sampling strategy that preserves structural diversity while remaining computationally tractable. On OpenCitations Meta and GESIS, it retains high predicate coverage with minimal triple loss and reduces runtime by over 80x; on ORKG, sampling is not just faster but the only tractable path to obtain complete metadata. Together, these results show that structured schema context and lightweight prompting can substantially reduce reliance on fine-tuning for scalable conversational access to KGs, though closing the remaining gap to fully fine-tuned approaches will likely require reducing dependence on curated question-query exemplars -- whether through synthetic generation or an execution-feedback-driven approach -- and validating these findings beyond a single benchmark.

AI.tldr: EXYGEN offers a retrieval-augmented framework for scalable conversational access to knowledge graphs, using VoID descriptions and ShEx schemas to perform text-to-SPARQL without task-specific fine-tuning. It achieves 0.419 exact-match on SciQA, highlighting that lexical metrics poorly predict query correctness, and shows that larger LLMs help with sufficient context. It also introduces a predicate-coverage-aware parallel graph sampling method to generate structured metadata efficiently, yielding major runtime reductions (over 80x) across several KG datasets and enabling complete metadata extraction on ORKG. Together, these show that structured schema context and lightweight prompting can reduce fine-tuning needs, though remaining gaps point to synthetic or feedback-driven exemplar generation and broader validation.
AI.motivation: The work targets scalable, conversational access to large knowledge graphs without heavy task-specific fine-tuning, addressing the dual challenges of effective text-to-SPARQL generation and scalable generation of structured metadata (schema/voID) for retrieval.
AI.method: 1) A retrieval-augmented generation pipeline incorporating VoID descriptions and ShEx schemas; ablation on KG-derived context using SciQA with and without retrieved triples and exemplars; best configuration combines ShEx, retrieved triples, and Q/A exemplars for 0.419 exact-match on execution results. 2) A predicate-coverage-aware parallel sampling strategy to generate structured metadata from large KGs, evaluated on OpenCitations Meta, GESIS, and ORKG, achieving high predicate coverage with minimal triple loss and dramatic runtime reductions.
AI.result: Best configuration (ShEx + retrieved triples + exemplars) achieves 0.419 exact-match on SciQA execution results without LLM fine-tuning. Lexical metrics (e.g., F1) are poor predictors of query correctness. Larger general-purpose LLMs outperform smaller code-specialized models given sufficient context. The sampling strategy maintains predicate coverage with minimal loss and reduces runtime by >80×; on ORKG sampling is essential to obtain complete metadata.
AI.conclusion: Structured schema context and lightweight prompting can substantially reduce reliance on fine-tuning for scalable KG-to-text/QA in conversational interfaces. Closing remaining gaps will likely require synthetic generation of exemplars or execution-feedback loops and broader validation beyond a single benchmark.

title: Predicting Privacy Leakage from Weight Spectral Density
summary: Membership inference attacks (MIAs) are widely used to audit the privacy disclosure risk of machine learning models, however current state-of-the-art attacks require training computationally expensive shadow models, making large-scale privacy evaluation impractical. In this work, we investigate whether inexpensive spectral metrics derived from the heavy-tailed self-regularisation framework can serve as proxies for MIA vulnerability. We evaluate several WeightWatcher spectral metrics on image and tabular classification tasks and compare their relationship with MIA privacy leakage against conventional measures of generalisation. Across datasets, stable rank exhibits a strong positive correlation with overall MIA success, while Log alpha-Norm shows a consistent negative correlation with MIA vulnerability at the low false-positive regime. These associations are observed to be stronger than those obtained using the generalisation gap. The results indicate that neural network spectra may contain information about privacy leakage that is not fully captured by conventional measures of overfitting, motivating spectral analysis as a promising direction for scalable privacy auditing.

AI.tldr: Spectral metrics from the WeightWatcher framework correlate with membership inference attack (MIA) vulnerability, offering a cheaper proxy than shadow-model training.
AI.motivation: To enable scalable privacy auditing by using inexpensive spectral proxies rather than computationally expensive shadow models for MIA evaluation.
AI.method: Assess multiple WeightWatcher spectral metrics (e.g., stable rank, Log alpha-Norm) on image and tabular classification tasks and correlate them with MIA leakage; compare against conventional generalisation measures.
AI.result: Across datasets, stable rank shows a strong positive correlation with overall MIA success, while Log alpha-Norm shows a consistent negative correlation with MIA vulnerability at low false-positive rates. These correlations often exceed those observed with the generalisation gap.
AI.conclusion: Neural network spectral properties carry information about privacy leakage not fully captured by overfitting metrics, supporting spectral analysis as a promising approach for scalable privacy auditing of ML models.

title: LangStreet: Persistent Language Fields for Anchor-Decoded Street Gaussians
summary: Language Gaussian fields implicitly assume that the primitive carrying semantics remains identifiable across views. This assumption breaks in scalable anchor-decoded representations, where persistent anchors generate view-conditioned child Gaussians whose geometry and appearance vary with the camera. We introduce Ours, a persistent language field for such structured Gaussian scenes. Our key idea is semantic ownership: transient children route observations, while persistent decoder slots and their parent anchors own the language field. We use alpha-compositing responsibilities to accumulate additive directional evidence at slots; these statistics marginalize exactly to anchors. We then complete weakly supported slots with anchor-aligned evidence while preserving the anchor direction, and represent slot detail through low-rank residuals in anchor-relative semantic coordinates. Our primary model, Ours (base), stores anchor features together with compact slot residuals. Ours (light) retains only anchor features, whereas Ours (max) stores the full-dimensional completed slot features explicitly. Without scene-specific semantic optimization, Ours (base) nearly matches Ours (max) across KITTI, Virtual KITTI, and Waymo. On KITTI, it achieves 34.19 2D mIoU with a 2.72 GiB effective feature footprint, compared with 34.20 mIoU and 12.90 GiB for Ours (max). The same accuracy-storage trend holds on Virtual KITTI and Waymo. These results show that language fields on view-conditioned splats require persistent semantic ownership, conserved evidence, and a hierarchy that balances stability, detail, and representation cost. Our code, checkpoints, and benchmark suite will be publicly available.

AI.tldr: Proposes Ours, a persistent language field for structured Gaussian scenes to fix semantic ownership issues in view-conditioned anchor-decoded representations; presents base/light/max variants with different storage/detail trade-offs; base nearly matches max performance with substantial storage savings across KITTI, Virtual KITTI, and Waymo; code and benchmarks to be released.
AI.motivation: Language Gaussian fields assume stable semantic identity across views, which fails for scalable anchor-decoded representations where anchors and view-conditioned splats shift geometry and appearance. A persistent, owner-based language field is needed to maintain semantic coherence and reduce storage while preserving detail where needed.
AI.method: Introduce Ours, a persistent language field with semantic ownership: transient children route observations; persistent decoder slots and their parent anchors own the language field. Use alpha-compositing responsibilities to accumulate additive directional evidence at slots, marginalizing exactly to anchors. Complete weakly supported slots with anchor-aligned evidence while preserving anchor direction, and encode slot detail via low-rank residuals in anchor-relative semantic coordinates. Define three model variants: Ours (base) stores anchor features plus compact slot residuals; Ours (light) stores only anchor features; Ours (max) stores full-dimensional completed slot features. Compare across KITTI, Virtual KITTI, and Waymo without scene-specific semantic optimization.
AI.result: Ours(base) nearly matches Ours(max) in accuracy across datasets. On KITTI, 34.19 2D mIoU with 2.72 GiB feature footprint vs 34.20 mIoU and 12.90 GiB for Ours(max). Similar trends on Virtual KITTI and Waymo, indicating substantial storage savings with minimal loss in performance.
AI.conclusion: Persistent semantic ownership and a hierarchical representation balance stability, detail, and cost in language fields for view-conditioned Gaussian scenes. The approach achieves strong accuracy with much reduced storage, and code/checkpoints/benchmarks will be publicly released.

title: Making Alternative Data Work: Context-Augmented LLMs for Financial Forecasting
summary: When forecasting a firm's future financial performance, alternative data - data collected from non-traditional sources such as consumer transactions, web traffic, and prediction markets - can provide timely signals about firms' operating activities and broader market conditions. These signals may reveal information that is not captured by traditional public sources and can therefore provide complementary information for forecasting firms' future financial performance. However, firm-level alternative data often have limited historical coverage, are relevant only to specific prediction targets or subsets of firms, and are distributed across numerous heterogeneous channels, making them difficult to incorporate flexibly into conventional forecasting approaches. Meanwhile, large language models (LLMs) can interpret instructions, learn from in-context examples, and generate predictions by combining heterogeneous information without task-specific parameter updates. Motivated by this potential flexibility, we investigate whether an LLM can forecast firm performance by integrating alternative data with other financial information through in-context learning. We propose a two-agent framework that first identifies the firms for which each alternative data channel is likely to be informative and then predicts revenue using firm- and channel-specific context. We evaluate the framework across four commercial alternative data channels. In our experiments, adding alternative data in context alongside other financial information improves the LLM's forecasting relative to either source alone, and these forecasts are more accurate than those of standard forecasting baselines. These findings suggest that LLMs provide a flexible and practical approach to integrating alternative data with heterogeneous financial information.

AI.tldr: An LLM-based two-agent approach integrates four commercial alternative data channels with standard financial information via in-context learning to forecast firm revenue, improving accuracy over using either source alone or standard baselines.
AI.motivation: Alternative data provide timely signals about firms' activities and market conditions but suffer from sparse history and heterogeneity across channels, making integration into forecasting challenging. LLMs offer flexible, in-context fusion without task-specific fine-tuning.
AI.method: Propose a two-agent framework: (1) channel-firm informer identifies which data channels are informative for which firms; (2) revenue predictor uses firm- and channel-specific context to forecast revenue through in-context learning in an LLM. Evaluation across four commercial alternative data channels, comparing against baselines and single-source forecasts.
AI.result: In-context integration of alternative data with traditional financial information improves forecasting performance relative to using either source alone and outperforms standard forecasting baselines.
AI.conclusion: LLMs provide a flexible, practical means to combine heterogeneous alternative data with financial information for firm revenue forecasting, addressing data heterogeneity and limited historical coverage.

title: Dynamic language model representations for multi-objective reaction optimisation
summary: Optimising chemical reactions across multiple objectives, such as yield, selectivity, and safety, is central to chemical synthesis, and model-driven approaches depend critically on how reaction components are represented. Established featurisations are either chemically uninformative, as with one-hot encodings, or, as with molecular descriptors, do not readily extend across chemically distinct components. For structurally and functionally diverse components, it is therefore unclear what a shared representation should contain. Constructing such a representation is itself a challenging research undertaking that must be revisited for each new reaction system. Here we bypass this step by learning the reaction representation dynamically from text. Textual descriptions of reaction conditions are encoded by a fine-tuned language model trained jointly with Gaussian process surrogates, yielding task-adaptive representations within a multi-objective Bayesian optimisation loop. Across nickel- and palladium-catalysed cross-couplings in both sequential and parallel experimentation regimes, this approach reaches optimisation convergence in fewer experiments than descriptor libraries or one-hot encoding. Applied prospectively to a palladium-catalysed cyanation spanning mixed ligand denticity and heterogeneous additives, and to a three-objective asymmetric hydrogenation across chiral iridium and ruthenium catalyst families, two rounds of high-throughput experimentation (192 reactions, under 3% of each design space) delivered conditions translating directly to gram scale in 94% and 84% isolated yield, the latter at 99.6% enantiomeric excess.

AI.tldr: A text-based, task-adaptive representation learned by fine-tuning a language model jointly with Gaussian process surrogates to drive multi-objective Bayesian optimization for diverse cross-coupling reactions, achieving faster convergence and enabling high-yield, high-ee results in few experiments.
AI.motivation: Fixed featurisations (one-hot, descriptors) struggle to generalize across chemically diverse components; there is a need for a shared, informative, adaptable representation that can be learned for each reaction system to enable efficient multi-objective optimization.
AI.method: Fine-tune a language model on textual descriptions of reaction conditions and couple it with Gaussian process surrogates within a multi-objective Bayesian optimization loop; evaluate across nickel- and palladium-catalysed cross-couplings in sequential and parallel experimental settings; extend prospectively to Pd-cyanation and triple-objective asymmetric hydrogenation over multiple catalyst families.
AI.result: Achieves optimization convergence in fewer experiments than descriptor libraries or one-hot representations; two rounds of high-throughput experiments (192 reactions, <3% of design space) delivered gram-scale conditions; isolated yields of 94% and 84%, with 99.6% ee for the latter.
AI.conclusion: Task-adaptive, text-derived representations enable efficient multi-objective optimization across diverse reaction systems, reducing experimental effort and enabling scalable, high-performance outcomes.

title: Vidu S2: Real-Time Interactive, Editable, and Spatial Video Generation
summary: We present Vidu S2, which comprises Vidu S2-Avatar, a real-time interactive digital-character model, and Vidu S2-Editing, a real-time video editing model. Moreover, we explore the feasibility of real-time spatial video generation for both Vidu S2-Avatar and Vidu S2-Editing. Compared with Vidu S1, Vidu S2-Avatar supports real-time 720p video generation, generation with dynamic references that can be updated at any moment, and stronger instruction following, such as dancing. Vidu S2-Editing supports editing a video stream in real time, including style rendering, clothing replacement, character replacement, and background replacement. Experiments show that Vidu S2 outperforms all baselines. A playable online demo is available at https://vidu.com/vidu-stream.

AI.tldr: Vidu S2 introduces a real-time, 720p avatar-based video generation and real-time video editing system with dynamic reference updates, showing superior performance over Vidu S1 and baselines; includes a playable online demo.
AI.motivation: To enable interactive, real-time digital humans and live video editing with updatable references, enabling dynamic tasks (e.g., dancing) in real time.
AI.method: Decomposed into Vidu S2-Avatar (real-time 720p generation with dynamic references) and Vidu S2-Editing (real-time video editing including style rendering, clothing, character, and background replacement); explores feasibility of real-time spatial video generation for both components and demonstrates stronger instruction following.
AI.result: Experiments show Vidu S2 outperforms all baselines; supports real-time 720p generation and dynamic reference updates; real-time editing capabilities demonstrated; online demo available.
AI.conclusion: Vidu S2 advances real-time digital-human generation and video editing by enabling spatial, interactive video generation for avatars and editing pipelines, with an accessible online demo to showcase feasibility.

title: Distributed Optimization of Modular Production Systems using Model-based Reinforcement Learning with Inverse Models
summary: This paper presents a novel approach for data-driven self-learning control of highly flexible, modular manufacturing systems. Specifically, we employ a novel framework for model-based reinforcement learning which introduces approximate inverse process models within the training of reinforcement policies. This approach disentangles the learning of actuation dynamics and the dynamics in state space, resulting in RL-based training solely within the task space. We propose a lightweight feedforward architecture for approximate inverse models and integrate them within the policy network of standard RL algorithms. We apply the approach to a laboratory modular production testbed with heterogeneous production modules. The results underline the efficiency improvements for modular manufacturing units in terms of both performance and training speed, particularly for off-policy algorithms.

AI.tldr: Proposes a model-based RL framework that uses approximate inverse process models to disentangle actuation and state dynamics, enabling RL in task space for modular manufacturing; shows faster training and better performance on a lab testbed, especially with off-policy methods.
AI.motivation: Improve data-driven control for highly flexible, modular manufacturing systems by increasing training efficiency and reducing the complexity of learning dynamics.
AI.method: Incorporates lightweight feedforward approximate inverse models into the policy network within a model-based RL framework; separates actuation dynamics from state dynamics; tasks are learned in task space; validated on a heterogeneous, laboratory modular production testbed; emphasizes off-policy RL.
AI.result: Demonstrates efficiency gains in both performance and training speed for modular units, with notable benefits for off-policy algorithms.
AI.conclusion: Disentangling actuation and state dynamics via inverse models within RL can enhance data efficiency and training speed in modular manufacturing; framework is adaptable to heterogeneous production modules.

title: Thinking with Looped Flows
summary: Humans and machines often solve harder problems by spending more time on computation. In deep learning, looped models implement this idea during inference by recurrently updating a hidden state. In practice, however, their training backpropagates through only one or a few updates, making it hard to train early updates to support future ones. We propose looped flows, an approach that sidesteps this issue by training the recurrence with local denoising objectives. By imposing temporal association across denoising objectives through progressively decreasing noise levels and shared noise, the model is incentivized to learn recurrent states that transfer useful computation over time, even when gradients cover only a few updates. We then formulate inference as integrating the velocity of a probability flow parameterized by the learned denoiser, coupled with recurrent states. This allows solving harder problems by spending more computation through a finer temporal grid and enables multiple valid predictions from different initial noise samples. Across six reasoning benchmarks including two multi-solution benchmarks, looped flows outperform prior state-of-the-art looped models overall, achieving 58.8% test accuracy on ARC-AGI-1 and 12.2% on ARC-AGI-2.

AI.tldr: Looped flows train recurrent models via local denoising objectives with progressively decreasing/shared noise to encourage transfer of computation across time, and perform inference by integrating a probability-flow velocity parameterized by a learned denoiser; this enables deeper computation and multiple valid predictions, improving over prior looped models on several benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Backpropagation through long recurrence during training is difficult, making it hard to train early updates to support future ones. A training objective that enforces temporal consistency over denoising steps can align early and later updates.
AI.method: Train the recurrence with local denoising objectives across noise levels, enforcing temporal association via shared noise and decreasing noise. During inference, solve by integrating the velocity of a probability flow parameterized by the learned denoiser, coupled with recurrent states; allow finer temporal grids for more computation and multiple predictions from different initial noise samples.
AI.result: On six reasoning benchmarks (including two multi-solution ones), looped flows outperform prior looped models, achieving 58.8% test accuracy on ARC-AGI-1 and 12.2% on ARC-AGI-2.
AI.conclusion: Local denoising objectives with temporal association can train recurrent models to transfer useful computation over time. Inference via probability-flow velocity enables deeper computation and diverse predictions, yielding strong performance on challenging reasoning tasks.

title: Self-Supervised Cardiac Phase Detection via Single-Parameter Latent Orbits
comment: Accepted for oral presentation at the ASMUS workshop at MICCAI 2026
summary: Accurate identification of end-diastole (ED) and end-systole (ES) in echocardiography underpins the quantification of ventricular function, yet manual selection of these key frames is subjective and introduces clinically significant inter-operator variability. Recent self-supervised methods either prescribe strict periodic trajectories or learn an unconstrained low-dimensional motion subspace from reconstruction or registration objectives. The former offers interpretability but imposes restrictive assumptions on temporal progression, whereas the latter leaves cardiac phase implicit and ED/ES must be recovered through post-hoc geometric processing of the learned trajectory. We translate the physiological observation that cardiac phase is a one-dimensional signal into a prior by constraining the latent motion component to a single-parameter latent orbit, i.e., a global linear trajectory in latent space indexed by a bounded scalar phase variable. Mapping this variable through a sinusoidal nonlinearity yields an oscillatory motion signal with consistent temporal ordering, enabling direct identification of ED and ES from the learned phase signal. This inductive bias allows the model to capture an interpretable representation of the cardiac cycle, while maintaining flexibility to capture irregular heartbeats. Trained on EchoNet-Dynamic without annotations, our minimal single-parameter cardiac phase model learns an effective latent orbit, significantly improves upon the previous state of the art in ED localisation and matches it in ES localisation while using a more constrained representation and fewer training epochs. This demonstrates that a principled physiological inductive bias can match or exceed the performance of more complex representations. Code is available at: https://github.com/BonniciJ/OrbitalEcho/

AI.tldr: A minimal one-parameter cardiac phase model with a latent sinusoidal trajectory captures the cardiac cycle, enabling direct ED/ES identification from unannotated echocardiography data and outperforming prior self-supervised methods in ED localization while matching ES localization.
AI.motivation: Manual ED/ES frame selection in echocardiography is subjective and introduces clinically significant inter-operator variability; existing self-supervised approaches either impose strict periodicity or learn unconstrained motion, but struggle with interpretability or phase recovery.
AI.method: Introduce a single-parameter latent phase variable that indexes a global linear latent orbit. Apply a sinusoidal nonlinearity to generate an oscillatory motion signal whose phase corresponds to the cardiac cycle. Train self-supervised on EchoNet-Dynamic without annotations, learning the latent orbit and phase signal, enabling direct ED/ES identification from the phase.
AI.result: The model learns an effective latent orbit under a physiological inductive bias, achieving superior ED localization compared to prior art and matching state-of-the-art ES localization, with fewer training epochs and a more constrained representation.
AI.conclusion: Imposing a principled physiological inductive bias (one-dimensional cardiac phase) can match or exceed performance of more complex representations in estimating ED/ES from echocardiography, even under irregular heartbeats; code is available.

title: MAPLE: Memory-Augmented Planning with Language and Evolution
summary: Domain practitioners understand their business constraints but may lack operations-research expertise or dedicated support. LLM-based optimization agents translate natural-language requirements into models or solver programs that established optimization tools can execute. This progress makes optimization more accessible, but real-world operations are dynamic: changing demand, resources, and priorities require updates to data, constraints, and objectives. Methods centered on isolated requests offer limited support for rapid adaptation that preserves earlier decisions and reuses useful search results. We introduce MAPLE (Memory-Augmented Planning with Language and Evolution), an agent for maintaining optimization problems through successive natural-language requests. MAPLE combines language-based problem construction with mathematical programming and evolutionary search. It retains the optimization program, accepted plans, earlier updates, and candidate solutions for subsequent requests. We introduce NLDO, a benchmark of 15 trajectories and 180 updates spanning selection, scheduling, rostering, routing, and cloud-resource placement. In the main evaluation, MAPLE completes all trajectories and achieves online scalar quality of 0.951 and a Pareto hypervolume ratio of 0.875. Controlled comparisons further show that maintaining executable state improves update validity and can preserve useful search information across substantial revisions.

AI.tldr: MAPLE is a memory-augmented planning agent for maintaining optimization problems across successive natural-language requests, achieving strong online performance on NLDO benchmark.
AI.motivation: Domain practitioners need to translate natural-language requirements into optimization models while dynamic real-world conditions demand updates and reuse of past computations; existing NL-based approaches lack persistent state to support rapid adaptation.
AI.method: Introduce MAPLE, a memory-augmented agent that stores the executable optimization program, accepted plans, prior updates, and candidate solutions; combines language-based problem construction with mathematical programming and evolutionary search; evaluates on NLDO, a benchmark of 15 trajectories and 180 updates across domains like selection, scheduling, rostering, routing, and cloud-resource placement.
AI.result: MAPLE completes all trajectories; online scalar quality 0.951; Pareto hypervolume ratio 0.875; controlled comparisons show that maintaining executable state improves update validity and preserves useful search information across substantial revisions.
AI.conclusion: Maintaining executable state via memory augmentation improves adaptability and reuse in NL-driven optimization, enabling better performance across dynamic updates compared to non-stateful approaches.

title: Model-Aware Schedules Improve Generation via Fiberwise Optimal Transport
comment: 11 pages, 2 figures. Keywords: Diffusion models; flow matching; schedule optimization; fiberwise optimal transport; time reparameterization; empirical universality
summary: Diffusion and flow-matching schedules control the signal and noise coefficients that mix data and noise along affine probability paths. Minimizing a kinetic action defined on coefficient paths, motivated by optimal transport, helps explain strong baselines but remains model-agnostic and ignores prediction error. Here we introduce a model-aware schedule construction based on fiberwise optimal transport. At a fixed time and state on the probability path, compatible signal/noise decompositions form an affine fiber. We define a fiberwise prediction risk by averaging optimal-transport costs between the true and predictor-induced decompositions within these fibers. On a fixed coefficient curve, combining this risk with coefficient-path kinetic action yields a closed-form optimal time allocation. This construction extends to general linear prediction targets, and the risk profile can be estimated from an early baseline checkpoint. We evaluate DDPMs and flow matching across prediction targets, training configurations, risk-estimation checkpoints, datasets, and architectures. Our model-aware schedules consistently outperform strong baselines, including a 38.6% relative FID reduction for flow matching on CIFAR-10 at 16 function evaluations. Each model-agnostic kinetic baseline determines its own kinetic reference coordinate. In these coordinates, fiberwise-risk profiles from independently trained models in different settings align closely after normalization to unit area. The resulting schedule deformations used in training also align, suggesting empirical universality across the evaluated models and settings. Pretrained-checkpoint diagnostics extend this normalized-risk agreement to larger conditional latent diffusion and 2-RF models. A frozen analytic allocation template retains most of the model-aware improvement without further risk estimation or model-specific fitting.

AI.tldr: Model-aware schedule for diffusion/flow-matching via fiberwise optimal transport; yields improved training schedules and outperforms baselines, with universal risk profiles and practical templates.
AI.motivation: Model-agnostic kinetic-action-based schedules explain baselines but ignore prediction error; need schedule that accounts for prediction risk and model structure.
AI.method: At fixed time/state, define affine fiber of signal/noise decompositions; define fiberwise prediction risk as average OT cost between true and predictor-induced decompositions. On a fixed coefficient curve, combine risk with kinetic action to obtain closed-form optimal time allocation. Extend to general linear targets; risk estimable from early baseline checkpoints; evaluate across datasets and architectures.
AI.result: Model-aware schedules consistently outperform baselines; e.g., 38.6% relative FID reduction on CIFAR-10 at 16 function evaluations for flow matching. Risk profiles align across independently trained models after normalization. Frozen analytic allocation template retains most improvements without extra risk estimation.
AI.conclusion: Fiberwise, model-aware scheduling reveals potential universal structures across diffusion models; risk-informed allocations facilitate transfer and robustness; practical template for schedule design.

title: Multimodal Taxonomic Conditioning for Generative Plankton Imagery
comment: European Conference on Computer Vision (ECCV) 2nd Workshop on Marine Vision
summary: Automated plankton imaging produces severely long-tailed datasets, where the rare taxa of greatest ecological interest have too few images to train or evaluate classifiers reliably. We generate synthetic plankton imagery conditioned on taxonomy: a CLIP encoder is adapted on a large plankton corpus with a ranked contrastive objective extended to deep, ragged taxonomies, then frozen to condition a parameter-efficient diffusion transformer. We evaluate synthetic sample quality on distributional fidelity and downstream classifier utility.

AI.tldr: Taxonomy-conditioned synthetic plankton images via CLIP adaptation and diffusion transformer to mitigate long-tailed data problem for rare taxa.
AI.motivation: Long-tailed distributions in automated plankton imaging; rare taxa are ecologically important but underrepresented; synthetic data could improve training and evaluation.
AI.method: Train/adapt a CLIP encoder on a large plankton corpus employing a ranked contrastive objective across a deep taxonomic tree with ragged taxonomy; freeze this encoder to condition a parameter-efficient diffusion transformer, enabling taxonomy-conditioned image synthesis; evaluate generated samples for fidelity and utility in downstream classifiers.
AI.result: Evaluation focuses on distributional fidelity and downstream classifier utility; the abstract reports evaluation metrics but does not provide explicit quantitative results in the provided text.
AI.conclusion: The approach demonstrates a pathway to produce taxonomy-conditioned synthetic plankton imagery to address data imbalance and support classifier development for rare taxa.

title: Autonomy, Social Norms, and Alignment: Towards a Developmental Framework for Autonomous Artificial Agents
comment: In publication in the proceedings of SIpEIA 2026 conference
summary: In recent years, artificial intelligence has made extraordinary progress thanks to large-scale models capable of generalization and the generation of complex outputs. However, transferring this potential into embodied agents reveals a significant limitation: the most advanced systems rely on pre-existing datasets and human feedback strategies that are powerful but insufficient in dynamic or unknown contexts. To adapt, an agent must acquire knowledge through direct interaction with its environment. One strategy to address this challenge involves introducing higher-level mechanisms, such as intrinsic motivations, which leverage curiosity and competence, to guide exploration and learning in complex environments. While this flexibility expands autonomy, it complicates the task of ensuring agents remain aligned with human goals. Alignment, already a challenge for artificial systems in general, becomes even more complex in unstructured and dynamic contexts where predefined rules prove insufficient. To be effective and adaptable, norms must be rooted in experience through an epistemological process that starting from simple, situated principles allows for the gradual construction of more complex rules through experience, autonomous learning, and cooperation with other moral agents. Similarly to children learning social norms by exploring their environment and participating in collective practices, artificial agents must also be educated toward alignment. Following Dennett, the status of a moral agent is not innate but is attributed gradually based on the ability to responsibly manage increasing degrees of freedom. From this perspective, the regulatory sandboxes can be viewed as pedagogical environments for AI: dynamic spaces where alignment develops as a formative process, progressively shaping autonomous behaviors through interaction and cooperation in scenarios of increasing complexity.

AI.tldr: Proposes a developmental, sandbox-based framework for AI alignment using intrinsic motivation and experiential learning, treating moral agency as gradually attributed through interaction and cooperation.
AI.motivation: Address the gap between powerful AI systems trained on static data and the need for autonomous agents to align in dynamic, unknown environments by leveraging curiosity-driven exploration and epistemic norm formation.
AI.method: Theoretical/conceptual synthesis: embed intrinsic motivations (curiosity, competence) to drive exploration; ground norm formation in experiential and cooperative learning; view alignment as a gradual process inspired by Dennett and child development; regulatory sandboxes serve as pedagogical environments for progressively complex alignment.
AI.result: A conceptual framework outlining how alignment can emerge through interaction in sandbox settings, with norms rooted in experience and cooperation; no empirical results are provided.
AI.conclusion: Alignment should be cultivated as a formative, experience-based process via regulatory sandboxes, enabling autonomous behaviors to mature through increasingly complex scenarios and collaboration with other agents.

title: AdamX: Cosine similarity meets gradient descent
summary: We introduce AdamX, a first-order optimizer that incorporates cosine similarity as an adaptive mechanism for controlling update magnitudes. The proposed method is scalable, model-agnostic, and straightforward to integrate into existing training pipelines. We further introduce a variance rectification scheme that promotes smoother optimization during the early stages of training. Overall, we provide empirical evidence that AdamX achieves competitive convergence rates across a range of benchmark datasets and architectures. Performance is evaluated in terms of the number of epochs required to reach predefined performance thresholds under a fixed hyperparameter budget. Code and Experiments available at: https://github.com/FranciscoCaldas/adamX.

AI.tldr: AdamX introduces cosine-similarity-based adaptive updates with a variance-rectified scheme, aiming for scalable, model-agnostic optimization and smoother early training, with competitive convergence measured by epochs to target performance under fixed hyperparameter budgets.
AI.motivation: Motivation is to dynamically scale update magnitudes using cosine similarity to improve convergence, while stabilizing early training via variance rectification; target is a simple, scalable optimizer that can be integrated into existing pipelines across diverse models and datasets.
AI.method: Proposes AdamX, a first-order optimizer where cosine similarity guides the adaptive update magnitude. Includes a variance rectification component to stabilize early optimization. Claimed to be model-agnostic and easy to integrate with standard training pipelines.
AI.result: Empirical evidence that AdamX achieves competitive convergence rates across various benchmarks and architectures. Evaluation focuses on epochs needed to reach predefined performance thresholds under a fixed hyperparameter budget. Code and experiments are provided at the project URL.
AI.conclusion: AdamX appears to be a competitive, scalable optimizer that leverages cosine similarity for adaptive updates and adds variance rectification to improve early-stage stability; its portability across models and datasets is emphasized, supported by public code and experiments.

title: Single-Stream Multi-Feature Fusion with Temporal Robustness for Gait Emotion Recognition
comment: Accepted at the 35th International Conference on Artificial Neural Networks (ICANN 2026)
summary: 3D skeleton-based gait emotion recognition faces high annotation costs, data scarcity, and poor generalization on heterogeneous data. This paper proposes SV-GCN, a single-stream multi-feature fusion framework with temporal invariance. We introduce intra-frame relative motion features to eliminate frame-rate sensitivity and embed heterogeneous cues at shallow layers, enabling early fusion without multi-stream complexity. For variable-length sequences, we design a global mask-guided valid-frame spatio-temporal graph convolution module, introducing frame-rate insensitivity for the first time in this domain. On the E-Gait dataset, our method achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art while demonstrating strong generalization across varying sequence lengths and frame rates, offering a viable pathway for pre-training on large-scale skeleton-based action recognition datasets.

AI.tldr: A single-stream, frame-rate invariant gait emotion recognition framework (SV-GCN) that fuses multi-feature cues in early layers and uses a global mask-guided valid-frame spatio-temporal graph convolution to achieve frame-rate insensitivity and robust generalization on E-Gait.
AI.motivation: Address high annotation costs, data scarcity, and poor cross-domain generalization in 3D skeleton-based gait emotion recognition, and reduce model complexity by avoiding multi-stream architectures.
AI.method: Propose SV-GCN with intra-frame relative motion features for frame-rate invariance, early fusion of heterogeneous cues, and a global mask-guided valid-frame ST-GCN module to handle variable-length sequences and frame-rate variability.
AI.result: Achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art on E-Gait and demonstrates strong generalization across different sequence lengths and frame rates; indicates potential for pre-training on large-scale skeleton-based action datasets.
AI.conclusion: SV-GCN provides a robust, efficient approach to gait emotion recognition with frame-rate invariance and cross-length generalization, enabling effective pre-training and deployment on heterogeneous data.

title: Geospatial AI, Dataverse Metadata, and the Study of Place-Based Government
