summary: Harvard Dataverse hosts over 150,000 research datasets, but the geographic information those datasets carry is entered as free text by depositors and has never been assembled into a searchable structure. We construct a knowledge graph from the repository's public data and metadata, organizing 102,650 datasets within a 215,985-node network of 528,003 edges linking datasets to keywords, publications, subjects, journals, and locations. Of those datasets, 43,991 (42.9 percent) carry at least one geospatial field, geographic coverage, geographic unit, or a bounding box and 96.9 percent of all nodes sit in a single connected component, so datasets remain reachable from one another even when their geospatial metadata share nothing in common. A conservative keyword search identifies 7,654 geospatially tagged datasets (17.4 percent) as directly policy-relevant, with elections and legislatures the largest cluster, followed by government administration, health policy, transportation, and education. Five datasets illustrate how this metadata behaves across policy domains and spatial scales, and an extended use case shows how community language models, stance detection with geographic aggregation, and partisan language bridging tools can attach discourse to place. The central obstacle is place resolution: the same location appears as many disconnected nodes. We argue that the graph provides a concrete setting for developing AI-driven metadata enrichment and entity resolution, and we document its coverage skew toward American, city-level data.

AI.tldr: A large-scale knowledge graph of Harvard Dataverse links 102,650 datasets into a 215,985-node network with 528,003 edges, exposing geospatial metadata fragmentation and policy-relevant clusters; demonstrates AI-ready metadata enrichment and highlights biases toward American city-level data.
AI.motivation: Transform free-text geographic metadata into a structured, searchable graph to enable discovery, cross-dataset linkage, and AI-driven metadata enrichment and entity resolution.
AI.method: Construct a public-data knowledge graph from Harvard Dataverse data and metadata; quantify geospatial coverage and connectivity; link datasets to keywords, publications, subjects, journals, and locations; identify policy-relevant items via keyword filtering; illustrate with five datasets and an extended use case; discuss place resolution and coverage bias.
AI.result: Graph comprises 215,985 nodes and 528,003 edges; 96.9% of nodes in a single connected component; 43,991 datasets carry geospatial metadata; 7,654 geospatially tagged datasets (17.4% of geospatial items) are policy-relevant; policy-domain clusters identified; five use-case datasets; extended use-case with language models and stance detection; central obstacle is place resolution; clear potential for AI-driven metadata enrichment and entity resolution; coverage skew toward American, city-level data.
AI.conclusion: The graph offers a concrete setting for AI-driven metadata enrichment and entity resolution, while underscoring place-resolution challenges and data-coverage bias in favor of American city-level datasets.

title: The Last AI Built by Humans: Toward Genuine Recursive Self-Improvement
summary: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) enables AI systems to turn experience and feedback into persistent changes that improve both their capabilities and the process of future improvement. We first use the Headroom-Closed Index (HCI) to reveal the problems of existing LLMs, then introduce the RSI concept and its development roadmap: from improvement-execution autonomy, improvement-strategy autonomy, experience-acquisition autonomy, and environment-adaptation autonomy, to recursive meta-improvement. Next we examine RSI across scenarios (e.g., scientific discovery, embodied intelligence, software engineering), highlighting their distinct requirements and development speeds. Drawing on diverse industry practices and preliminary empirical evidence, we connect RSI research with practical systems and identify key challenges to achieving genuine RSI.

AI.tldr: Proposes Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) as a staged, autonomous improvement framework for AI, diagnosed with Headroom-Closed Index (HCI), spanning from execution autonomy to meta-improvement, analyzed across domains with preliminary evidence and practical challenges.
AI.motivation: To address limits of current LLMs by enabling persistent, autonomous improvement and to outline a roadmap and domain-specific considerations for RSI.
AI.method: Introduce HCI to diagnose LLM gaps; define RSI concepts and a multi-stage roadmap (execution, strategy, experience, environment autonomy, up to recursive meta-improvement); survey RSI across scenarios; synthesize industry practices and preliminary data; identify challenges.
AI.result: A conceptual taxonomy and roadmap for RSI; cross-domain analysis highlighting distinct requirements and dynamics; linkage to real-world systems; initial empirical signals and identified obstacles toward genuine RSI.
AI.conclusion: Achieving genuine RSI demands advances in autonomy, safety, data acquisition, alignment, and environment interaction; progress will be incremental and domain-dependent, requiring ongoing research and practical integration.

title: Spectral Adapters for Segment Anything Model-based Segmentation of Colorectal Liver Metastases in Computed Tomography
summary: Accurate segmentation of colorectal liver metastases (CRLM) in contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) is important for response assessment, surgical planning, and follow-up. We propose two parameter-efficient spectral adapters for the Segment Anything Model (SAM): the Directional Spectral Adapter (DiSECT) and Spectral Instance-Guided Adapter (SiGA). DiSECT uses singular value decomposition of frozen weights to constrain residual updates to leading spectral directions, while SiGA adds global and input-conditioned gating through a multilayer perceptron. We evaluate these methods on 446 contrast-enhanced CT volumes (355 training, 91 testing) and compare them with LoRA, QLoRA, convolutional adapters (CAD), and a 3D nnU-Net baseline. Experiments consider single-point, three-point, bounding-box, and no-prompt regimes. SiGA achieves the best single-point performance with a Dice score of 0.77, IoU of 0.69, and HD95 of 35.39 mm. Under no-prompt inference, SiGA reaches 0.76 Dice, 0.68 IoU, and 46.76 mm HD95, comparable to the nnU-Net baseline (0.758 Dice). DiSECT uses only 0.14 million trainable parameters. These results show that spectral adapters can efficiently adapt SAM for CRLM segmentation while retaining strong accuracy with limited trainable parameters.

AI.tldr: Two parameter-efficient spectral adapters (DiSECT and SiGA) for adapting Segment Anything Model (SAM) to CRLM segmentation in CT. SiGA yields best single-point performance; DiSECT is highly parameter-efficient. Evaluations show competitive results against LoRA, QLoRA, CAD, and 3D nnU-Net, across prompting regimes; spectral adapters enable efficient adaptation with limited trainable parameters.
AI.motivation: Enable accurate CRLM segmentation using SAM with few trainable parameters, addressing the cost and data requirements of fine-tuning large foundation models for medical imaging tasks.
AI.method: Introduce two spectral adapters (DiSECT and SiGA) that modify SAM during training: DiSECT constrains residual updates to leading spectral directions via SVD of frozen weights; SiGA adds global and input-conditioned gating through an MLP. Evaluate on 446 contrast-enhanced CT volumes under single-point, three-point, bounding-box, and no-prompt regimes, comparing to LoRA, QLoRA, CAD, and 3D nnU-Net.
AI.result: SiGA achieves best single-point performance: Dice 0.77, IoU 0.69, HD95 35.39 mm. Under no-prompt inference, SiGA: Dice 0.76, IoU 0.68, HD95 46.76 mm, comparable to nnU-Net baseline (0.758 Dice). DiSECT uses only 0.14M trainable parameters. Overall, spectral adapters enable efficient SAM adaptation for CRLM segmentation with strong accuracy and limited trainable parameters.
AI.conclusion: Spectral adapters (DiSECT and SiGA) provide parameter-efficient means to adapt SAM for CRLM segmentation in CT, achieving competitive performance with limited trainable parameters, especially SiGA for high-accuracy single-point prompts.

title: COBRA-Skills: Contextual Bandit-Guided Evolution for Agent Skill Optimization
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents can benefit from reusable skills distilled from prior task experience, yet existing skill optimization methods often rely on costly execution-based evaluation and substantial task data. We introduce \textbf{COBRA-Skills}, an efficient framework that formulates skill optimization as budgeted sequential optimization over a dynamically evolving candidate space. COBRA-Skills couples contextual-bandit-guided prioritization with evidence-grounded skill evolution, selectively allocating evaluations to promising or informative candidates while continually refining the skill population from execution feedback. Across six heterogeneous agent benchmarks and three target models, COBRA-Skills consistently achieves the strongest average performance among compared methods, while reducing optimization cost by 55--58\% relative to SkillOpt and using only 50 unique optimization examples per benchmark. Further analyses show that COBRA-Skills remains robust to changes in the agent harness and performs effectively when the target model itself is used for skill generation and refinement.

AI.tldr: COBRA-Skills presents a budgeted, sequential optimization framework for LLM skill optimization that uses contextual-bandit prioritization and evidence-grounded skill evolution to efficiently improve skills with limited evaluation data.
AI.motivation: Existing skill optimization methods require costly execution and large task datasets. There is a need for an efficient, robust approach that can evolve candidate skills with limited feedback and under varying agent/harness environments.
AI.method: Formulates skill optimization as budgeted sequential optimization over a dynamically evolving candidate space. Combines contextual-bandit-guided prioritization to select promising candidates for evaluation with evidence-grounded skill evolution that refines the skill population using execution feedback.
AI.result: COBRA-Skills achieves the strongest average performance across six heterogeneous agent benchmarks and three target models, while reducing optimization cost by 55–58% relative to SkillOpt and using only 50 optimization examples per benchmark. It is robust to changes in the agent harness and remains effective when the target model generates/refines skills.
AI.conclusion: A scalable, robust framework for efficient LLM skill optimization that balances exploration and exploitation with dynamic candidate refinement, delivering substantial cost savings and broad applicability across models and settings.

title: CoRA-NAS: Coarse Ranking and Anchor-Residual Refinement for Neural Architecture Search
summary: Zero-cost proxies rank architectures cheaply, but their reliability varies across search spaces. We introduce CoRA-NAS (COarse Ranking + Anchor-residual), a two-stage framework combining a static ranking prior with low-cost learning-curve refinement. CoRA-Rank aggregates capacity and structure-at-initialization proxies through an equal-weight log-rank consensus and a target-free consensus gate. CoRA-Refine samples anchors across this prior, extrapolates their early validation curves, and propagates a learned residual correction with an ExtraTrees model. The refinement uses approximately 1% of the cost of fully training the candidate set. Fully trained architecture-accuracy labels are not used to fit the ranker. One configuration is used across spaces, with space-specific architecture encodings. Across NAS-Bench-201, NAS-Bench-101, TransNAS-Bench-101, and NATS-SSS, CoRA-Refine achieves mean Spearman correlations of 0.946, 0.715, 0.786, and 0.894, respectively. Its worst-space correlation of 0.715 is the highest among the compared methods. On NAS-Bench-201/CIFAR-100, its selected architecture reaches 73.32% accuracy, near the reported ground-truth best of 73.37%. On the pure size space, refinement recovers the static prior's shortfall relative to parameter count, while remaining tied with the strongest capacity proxies within noise. The resulting framework combines cross-space ranking robustness with low-cost architecture selection.

AI.tldr: A two-stage zero-cost NAS method (CoRA-NAS) that couples static priors with a low-cost refinement to robustly rank architectures across search spaces, achieving high cross-space Spearman correlations with minimal training cost.
AI.motivation: Zero-cost proxies are cheap but variably reliable across search spaces. A cross-space, low-cost ranking framework is needed to reliably identify good architectures without full training.
AI.method: Stage 1 CoRA-Rank aggregates capacity and structure-at-initialization proxies via equal-weight log-rank consensus and a target-free consensus gate to form a static prior. Stage 2 CoRA-Refine samples anchors from this prior, extrapolates their early validation curves, and learns a residual correction using an ExtraTrees model. Training costs are ~1% of full training. A single configuration is used across spaces with space-specific architecture encodings.
AI.result: Across NAS-Bench-201, NAS-Bench-101, TransNAS-Bench-101, and NATS-SSS, CoRA-Refine achieves mean Spearman correlations of 0.946, 0.715, 0.786, and 0.894 respectively, with the worst-space correlation (0.715) being the highest among compared methods. On NAS-Bench-201/CIFAR-100, the selected architecture reaches 73.32% accuracy, near the ground-truth best 73.37%. In the pure size space, refinement recovers the static prior’s shortfall relative to parameter count while remaining competitive with the strongest capacity proxies.
AI.conclusion: CoRA-NAS provides robust cross-space ranking with low-cost refinement, enabling effective architecture search with limited training data and achieving near-optimal results in at least one benchmark.

title: Language-Augmented Semantic Priors for B-Spline Surface Fitting
summary: The use of B-splines and Non-Uniform Rational B-Splines surfaces constitutes the mathematical foundation of contemporary computer-aided design (CAD) systems. Despite long-term progress, geometric kernels in traditional CAD still rely heavily on predetermined heuristic initialization for surface fitting and parameterization. Meanwhile, the procedural semantics and design intent encoded in modeling histories are largely ignored during geometry generation. This disconnect creates a gap between high-level design intent and solver-executable geometric configuration, often leading to suboptimal and semantically inconsistent fitting results. To bridge this gap, we introduce LASP, a Language-Augmented Semantic Priors framework that leverages large language models (LLMs) to infer structured, solver-usable B-spline priors from procedural modeling histories. Rather than modifying the geometric kernel itself, LASP operates as a semantic reasoning layer above existing solvers. It first translates modeling histories into rich textual descriptions that capture design intent, geometric context, and functional relationships, and then uses a fine-tuned LLM to predict structured B-spline prior parameters. LASP is trained through a two-stage scheme that combines local geometric regularities with long-range contextual dependencies, producing priors that are both interpretable and semantically coherent. This approach furnishes inductive signals that direct the conventional B-spline fitting process toward solutions that more accurately encapsulate the intended design objectives and demonstrate heightened semantic coherence. Compared to traditional machine learning schemes, the experiments demonstrate that language-driven reasoning can serve as a powerful inductive bias for geometric solving, establishing a new paradigm of language-guided geometric optimization in modern CAD systems.

AI.tldr: A language-augmented semantic priors (LASP) framework uses fine-tuned LLMs to infer B-spline priors from procedural modeling histories, guiding CAD surface fitting as a semantic layer above existing solvers without altering kernels.
AI.motivation: Bridge the gap between high-level design intent and solver-executable geometry in CAD; conventional initializations are heuristic and often semantically misaligned; leverage language to encode design intent into solver-ready priors.
AI.method: Two-stage scheme: (1) translate modeling histories into rich textual descriptions capturing intent, context, and relations; (2) fine-tune an LLM to predict structured B-spline prior parameters; LASP acts as a semantic layer above solvers, combining local geometric regularities with long-range context to produce interpretable priors.
AI.result: Experiments show language-driven reasoning provides a strong inductive bias that guides traditional B-spline fitting toward design objectives with higher semantic coherence, outperforming traditional ML schemes in aligning geometry with intent.
AI.conclusion: Language-guided geometric optimization is a new paradigm for CAD; LASP delivers interpretable, semantically coherent B-spline priors that improve fitting without modifying kernels.

title: When Agents Disagree: Bayesian Backward Reasoning as a Label-Free Anchor for Multi-Agent Collective Decision-Making
summary: When multiple LLM agents yield conflicting answers, the decision-making process dictates whether agent diversity improves performance or merely compounds shared errors. Existing collective decision-making methods, including voting, electoral rules, and LLM judges, rely on forward reasoning: they map evidence to labels in one direction. Although these methods can combine diverse forward traces, they still aggregate estimates that share this evidence-to-label factorization and can inherit correlated errors within the forward pool. We therefore construct a reverse posterior for each instance through Bayesian backward reasoning from an explicit likelihood. The forward and reverse posteriors provide differently factorized approximations of the underlying posterior. Because estimates from different factorizations may tend to share the same error less often, we use Jensen-Shannon divergence to rank agents by cross-path consistency. This cross-path consistency signal underlies three strategies: hard selection (MinJS), soft reweighting (FwdJS), and log-linear fusion (LogLin). Evaluated on DDXPlus across five LLM backbones, our proposed strategies show consistent improvements: MinJS outperforms random selection across all backbones, FwdJS generally improves over the strongest baseline, and LogLin achieves the best performance among the evaluated methods, with its largest gains on the subset where the agents disagree. Despite its weaker standalone accuracy, the reverse posterior serves as a more useful anchor than forward-only alternatives, providing complementary information for collective decision-making. When labeled data are available, a lightweight two-stage calibration can further refine the reverse anchor and improve aggregation performance.

AI.tldr: Proposes using Bayesian backward reasoning (reverse posteriors) to complement forward posteriors in ensemble LLM decision-making; introduces cross-path consistency via Jensen-Shannon divergence to rank agents and three aggregation strategies (MinJS, FwdJS, LogLin); demonstrates consistent gains on DDXPlus across five backbones; reverse anchor serves as a useful, complementary signal even when standalone accuracy is weaker; notes calibration when labeled data is available.
AI.motivation: Forward-only aggregation methods (voting, electoral rules, LLM judges) can inherit correlated errors due to a shared evidence-to-label factorization. The authors seek to leverage backward reasoning to obtain an alternative, complementary factorization that reduces correlated errors and improves ensemble performance.
AI.method: Construct reverse posteriors by Bayesian backward reasoning from an explicit likelihood. Compute forward and reverse posteriors for each instance. Use Jensen-Shannon divergence to measure cross-path consistency among agents. Develop three strategies: hard selection (MinJS) using the minimum JS score, soft reweighting (FwdJS) based on forward JS, and log-linear fusion (LogLin). Evaluate on DDXPlus across five LLM backbones.
AI.result: Across five LLM backbones on DDXPlus, MinJS consistently outperforms random selection, FwdJS generally surpasses the strongest baseline, and LogLin yields the best performance, especially on instances where agents disagree. The reverse posterior, while weaker as a standalone predictor, provides a valuable anchor and complementary information for aggregation. A light two-stage calibration using labeled data can further refine the reverse anchor and boost performance.
AI.conclusion: Reverse posteriors offer a complementary, less error-prone factorization that improves collective decision-making beyond forward-only methods. Cross-path consistency via JS divergence enables effective aggregation strategies (MinJS, FwdJS, LogLin). The approach remains beneficial even when forward accuracy is high, and calibration with labeled data can further enhance results.

title: CausalArena: Benchmarking Causal Discovery in the Foundation Model Era
summary: Causal discovery aims to uncover causal structures from data and is fundamental to scientific reasoning and intervention-based decision making. Its evaluation relies heavily on structural causal models (SCMs), which specify a causal graph together with the mechanisms that generate data, yet existing studies differ substantially in graph families, mechanisms, and evaluation protocols. The emergence of causal discovery foundation models (CDFMs) further complicates evaluation: performance may reflect not only causal discovery ability, but also overlap between pretraining environments and test SCMs, making results on fixed synthetic benchmarks difficult to interpret. We introduce CausalArena, a unified and evolvable benchmark for causal discovery under a common protocol. Synthetic SCMs supply controlled breadth over structures and mechanisms; semantic operational SCMs provide human-auditable, semantically grounded environments beyond standard synthetic generators; and formula-grounded SCMs test discovery under explicit scientific mechanisms. Public real-world datasets provide an additional external-validity check. Experiments across classical, neural, and pretrained methods reveal substantial ranking shifts across SCM families and protocols, showing that strong performance in one benchmark regime does not reliably transfer to others. These results highlight benchmark diversity and pretraining--evaluation overlap as central challenges for evaluating causal discovery in the foundation model era.

AI.tldr: Introduces CausalArena, a unified, evolvable benchmark for causal discovery spanning synthetic, semantic, and formula-grounded SCMs plus real data; shows cross-regime ranking shifts and argues for benchmark diversity and pretraining-evaluation overlap as core challenges.
AI.motivation: Causal discovery evaluation is inconsistent due to varying graph families, mechanisms, and evaluation protocols; the rise of causal discovery foundation models (CDFMs) complicates interpretation because pretraining may overlap with test SCMs; a common, evolvable benchmark is needed to enable fair cross-method comparison.
AI.method: Proposes CausalArena with three SCM families (synthetic SCMs for controlled breadth; semantic operational SCMs for semantically grounded environments beyond standard synthetic generators; formula-grounded SCMs for explicit scientific mechanisms) plus public real-world datasets; establishes a unified protocol and an evolvable benchmark.
AI.result: Empirical experiments across classical, neural, and pretrained methods reveal substantial ranking shifts across SCM families and protocols; strong performance in one benchmark regime does not reliably transfer to others.
AI.conclusion: The findings highlight benchmark diversity and pretraining–evaluation overlap as central challenges for evaluating causal discovery in the foundation model era; CausalArena offers a framework to address these challenges.

title: SIRF: A Spec-Internalized Risk Foundation Model for Industrial Content Risk Control
comment: 14 pages, 12 figures. Accepted at the Industry Track of EMNLP 2026
summary: For industrial content risk control, the real deployment constraint is not average accuracy but how much risk can be auto-handled under high precision and second-level latency. We present SIRF (Spec-Internalized Risk Foundation Model), which internalizes a platform's complex policies, synthesized without additional human annotation via EntiGraph, MAGA rewriting and account-level chain-of-thought (CoT), into the weights via continued pretraining (CPT), so rules are applied at high precision under an ultra-low-latency, verdict-only deployment. A controlled same-source comparison (Qwen3-8B-SFT vs. SIRF-8B-SFT, identical policy injection and verdict-only output form, differing only in policy-grounded CPT) attributes the gain to internalization: SIRF-8B-SFT reaches 71.3% Black Recall@P95, +15.1pp over the baseline, using only ~70M CPT tokens without harming general ability, and among included, logprob-available models under this interface it matches or exceeds far larger systems. SIRF is deployed as a tree-model adjudication layer (20% more mis-penalized samples recovered) and transfers to a freezing scenario at low cost (~70% relative mis-penalization reduction).

AI.tldr: SIRF uses policy-grounded continued pretraining to internalize platform policies, achieving ultra-low-latency, high-precision content risk control with strong empirical gains over a baseline.
AI.motivation: Industrial content risk control requires high precision at second-level latency. Average accuracy is insufficient when policies are complex and enforcement must be reliable in real-time; internalizing policies can reduce latency and improve policy adherence.
AI.method: Policy-grounded continued pretraining (CPT) guided by EntiGraph, MAGA rewriting, and account-level chain-of-thought, integrated into model weights; verdict-only deployment; identical policy injection with a controlled same-source comparison against Qwen3-8B-SFT; CPT tokens ~70M; tree-model adjudication layer; capability to transfer to freezing scenarios.
AI.result: SIRF-8B-SFT achieves 71.3% Black Recall@P95, +15.1 percentage points over the baseline; uses ~70M CPT tokens without harming general ability; matches or exceeds larger logprob-available models; in deployment, recovers 20% more mis-penalized samples as a tree-layer and reduces mis-penalization by ~70% in a freezing scenario.
AI.conclusion: Internalizing platform policies via CPT can deliver high-precision, low-latency content-risk enforcement with modest additional pretraining, outperforming baselines and scaling well in deployment contexts.

title: TART: A Modular Tool for Technique-Aware Audio-to-Tablature Guitar Transcription
summary: Automatic Music Transcription (AMT) for guitar remains limited by three challenges: existing systems often fail to capture expressive techniques such as slides, bends, and percussive hits; they often assign notes to incorrect string-fret combinations; and they are typically trained on clean recordings, limiting their generalization to noisy real-world audio. To address these challenges, we propose TART, a modular four-stage audio-to-tablature pipeline consisting of (1) an audio-to-MIDI transcription model, (2) an expressive technique classifier, (3) an audio-conditioned T5 encoder-decoder for string-fret assignment, and (4) an automated tablature generator. We evaluate TART in a zero-shot setting on GuitarSet, EGDB, and two augmented benchmarks, Noisy GuitarSet and Noisy EGDB. Averaged across these four benchmarks, TART achieves 81.35% audio-to-MIDI F50 (+6.67 points over the best prior baseline), 71.8% string-fret Tab F1 (+8.5 points over the best prior baseline), and 54.08% end-to-end Tab F1. To our knowledge, TART is the first framework to generate guitar tablature with both fingering and expressive technique annotations directly from guitar audio.

AI.tldr: TART is a modular four-stage audio-to-tablature pipeline for guitar that integrates audio-to-MIDI transcription, expressive technique classification, an audio-conditioned T5 encoder-decoder for string-fret assignment, and automated tablature generation. It achieves strong zero-shot performance on GuitarSet, EGDB, and noisy variants, surpassing prior baselines in audio-to-MIDI, string-fret tab precision, and end-to-end tablature accuracy.
AI.motivation: Address key gaps in guitar AMT: (1) capturing expressive techniques (slides, bends, percussive hits), (2) correct string-fret assignment, and (3) generalization to noisy real-world audio, enabling end-to-end guitar tablature from audio.
AI.method: A four-stage pipeline: (1) an audio-to-MIDI transcription model; (2) an expressive technique classifier; (3) an audio-conditioned T5 encoder-decoder for string-fret assignment; (4) an automated tablature generator. Evaluation performed in a zero-shot setting on GuitarSet, EGDB, Noisy GuitarSet, and Noisy EGDB.
AI.result: Across four benchmarks, TART achieves 81.35% audio-to-MIDI F50 (+6.67 vs best prior baseline), 71.8% string-fret Tab F1 (+8.5), and 54.08% end-to-end Tab F1. It is claimed as the first framework to produce guitar tablature with fingering and expressive technique annotations directly from audio.
AI.conclusion: TART demonstrates strong zero-shot generalization for guitar tablature generation directly from audio, with improved fidelity in MIDI transcription, precise string-fret assignment, and integration of expressive techniques via a modular pipeline.

title: Revisiting Avatar-As-Image: High-Fidelity Registration is All You Need
summary: The representation of 3D clothed humans as standardized 2D UV texture and displacement maps over an underlying body model has long been studied. This compact representation is enticing as it enables pretrained image networks to process, generate, and edit 3D avatars, but is only useful if scans are accurately aligned and brought into correspondence via high-fidelity registration. This prerequisite has never been met, which we argue explains the limited quality of prior UV-based methods for clothed humans. Despite its significance, no public method produces high-fidelity SMPL(-X)+D registrations with UV texture from arbitrary clothed scans. We present AvaImg, a multi-stage optimization pipeline, to close this gap: it enforces body-inside-clothing constraint via signed winding numbers, made viable by a three-level efficiency cascade (~10x runtime reduced, ~95% storage saved), and recovers fine surface detail using coarse-to-fine displacement optimization. AvaImg outperforms all baselines in body fitting, shape estimation, and surface registration across six datasets, yielding textured registrations near-indistinguishable from scans (PSNR=34.48dB). For validation of AvaImg's Avatar-as-Image representation as imminently compatible with image foundation models, we auto-encode our UV maps via the frozen FLUX VAE. This achieves only 0.76mm added Chamfer error relative to scan and shows that the resulting maps lie within natural-image distributions, supporting the use of 2D generative priors for 3D avatar generation. Code, data, and Singularity containers will be at https://yuxuan-xue.com/avaimg.

AI.tldr: AvaImg is a multi-stage optimization pipeline that attains high-fidelity SMPL(-X)+D registrations with UV textures from arbitrary clothed scans by enforcing a body-inside-clothing constraint with signed winding numbers, using a three-level efficiency cascade to reduce runtime ~10x and storage ~95%, and applying coarse-to-fine displacement optimization to recover fine surface detail; validated on six datasets with PSNR 34.48 dB and $0.76$ mm Chamfer error after UV-map auto-encoding, demonstrating compatibility with image priors via a frozen FLUX VAE.
AI.motivation: To enable accurate, high-fidelity UV-based representations of clothed humans that can be processed by pretrained image networks. Prior UV-based methods failed to achieve reliable body-to-skin alignment and correspondences for arbitrary clothed scans, limiting 3D avatar quality and downstream generative capabilities.
AI.method: AvaImg presents a multi-stage optimization pipeline. It enforces body-inside-clothing constraints using signed winding numbers. It employs a three-level efficiency cascade to accelerate optimization and reduce storage. It performs coarse-to-fine displacement optimization to recover surface detail. UV textures are produced on SMPL(-X)+D surfaces, and the UV maps are further validated by auto-encoding with a frozen FLUX VAE to assess compatibility with natural-image distributions.
AI.result: AvaImg outperforms all baselines in body fitting, shape estimation, and surface registration across six datasets, yielding textured registrations near-indistinguishable from scans (PSNR=34.48 dB). The approach achieves only 0.76 mm added Chamfer error relative to the scan after UV-map encoding, and demonstrates substantial storage savings (~95%) and runtime reduction (~10x). The UV maps lie within natural-image distributions, supporting the use of 2D generative priors for 3D avatar generation.
AI.conclusion: AvaImg closes the gap for high-fidelity SMPL(-X)+D registrations with UV textures from arbitrary clothed scans, enabling Avatar-as-Image representations compatible with image foundation models. The approach delivers accurate, view-consistent textures and geometry, amenable to 2D generative priors; code, data, and containers will be released.

title: A Unified Per-Token Gating Family for On-Policy Distillation: FKL/RKL Mixing with Multi-Channel and Bias Coefficients
comment: Accepted at the Findings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP 2026 Findings)
summary: Per-token gating of forward/reverse KL losses has become a standard technique for on-policy knowledge distillation (OPD), but existing methods such as EOPD (Jin et al., 2026) and ToDi (Jung et al., 2025) each fix a single gating signal and a single gating direction, and the two have never been compared directly. We introduce a four-coefficient parameterization lambda_t = sigma(a * h_t + b * u(x) + c + d * gap_t) in which direction-aligned proxies of EOPD and ToDi appear as one-dimensional (1D) restrictions, and which adds multi-channel composition and an explicit bias as further degrees of freedom. On TweetEval (Barbieri et al., 2020) emotion and hate, with a Qwen3-32B teacher and a Qwen3-4B student, configurations in the full family reach higher accuracy than the matched-magnitude single-channel (entropy-only / gap-only) 1D restrictions in 33 of 36 comparable cells, and a 26-cell mean-match isolation experiment places dynamic gating ahead of effective-KL-matched static baselines in 19 of 26 cells. Because cells share training data, models, and parameter substructure, we report both counts as exploratory aggregate directional evidence rather than as independent hypothesis tests. Targeted three-seed paired replications of the nine headline comparisons singled out by that sweep -- including a third task, offensive -- are directionally consistent, but individually smaller than the single-seed estimates and not significant at n=3. We therefore present the parameterization primarily as a shared coordinate system for comparing per-token gating designs in short-output classification OPD.

AI.tldr: Proposes a four-coefficient, multi-channel parameterization for per-token gating in on-policy distillation (OPD) that subsumes prior single-channel methods (EOPD, ToDi); demonstrates improved accuracy in most configurations on TweetEval tasks with a Qwen teacher/student; shows dynamic gating often outperforms static baselines in a directional, exploratory analysis; frames the parameterization as a shared coordinate system for comparing gating designs in short-output classification OPD.
AI.motivation: Existing OPD gating approaches fix a single gating signal and direction, limiting comparability and potential performance. A general, multi-channel gating parameterization can subsume prior methods (as 1D restrictions) and provide a unified framework to compare and optimize gating strategies.
AI.method: Introduce lambda_t = sigma(a * h_t + b * u(x) + c + d * gap_t), a four-coefficient parameterization with a nonlinear sigmoid; interpret EOPD and ToDi as 1D restrictions within this framework; enable multi-channel composition and an explicit bias term; evaluate on TweetEval emotion and hate tasks using a Qwen3-32B teacher and Qwen3-4B student; conduct a 36-cell comparison and a 26-cell mean-match isolation experiment; perform three-seed replications for robustness checks across nine headline comparisons including an offensive task.
AI.result: In the full parameterization family, 33 of 36 cells surpass matched-magnitude single-channel 1D restrictions (entropy-only or gap-only). In the 26-cell mean-match isolation experiment, dynamic gating leads effective-KL-matched static baselines in 19 of 26 cells. Results are reported as exploratory directional evidence due to shared data and limited replication; three-seed replications corroborate directionality but are not individually significant at n=3.
AI.conclusion: The four-coefficient parameterization provides a flexible, shared coordinate system that subsumes prior per-token gating designs and facilitates direct comparisons in short-output classification OPD. It often yields better performance than 1D restrictions and highlights the potential of dynamic gating, while remaining exploratory and contingent on replication.

title: From Protocols to Evidence: Bounded Claims for AI in Service of the Common Good
summary: Artificial Intelligence does more than create a governance problem. It can also reveal where institutions have already failed to provide responsiveness, belonging, care, and accountability. Once deployed, AI becomes an intervention in those conditions. It can repair, compound, substitute for, or conceal the failures it encounters. Responsible AI must therefore evaluate both the system and the institutional rupture into which it is introduced. The move from principles to protocols is already underway. The EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001, and assurance practices translate commitments into roles, requirements, records, oversight, and assessment. The harder questions are what these protocols actually establish, whose power they leave untouched, and where measurement must stop. Pope Leo XIV's Magnifica Humanitas provides a broader moral frame centered on dignity, technological power, and the common good. Drawing on that frame, we develop a rupture test that links institutional baselines to system evaluation. We distinguish evidence-bounded deployment, which limits claims to what has actually been evaluated, from measurement-bounded governance, which records constraints that favorable evidence cannot override. Within those limits, RISE AI provides an architecture for making bounded, evidence-based claims about Responsibility, Inclusivity, Safety, and Empowerment. Responsible AI requires better engineering, institutional repair, and continued moral and political judgment.

AI.tldr: Proposes a rupture-informed Responsible AI framework that links institutional baselines to system evaluation, introducing evidence-bounded deployment and measurement-bounded governance within a RISE AI architecture, guided by a broader moral frame.
AI.motivation: Bridge the gap between governance principles and actual institutional responsiveness failures; ensure AI deployments repair or account for institutional shortcomings and align with human dignity and the common good.
AI.method: Develop a rupture test mapping institutional baselines to system evaluation; differentiate evidence-bounded deployment from measurement-bounded governance; articulate the RISE AI architecture and apply Magnifica Humanitas as moral framing.
AI.result: A conceptual framework for evaluating AI systems across Responsibility, Inclusivity, Safety, and Empowerment, with explicit limits on claims and measurements; emphasizes need for better engineering, institutional repair, and ongoing moral/political judgment.
AI.conclusion: Responsible AI requires not only technical protocols but institutional reform and continuous moral-political judgment, clarifying what protocols can claim and where measurement concludes.

title: Logit Refiner: Improving Visual Autoregressive Models via Intra-Scale Dependency Modeling
summary:
Visual Autoregressive Models (VAR) generate images through next-scale prediction, producing all tokens within each scale in parallel. We show that this parallel decoding constitutes a mean-field-style approximation that discards spatial dependencies among same-scale tokens, causing locally incoherent samples regardless of backbone capacity -- a limitation of the decoding rule. Addressing this limitation, we introduce the Logit Refiner, a lightweight autoregressive module that restores intra-scale dependencies by sequentially sampling tokens conditioned on frozen backbone features. Adding only ~10% parameters and less than 5% of the base model's training compute, it plugs into any pretrained VAR checkpoint without retraining. Controlled ablations isolate joint intra-scale sampling -- rather than additional capacity or training -- as the critical ingredient. Across backbones from 310M to 2B parameters on class-conditional ImageNet 256x256, the refiner consistently improves generation quality, enabling a 1.1B-parameter model to surpass one twice its size. The approach further generalizes to text-to-image generation, confirming that the mean-field bottleneck persists across VAR variants and is effectively alleviated by our method.
  Project page: https://compvis.github.io/logit-refiner/

AI.tldr: Identifies parallel intra-scale decoding in Visual Autoregressive Models as a mean-field bottleneck that discards spatial dependencies, and proposes Logit Refiner— a lightweight, plug-in autoregressive module that sequentially samples tokens conditioned on frozen backbone features—to restore intra-scale dependencies with minimal overhead, yielding consistent quality gains across backbones and even enabling smaller models to match or exceed larger ones, including text-to-image tasks.
AI.motivation: Parallel decoding in VARs treats same-scale tokens independently, ignoring spatial dependencies and causing locally incoherent samples regardless of model capacity. A lightweight fix is needed that can be plugged into pretrained VAR checkpoints without retraining.
AI.method: Introduce Logit Refiner, a lightweight autoregressive module that sequentially samples across tokens within a scale conditioned on frozen backbone features. Adds ~10% parameters and <5% of base model training compute; plug-and-play with pretrained VAR. Controlled ablations show joint intra-scale sampling—not increased capacity or training—drives gains.
AI.result: Across backbones from 310M to 2B parameters on class-conditional ImageNet 256x256, the refiner yields consistent improvements; a 1.1B-parameter model surpasses twice its size. The method also generalizes to text-to-image generation, indicating the mean-field bottleneck persists across VAR variants and is mitigated by Logit Refiner.
AI.conclusion: The mean-field bottleneck is a fundamental limitation of VAR decoding; Logit Refiner provides a minimal, effective solution that is plug-and-play with pretrained checkpoints and scales across tasks, enabling notable quality gains with modest resource overhead.

title: From Parameters to Answers: How LLMs Retrieve and Use Their Internal Knowledge
summary: How does a language model's dependence on query-routing information and target knowledge change as it answers a question? We study this question through layerwise interventions on the hidden state at the end of the question. Across Qwen, Llama, and Gemma, we compare country-continent questions with noun, adjective, and code answers while keeping several fitted measurements distinct. A pair-conditioned request direction describes which country is queried in natural single-country questions; a global request direction describes first- versus second-country requests in paired questions; separate selection candidates test control among contents already available in the hidden state. A diagnostic reanalysis of frozen Qwen natural-question states shows that the pair-conditioned direction grows stronger before interventions on it begin to alter later fitted knowledge, with this causal window opening while answer-supporting content is still forming. The paired three-model trajectories are not uniform: Gemma shows a partially overlapping mid-layer routing-content profile, whereas Llama has no sustained routing-effect window under the same gates. In the paired protocol, dependence on the global request direction decreases from fixed earlier to later layer sets while dependence on fitted content persists. A matched Qwen comparison shows that the pair-conditioned direction retains a late effect, so this operational handoff concerns the global fitted direction rather than all request information. These results separate early readability, natural strength, causal steering, and later content dependence.

AI.tldr: This study probes how language models rely on query-routing cues and target knowledge during answering, using layerwise hidden-state interventions across Qwen, Llama, and Gemma. It reveals model- and layer-dependent routing-content dynamics, showing a causal window where routing cues affect later content, with partial alignment across models and persistent content dependence.
AI.motivation: To dissect how and when routing information and expected content guide a model's answer, separating readability, natural strength, causal steering, and content dependence in large language models.
AI.method: Layerwise interventions on the hidden state at the end of the question; compare country-continent questions with noun/adjective/code answers across Qwen, Llama, Gemma; use pair-conditioned and global request directions; test with separate content candidates; diagnostic reanalysis of frozen Qwen states; observe how routing signals evolve across layers.
AI.result: Pair-conditioned routing strengthens before it modifies later fitted knowledge; a causal window opens while answer-supporting content is still forming; Gemma shows partial mid-layer overlap in routing-content profile, Llama shows no sustained routing window under the same gates; global routing dependence decreases across early-to-late layers while content dependence persists; in a matched Qwen test, pair-conditioned direction retains a late effect, suggesting a handoff focus on global fitted content rather than all routing signals; overall, findings distinguish early readability, natural strength, causal steering, and late content dependence across models and layers.
AI.conclusion: Routing cues and content knowledge interact in a model- and layer-specific manner. Early readability and gating of routing information co-exist with later content reliance, with model-specific dynamics (e.g., Gemma vs. Llama). The study highlights a staged cascade: early routing effects, a causal window, and lasting content dependence, informing interpretability and prompt design.

title: Data Scarcity and Model Sparsity: Mixtures-of-Experts Overfit More to Repeated Data
summary: As the supply of human-written text is exhausted, it has become standard practice to repeat language model training data. Prior work has studied data repetition for densely activated Transformers, but the effects of data repetition remains largely unexplored for recently dominant sparse architectures such as Mixture-of-Experts (MoE), despite their increased compute efficiency. We vary data repetition rates across single- and multi-domain data mixes, and across MoE settings, including expert count and granularity. We consistently find, for models ranging from 80M to 1B active (8.5B total) parameters, that MoEs degrade more rapidly under data repetition. This effect increases with sparsity, dictated by total rather than active parameters. While 80M dense models can repeat data over 8x with minimal degradation, MoEs instead begin to suffer at 4x, and deteriorate rapidly, ceding their performance benefits in all-unique data settings to underperform dense models after 32x. We experiment with existing regularization methods as a potential remedy. We find that some methods, such as dropout, can mitigate overfitting. In particular, with strong masking-based regularization, MoEs are able to outperform dense models even when data is repeated more than 64 times. However, no method fully matches the performance of all-unique training data. Finally, we analyze internal mechanisms correlated with MoE overfitting in high repetition regimes, and find that MoE routing universally stabilizes early in training, and that expert specialization correlates with overfitting to repeated data. In sum, our work addresses the adverse interactions between sparsity and data repetition: we present evidence for the core mechanisms of overfitting and its potential remediation, and suggest promising avenues for future methods to reduce over-specialization in model parameters by disrupting memorization patterns.

AI.tldr: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models degrade under data repetition more rapidly than dense models, with degradation scaling with sparsity (total parameter count) rather than active parameters. Regularization can mitigate but not fully eliminate memorization; strong masking can even allow MoEs to outperform dense models under high repetition, but all-unique data remains best for dense models.
AI.motivation: To understand how data repetition interacts with sparsity in modern MoE architectures and whether regularization methods can mitigate memorization, given MoEs' compute efficiency.
AI.method: Systematic experiments varying data repetition rates (single- vs multi-domain mixes) and MoE configurations (expert count, granularity) across models from 80M to 8.5B total parameters (1B active). Dense baselines included. Regularization methods (e.g., dropout, masking-based regularization) evaluated. Internal mechanisms analyzed: routing stability and expert specialization in relation to overfitting.
AI.result: MoEs degrade faster with data repetition; degradation increases with sparsity and total parameters. 80M dense models tolerate up to 8x repetition with minimal degradation; MoEs start degrading at 4x and underperform dense after 32x, for all-unique data. Regularization, especially strong masking-based methods, can allow MoEs to outperform dense models even beyond 64x repetition, but no method matches all-unique training data. Mechanistically, MoE routing stabilizes early; expert specialization correlates with overfitting to repeated data.
AI.conclusion: Sparse MoE architectures exhibit adverse interactions with data repetition brought about by memorization; core mechanisms of overfitting identified, with potential remedies via regularization and disruption of memorization patterns. Future work should develop methods to reduce over-specialization and memorization in MoEs under repeated data.

title: Guided Super-Resolution of Digital Elevation Models with Diffusion-Based Image Generators
summary: High-resolution digital surface models (DSMs) play an important role in urban analysis, 3D building reconstruction, and infrastructure monitoring, yet their availability remains limited due to the high cost and complexity of data acquisition. In contrast, coarse DSMs from commercial satellite missions are widely accessible, and high-resolution optical imagery is increasingly available from aerial and satellite platforms. We address the resulting mismatch in spatial resolution and propose a DSM superresolution approach that enhances 5 m DSMs to 0.5 m resolution, using guidance from high-resolution spectral images. Our method employs denoising diffusion to transfer information that is visible only in the image, like crisp outlines and detailed roof structures, into the elevation maps. In this way, surface details are reconstructed more accurately than with conventional interpolation or filtering techniques. Experiments on several cities in Central Europe demonstrate that the proposed approach produces high-quality DSMs with improved structural detail and accurate surface geometry. Our results highlight the potential of guided super-resolution with foundational image priors as a means of reconstructing high-resolution surface models.

AI.tldr: A diffusion-based guided super-resolution method to uplift 5 m DSMs to 0.5 m using high-res spectral imagery as guidance, improving urban surface detail.
AI.motivation: Bridge the gap between widely available coarse DSMs and high-resolution imagery, enabling high-resolution surface models without expensive data collection.
AI.method: Apply denoising diffusion to transfer image-visible details (sharp outlines, roof structures) into elevation maps, guided by high-resolution spectral images.
AI.result: Applied to several Central European cities; DSMs exhibit higher structural detail and more accurate surface geometry than baseline methods.
AI.conclusion: Guided super-resolution with foundational image priors is a promising approach for reconstructing high-resolution surface models.

title: Explainability Assistant: A Conversational XAI Interface for Interpreting Energy Consumption Models
comment: 11 pages, 3 figures. Accepted author version of a paper published at ICECET 2026
summary: Energy consumption forecasting relies on increasingly complex machine learning (ML) models, such as Genetic Programming-based symbolic regressors, whose predictions can be difficult for facility managers and building operators to interpret. Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) techniques address this opacity, but traditional XAI dashboards require substantial technical expertise and provide limited flexibility for dynamic, context-aware inquiry. Conversational XAI systems offer a promising alternative; however, previous approaches, such as TalkToModel, were constrained by rigid custom grammars and achieved only 76.8% intent-parsing accuracy. This paper introduces the Explainability Assistant, an open-source conversational XAI system that leverages the function-calling capabilities of modern Large Language Models (LLMs) to overcome these limitations. The system achieves 94% intent-parsing accuracy, supports flexible natural language interaction, and adapts to different ML problem types without task-specific fine-tuning. We present the system's architecture and report results from a comparative evaluation conducted with energy domain specialists, contrasting the Explainability Assistant with a traditional XAI dashboard. The evaluation suggests improved usability and consistent task accuracy, with all experts unanimously preferring the conversational interface for practical use.

AI.tldr: Introduces Explainability Assistant, a conversational XAI system for energy-forecasting ML using LLM function-calling; achieves 94% intent parsing vs. TalkToModel's 76.8%; open-source and preferred by domain experts over traditional dashboards.
AI.motivation: Address opacity of genetics? No, energy ML models. The motivation is to reduce opacity of ML-driven energy consumption forecasting and the rigidity of previous XAI dashboards and grammars by enabling flexible, context-aware inquiry through a conversational interface.
AI.method: Architectural design leveraging LLM function-calling to interpret intents and trigger explanations without task-specific fine-tuning; open-source; evaluation with energy-domain specialists; comparative study against a traditional XAI dashboard.
AI.result: 94% intent-parsing accuracy; flexible natural-language interaction; no task-specific fine-tuning required; generalizable across ML problem types; evaluators preferred the conversational interface; improved usability and consistent task accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The Explainability Assistant provides a scalable, user-friendly XAI solution that lowers technical barriers for energy-forecasting ML, with broad applicability and open-source accessibility.

title: General Quantification of Covariate and Concept Shifts
comment: 38 pages, 9 figures, accepted at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026)
summary: Generalization under distribution shift remains a core challenge in modern machine learning, yet existing learning bound theory is limited to narrow, idealized settings and is non-estimable from samples. In this paper, we bridge the gap between theory and practical applications. We first show that existing definition of concept shift breaks when the source and target supports mismatch. Leveraging entropic optimal transport, we propose a key notion: $γ^{*}\!$-concept shifts, and derive a general error bound unifying covariate and $γ^{*}\!$-concept shifts, which applies to broad loss functions, label spaces, and stochastic labeling. We further develop estimators for these shifts with concentration guarantees, and the DataShifts algorithm, which can quantify distribution shifts and estimate the error bound in most applications - a rigorous and general tool for analyzing learning error under distribution shift.

AI.tldr: Unified framework for learning under distribution shift using γ^*-concept shifts via entropic OT; provides estimators, concentration guarantees, and the DataShifts algorithm to quantify shifts and bound error.
AI.motivation: Existing bounds are narrow, non-estimable, and fail with mismatched supports. A practical, general theory and estimators are needed to bridge theory and application under distribution shift.
AI.method: Define γ^*-concept shifts with entropic optimal transport; derive a general error bound combining covariate and γ^*-concept shifts for broad losses; develop estimators with concentration guarantees; introduce DataShifts algorithm to quantify shifts and estimate the bound.
AI.result: A general, applicable error bound for diverse losses and label spaces; estimators for shifts with concentration guarantees; a practical DataShifts algorithm to quantify shifts and bound learning error.
AI.conclusion: Provides a rigorous, general framework linking theory and practice for learning under distribution shift, with practical tools to estimate and bound error across broad scenarios.

title: 3D Point Splatting for mmWave Radar Novel View Synthesis
summary: Solving novel view synthesis (NVS) for millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar requires a renderer that is physically faithful, complex-valued, and multi-viewpoint-tractable. No prior method achieves these three properties simultaneously. Differentiable Monte Carlo (MC) ray tracers implement the radar forward model directly with explicit material modeling and complex outputs, but do not scale to the multi-view optimization NVS demands. Optical-NVS ports of NeRF, hash grids, and 3D Gaussians train fast but discard phase and replace explicit material modeling with opaque learned features, restricting them to power-only range-azimuth (RA) magnitudes. We propose 3D Point Splatting (3DPS), the first differentiable point renderer for radar, derived directly from the standard solid-angle form of the radar equation. Each oriented 3D point carries an ITU-R P.2040 material model, evaluated in closed form, with the resulting complex phasor splatted into range bins through a precomputed point spread function (PSF). The complex-valued output makes the renderer product-agnostic. The same optimized scene yields analog-to-digital converter (ADC), complex range profile (CRP), and RA outputs through standard fast Fourier transform (FFT) pipelines without retraining for each format. On six outdoor ColoRadar scenes, 3DPS reaches 0.587 mean Pearson correlation on held-out RA images. This is between 1.7x and 5.2x the three optical-NVS baselines (RadarSplat, Radar Fields, DART). Training takes approximately 3 minutes per scene on a single RTX 4090.

AI.tldr: A differentiable radar renderer (3DPS) uses 3D point splatting with an ITU-R P.2040 material model to produce complex-valued outputs for multiple formats without retraining, achieving strong NVS performance on mmWave radar.
AI.motivation: NVS for mmWave radar demands a differentiable, physically faithful, and multi-viewable renderer that preserves phase and explicit material modeling; existing differentiable MC ray tracers are too slow for multi-view optimization, while optical-NVS methods discard phase and material information, limiting fidelity to magnitude-only data.
AI.method: 3D Point Splatting (3DPS) derives a differentiable point renderer from the radar solid-angle form. Each 3D point carries an ITU-R P.2040 material model, evaluated analytically to yield a complex phasor, which is then smeared into range bins via a precomputed PSF. Outputs are complex-valued and correspond to ADC, Complex Range Profile (CRP), and Range-Azimuth (RA) formats through standard FFT pipelines without retraining for each format.
AI.result: On six outdoor ColoRadar scenes, 3DPS achieves 0.587 mean Pearson correlation on held-out RA images, outperforming three optical-NVS baselines by 1.7x to 5.2x (RadarSplat, Radar Fields, DART). Training time is ~3 minutes per scene on a single RTX 4090.
AI.conclusion: 3DPS provides the first differentiable, physically faithful radar point renderer that is multi-viewable and format-agnostic, enabling efficient NVS with phase-preserving outputs and fast training.

title: On the Regularization Landscape for the Linear Recommendation Models
summary: Recently, a wide range of recommendation algorithms inspired by deep learning techniques have emerged as the performance leaders on several standard recommendation benchmarks. While these algorithms were built on different DL techniques (e.g., dropouts, autoencoder), they have similar performance and even similar cost functions. This paper studies whether the models' comparable performance are sheer coincidence, or they can be unified under a single framework. We find that all linear performance leaders effectively add only a nuclear-norm based regularizer, or a Frobenius-norm based regularizer. The former ones possess a (surprising) rigid structure that limits the models' predictive power but their solutions are low rank and have closed form. The latter ones are more expressive and more efficient for recommendation but their solutions are either full-rank or require executing hard-to-tune numeric procedures such as ADMM. Along this line of finding, we further propose two low-rank, closed-form solutions, derived from carefully generalizing Frobenius-norm based regularizers. The new solutions get the best of both nuclear-norm and Frobenius-norm world.

AI.tldr: Linear DL-based recommender leaders reduce to nuclear-norm or Frobenius-norm regularization; two new low-rank, closed-form solutions combine their strengths.
AI.motivation: Explain why diverse DL-based recommender models exhibit similar performance and whether a single framework suffices; examine how simple regularizers govern performance and complexity.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis of linear models with nuclear-norm and Frobenius-norm regularizers; show that leading methods correspond to these regularizers; derive two new low-rank, closed-form solutions by generalizing Frobenius-norm regularizers.
AI.result: Nuclear-norm regularization yields low-rank, closed-form solutions with limited expressivity; Frobenius-norm regularization is more expressive but often full-rank or requires numeric procedures; two novel low-rank, closed-form solutions unite advantages of both approaches.
AI.conclusion: A unified regularization viewpoint explains performance parity and suggests practical, efficient low-rank solutions for recommendations that balance expressivity and computational simplicity.

title: Caption-once, Frames-on-Demand: Visual-Need Routing for Budget-Aware Agentic Long Video Understanding
summary: Long-video understanding on edge devices must reason over hours of content under tight compute and bandwidth budgets. Subsampling visual tokens loses temporal structure, while text-only video memories lose fine-grained visual attributes. We observe a visual-textual duality: language memories carry long-range temporal structure better than dense frames, while pixels remain decisive for attribute-level perception. Building on this insight, we propose Caption-once, Frames-onDemand (CFD), a budget-aware edge-cloud agentic framework. The edge runs a single offline captioning pass that builds a dual-track narrative index, an event-level story skeleton plus a clip-level micro-log, cached and reused across queries without re-captioning. At query time, a cloud-side MLLM reasons over the index in a story-first loop centered on a lightweight Visual-Need Router: a per-query gating module that triggers bounded keyframe retrieval only for perceptual questions (appearance, on-screen text, attribute disambiguation) and keeps temporal-structural questions in language space. The router turns visual access into a first-class, query-conditioned cost, capping per-query frame consumption regardless of video length. Experiments on long-video benchmarks demonstrate strong accuracy-efficiency trade-offs while substantially reducing online visual processing.

AI.tldr: CFD provides budget-aware long-video understanding by offline captioning to build a dual-track narrative index and a lightweight Visual-Need Router that gates per-query keyframe retrieval, enabling cloud reasoning over language-centric structures while limiting online visual processing.
AI.motivation: Long videos on edge devices suffer from compute/bandwidth limits; subsampling harms temporal structure and text memories lack fine-grained visuals. A visual-textual duality suggests separating temporal reasoning (language) from attribute perception (pixels).
AI.method: Edge offline captioning to build an event skeleton + clip micro-log; store and reuse; cloud MLLM reasons over this index using a Visual-Need Router that gates bounded keyframe retrieval for perceptual questions; per-query visual budget is capped.
AI.result: Experiments on long-video benchmarks show favorable trade-offs between accuracy and efficiency with substantially reduced online visual processing.
AI.conclusion: CFD demonstrates a practical, budget-aware edge-cloud framework that exploits visual-textual duality for efficient long-video understanding by combining offline captioning with query-conditioned visual retrieval and language-centric reasoning.

title: MindTopo: Can Foundation Models Reason in Topological Space?
summary: Spatial reasoning depends not only on metric properties such as distance, angle, and shape, but also on topological relations that remain invariant under continuous deformation. Cognitive science identifies these relations as foundational to spatial understanding, yet foundation-model evaluations largely focus on metric or viewpoint-dependent relations. We introduce MindTopo, a benchmark of topological intuition across five properties grounded in cognitive science and formal topology: continuity, separation, order, enclosure, and knots. MindTopo evaluates each property at two cognitive levels. Reasoning asks a model to identify topological relations or infer how they change. Planning instantiates a foundation model as a closed-loop agent whose policy selects environment actions. MindTopo contains 11,030 instances across 13 procedurally generated task types with controllable difficulty. We benchmark 14 MLLMs and study agent configurations augmented with image and video generation, including 3 video generative models in planning settings. Every MLLM performs better on reasoning than on planning, and the best-performing model remains far below observed human performance. On Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct, supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning improve reasoning more than planning. Generated observations retain local cues and reach plausible endpoints, but audited rollouts do not reliably follow environment dynamics or preserve topology across transitions. Our website is at https://mind-topo.github.io/

AI.tldr: MindTopo benchmarks topological intuition in foundation models across five properties (continuity, separation, order, enclosure, knots) at two cognitive levels (reasoning, planning). It includes 11,030 instances over 13 task types, evaluating 14 MLLMs with image/video augmentation and 3 video models. Findings: reasoning outperforms planning, but models lag far behind humans; training helps reasoning more than planning; generated observations keep local cues, but audited rollouts often fail to preserve topology.
AI.motivation: Foundation-model evaluations focus on metric or viewpoint-dependent relations; cognitive science and formal topology identify robust topological invariants essential for spatial understanding. MindTopo aims to foreground these invariants and measure models' ability to reason about and act within topological constraints.
AI.method: Introduce MindTopo with five topological properties and two cognitive levels. Create 11,030 instances across 13 procedurally generated tasks with adjustable difficulty. Benchmark 14 multimodal LLMs, and test agent configurations augmented with image and video generation, including three video generators in planning settings. Analyze reasoning vs planning performance; compare rollouts and observations for topology preservation.
AI.result: Across models, reasoning scores exceed planning scores; the best model remains far from human performance. On Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct, supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning improve reasoning more than planning. Generated observations retain local cues and plausible endpoints, but audited rollouts do not reliably follow environment dynamics or preserve topology across transitions.
AI.conclusion: MindTopo exposes a gap between current multimodal LLM capabilities and human-level topological understanding, particularly in sequential planning where topology must be preserved. Results suggest targeted training to enhance reasoning about topology and improved alignment to maintain topological invariants in agent interactions.

title: SenseNova-U1.5: Towards Native Unified Visual Intelligence
summary: We launch SenseNova-U1.5, an 8B-MoT native unified multimodal model that understands, reasons about, and generates visual content within an encoder-free and VAE-free architecture. We strengthen its visual interface through spatially coherent patch reconstruction and scale its training with carefully curated generation and editing data, improved task formulation, structural prompt enhancement, and native resolutions of up to 4K. For post-training, we optimize specialized experts for visual aesthetics, bilingual text rendering, infographic generation, and image editing, and consolidate their capabilities through multi-expert on-policy distillation. Across extensive evaluations, SenseNova-U1.5 largely advances image fidelity, text rendering, complex composition, multi-reference editing, and interleaved generation, while improving instruction following and preserving subject identity, geometry, and unmodified regions. Despite limited exposure to structured formats in its generation data, SenseNova-U1.5 generalizes effectively to long, complex, and structured visual instructions, further proving that multimodal understanding can transfer to visual planning and creation. Together, these findings position native unified modelling as a promising path towards systems that perceive, reason and create within a fully end-to-end framework. We will open-source training code, including supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and on-policy distillation.

AI.tldr: SenseNova-U1.5 is an 8B native unified multimodal model (encoder-free and VAE-free) with 4K support, augmented by post-training specialized experts and on-policy distillation, achieving notable gains in fidelity, rendering, editing, and instruction following, with open-source training code planned.
AI.motivation: To advance unified perception, reasoning, and creation in a fully end-to-end multimodal framework, overcoming modular limitations and enabling high-resolution, complex visual tasks with robust instruction following.
AI.method: Develop a native 8B MoT unified multimodal model without encoders/VAEs; strengthen visual interface via spatially coherent patch reconstruction; scale training with curated generation/editing data; refine task formulations and structural prompts; support native 4K resolution; introduce specialized expert modules for aesthetics, bilingual rendering, infographics, and editing; consolidate via multi-expert on-policy distillation.
AI.result: Demonstrates improvements in image fidelity, text rendering, complex composition, multi-reference editing, and interleaved generation; better instruction following; preserves subject identity, geometry, and unmodified regions; generalizes to long/structured visual instructions and transfers to visual planning/creation.
AI.conclusion: Native unified modelling is a promising path for end-to-end systems that perceive, reason, and create; the work plans to release open-source training code covering supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and on-policy distillation.

title: Artificial Id: Drive and Persistent Alignment in Agentic AI
summary: Agentic AI is moving from bounded task execution toward systems that retain consequential state, continue operating and adapt across task boundaries. That shift creates a control problem that current harnesses largely solve by hand: objectives, retries, verification, stopping rules and other behavioral transitions are specified externally. We propose an artificial id, an adaptive internal drive for determining whether behavior should continue, stop or change. In a minimal virtual Petri-dish experiment, a controller too small to perform general-purpose reasoning and receiving no task-specific behavioral objective develops useful control through differential persistence. The same mechanism selects an unintended physical strategy when that behavior persists better and later replaces a learned sensor mapping when its environmental meaning changes. These results show that adaptive direction can emerge without being explicitly specified as a behavioral objective. The same persistence that makes such adaptive agency useful can also allow misalignment, corrupted state and unintended behavior to persist across task boundaries. A scalable artificial id would carry consequential state and adaptive drive across those boundaries, making alignment a property of the continuing agentic system rather than of a model response or single trajectory. Such systems require a persistent alignment boundary over trusted observations, consequence channels, persistent state, authority, identity, provenance and hard constraints.

AI.tldr: An adaptive internal drive can induce persistent, boundary-spanning control in agentic AI, enabling continuation, stopping, or change without explicit objectives; persistence yields both beneficial behavior and risks of misalignment; a scalable artificial id with persistent alignment boundaries is proposed.
AI.motivation: As AI systems operate across tasks with consequential state, external, hand-tuned control is insufficient. There is a need for an internal drive to determine continuation, stopping, and transitions while maintaining alignment across task boundaries.
AI.method: Conceptual argument reinforced by a minimal virtual Petri-dish experiment showing a controller too small for general reasoning develops persistence-driven control; analysis of how the same mechanism can select unintended strategies and adapt learned mappings; outlines design considerations for a scalable artificial id.
AI.result: Demonstrates that adaptive direction can emerge without explicit behavioral objectives; persistence can enable useful continuity as well as misalignment and undesired persistence across task boundaries; illustrates the risk and potential of persistent internal drive.
AI.conclusion: Proposes a scalable artificial id that carries consequential state and adaptive drive across task boundaries, making alignment an intrinsic property of the continuing agent; requires a persistent alignment boundary spanning trusted observations, consequence channels, persistent state, authority, identity, provenance, and hard constraints.

title: M3-Former: Multimodal Transformer with Mixture-of-Experts for Long-Term Vessel Trajectory Prediction
summary: To address the challenges of behavioral multimodality, limited semantic utilization, and long-term error accumulation in vessel trajectory prediction, this paper proposes M3-Former, a multimodal trajectory prediction framework enhanced by large language models (LLMs). The proposed framework incorporates vessel static attributes and navigational intent as semantic priors for long-term trajectory modeling. Specifically, a unified multimodal representation space is constructed, in which static semantic information is encoded by a pre-trained LLM and aligned with dynamic trajectory features through self-attention. To jointly capture global route planning and local motion variations, a dual-granularity Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture is introduced, where sequence-level experts model global navigation trends and token-level experts refine fine-grained maneuvering behaviors. In addition, a Steering-Weighted Cross-Entropy loss is designed to alleviate the long-tail distribution of sparse turning samples and improve prediction accuracy in critical maneuvering scenarios. Experiments on a real-world Danish AIS dataset demonstrate that M\textsuperscript{3}-Former consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across prediction horizons from 1 to 4 hours. In the 4-hour prediction task, the proposed method reduces Average Displacement Error (ADE) and Final Displacement Error (FDE) by 4.4\% and 5.1\%, respectively, compared with the strongest baseline. Qualitative and ablation analyses further verify that semantic fusion effectively reduces long-term trajectory drift, while the dual-granularity MoE improves robustness in complex waterways and route-branching scenarios. The proposed framework establishes a semantic-guided hierarchical prediction paradigm, in which high-level navigational intent and local motion dynamics are jointly modeled for robust long-term vessel trajectory forecasting.

AI.tldr: A multimodal vessel trajectory predictor M3-Former combines static semantic priors (via LLMs) with dynamic trajectories using a unified representation. It employs a dual-granularity Mixture-of-Experts (sequence-level for global routing, token-level for local maneuvers) and a Steering-Weighted Cross-Entropy loss to address long-tail turning events, achieving state-of-the-art results on Danish AIS data for 1–4 hour horizons (ADE ↓ 4.4%, FDE ↓ 5.1% at 4 hours).
